title: Intriguing players to watch in Falcons vs. Saints
summary: A victory for the Atlanta Falcons in a high-stakes divisional clash against the New Orleans Saints will help strengthen the former’s position in the NFC South divisional race. That creates plenty of intrigue as five Falcons face critical questions in this Week 4 rivalry. QB Michael Penix Last week’s win over the Green Bay Packers […]
full_text: Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson (7) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Falcons won the game, 35-14. Tork Mason/Green Bay Press-Gazette | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co A victory for the Atlanta Falcons in a high-stakes divisional clash against the New Orleans Saints will help strengthen the former’s position in the NFC South divisional race. That creates plenty of intrigue as five Falcons face critical questions in this Week 4 rivalry. QB Michael Penix Last week’s win over the Green Bay Packers was an impressive debut for Penix, but the Falcons still have 14 more starts to answer the big question facing them this year: Is Penix their long-term answer at quarterback ? That may take years to answer definitively, but Penix can steadily prove each week that he should remain the guy at present. Right now, he has an opportunity to lead the Falcons to another impressive road win in a hostile environment. Last week’s win in Lambeau increases hopes that Penix’s road woes are behind him. He and the rest of the Falcons offense have a great opportunity to pummel the Saints because of several favorable matchups. RB Bijan Robinson The most favorable matchup centers on Atlanta’s best player: Bijan Robinson, raising the question of whether Bijan can continue to dominate . Fresh off a 213-yard performance against the Packers, Robinson can keep shining against the Saints defense battling critical injuries to linebackers Kaden Elliss and Pete Werner. With Elliss’s blitzing abilities sidelined, Bijan should have more opportunities as a pass-catcher instead of being stuck in pass protection. With Werner’s injury making the Saints more vulnerable in coverage, Robinson can have another superhuman performance in primetime . OT Jake Matthews Given the positive outlook for the offense, the only thing that might derail Atlanta’s hopes is losing the battle in the trenches. Left tackle Jake Matthews’ battle against Chase Young will become pivotal to deciding the outcome of that battle. Matthews is making his 200th career start on Monday night , a remarkable achievement and the epitome of durability, reliability, and stability at a cornerstone position. However, Matthews has had a few too many uncharacteristic, unsightly losses to start in 2026, prompting questions over whether his trademark consistency remains. Young has been a difficult challenge for Matthews over the past few years, pressuring the latter and the rest of the Falcons offensive line to rise once more and win the battle up front. CB Avieon Terrell Rookie cornerback Avieon Terrell is another who must rise to the challenge, alongside the rest of the secondary against Saints wideout Chris Olave. For Terrell, the intriguing question is whether he will get more snaps playing outside cornerback against one of the league’s most productive pass-catchers . Terrell deserves more than the 13 snaps he got against the Packers, rotating with Mike Hughes and C.J. Henderson. While we can debate whether the Falcons’ trust in the Hughes-Henderson tandem is prudent, the veteran duo certainly brings value now, but Terrell’s youth and upside offer more for the future . Finding out whether Avieon can pick up the slack left by his injured elder sibling A.J.’s absence could pay off both on Monday night and in many games beyond. DT Gervon Dexter Speaking of paying off, Falcons defensive tackle Gervon Dexter just signed a very lucrative extension, leaving some to question if it’s premature. Despite Dexter’s brilliant start to the season, the raise puts more pressure on him to keep showing why he earned it . Dexter can do so by continuing to lead a surprising, impressive Falcons pass rush . If Dexter continues to be a force along the interior and put the quarterback on his back, it makes things easier for Terrell and others on the back end of the defense. A win in the Superdome will not only boost the Falcons’ divisional momentum but also keep building their confidence. Can you name other Falcons who excite and intrigue you in this primetime battle?

title: Falcons vs. Saints: What will Week 4’s win or loss mean for Atlanta?
summary: The Falcons may have stumbled out of the starting of the 2026 season, but they regained their footing in a major way on the national stage, against the Green Bay Packers. Behind the heroics of Bijan Robinson and Drake London, Atlanta declassed the hosts in their home opener and really gave the early portion of […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - DECEMBER 24: Mohamed Sanu #12 of the Atlanta Falcons catches the ball as Marshon Lattimore #23 of the New Orleans Saints defends during the second half of a game at the Mercedes-Benz Superdome on December 24, 2017 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Falcons may have stumbled out of the starting of the 2026 season, but they regained their footing in a major way on the national stage, against the Green Bay Packers. Behind the heroics of Bijan Robinson and Drake London, Atlanta declassed the hosts in their home opener and really gave the early portion of this season a much needed shot in the arm. Next, the prime time festivities continue as the Birds head into the most hostile of environments with a game against the New Orleans Saints, on what will be the 20th anniversary of the re-opening of the Superdome following Hurricane Katrina, on Monday Night Football. For those who remember, the Falcons spoiled the festivities on the 10th such anniversary on Monday night exactly a decade ago. Following the short week, Atlanta has the longest possible rest that’s not a bye week, with a full 11 days between their game in Green Bay and the one upcoming in New Orleans. Here is the scenario the Falcons face if they beat the New Orleans Saints in Week 3, as well as if they lose. If the Falcons win They will essentially pull a lot of the fanbase back in and regain a lot of trust, especially playing in what increasingly continues to look like a pathetic division. Kevin Stefanski will pass a major early test in the consistency department after we witnessed this team routinely lay an egg after nearly ever huge win last season. Speaking of that division, the Falcons will move to 2-2 overall as well as 1-1 in the NFC South. If the Carolina Panthers lose a game they are not favored in against the Detroit Lions on Sunday Night Football that would give the Birds sole possession of first place. With the Bucs and Panthers struggling and the Saints at that point already once vanquished, Atlanta would emerge as an early favorite to win their first division title since 2016. They would also win their third consecutive win head to head against New Orleans, the first such instance of that occurring since 2017, which is also the last time we watched Atlanta compete in the playoffs. This will also be the first time they have won four games in five tries head to head over the Saints since the turn of the millennia. If the Falcons lose Despite the coaching and front office turnover, this will just feel like another case of it being the “same old Falcons.” While this regime has nothing to do with the failures of their predecessors, the stigma and stench of this organization over the past decade of losing is hard to wipe away. It would be New Orleans who would have the early inside track in the division, going 2-2 and likely taking over first place. If Carolina were to also win their game, Atlanta would be trailing two separate teams in the standings while already possessing a worrisome 0-2 record against the NFC South. A Tampa victory puts the Birds in the cellar. New Orleans would put a stop to the modest two game losing streak they have over the Falcons and once again pull within one game of the all time head to head mark, making their new record against Atlanta 57-58, and putting them in position to tie things up with another win later in the season. The meat of the schedule comes right after this game, with Baltimore, Chicago and San Francisco coming to town. Going into that run of games at 1-3 and the arrow pointing down feels like it could be catastrophic before we even hit November.
author: Adnan Ikic

title: NFL predictions: Can the Falcons continue their winning streak against the Saints?
summary: There’s a very special matchup on Monday Night Football, as the Atlanta Falcons travel to take on the New Orleans Saints in Week 4. This is a heated rivalry between two teams that truly seem to loathe each other, and things only get more intense when both teams are in the thick of the NFC […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - JANUARY 04: Atlanta running back Bijan Robinson (7) runs the ball during the NFL game between the New Orleans Saints and the Atlanta Falcons on January 4th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There’s a very special matchup on Monday Night Football, as the Atlanta Falcons travel to take on the New Orleans Saints in Week 4. This is a heated rivalry between two teams that truly seem to loathe each other, and things only get more intense when both teams are in the thick of the NFC South race. That’s the case as we reach the start of October, as the Falcons and Saints both sit at 1-2 with an opportunity to take at least a share of the lead on Monday night. While the Falcons started out playing abysmal football with third-string quarterback Cooper Rush, they looked like a completely different offense with Michael Penix Jr. against the Green Bay Packers in Week 3. Meanwhile, the Saints have played pretty great offensive football, but dropped two games thanks to inconsistency and turnovers. FanDuel currently has Atlanta as 2.5-point road underdogs , showing how close this game is projected to be. This is a tough game to get a read on for a number of reasons. For one, we only have a one-game sample size of Atlanta with a real quarterback in 2026. Not exactly much to base opinions on, although the fact that it was a great game certainly bodes well. New Orleans also can’t seem to play a consistent game, as their 1-2 record and massive point swings from quarter to quarter suggest. There’s also the matter of a pretty large injury report for the Saints, who could be down multiple major contributors on Monday night. Falcons vs Saints Week 4 predictions There are a few reasons why I’m bullish on the Falcons to win this game. For one, Atlanta already took down Tyler Shough and a very similar Saints team twice in 2025—and I’d argue that the 2025 Falcons were not as well coached as this year’s iteration. The Falcons defense found ways to stymie Shough and the passing game, and that will be critical once again in this matchup. Second, Atlanta has been downright dominant in primetime. The Falcons are 8-3 on all primetime games going back through the 2024 season, and they’ve been particularly good on Monday Night Football. Atlanta is 4-0 on MNF since 2024, including two away games. If you take it back even further to 2015, the Falcons are a startling 9-1 (including a road win against the Saints in 2016). This team plays its best football under the bright lights, and I’d expect that to continue this week. Getting to the game itself, the Falcons match up well with the Saints in a number of key areas. Even though the passing game is coming along with Penix at the helm, the is still a team that wants to run the ball as much as possible with Bijan Robinson. Atlanta is second in rushing yards and seventh in yards per carry, and they did all that with no passing game to speak of in the first two weeks. Meanwhile, the Saints are a poor run defense, ranking 27th in rushing yards allowed and 27th in yards per carry allowed. This could be a recipe for disaster, particularly with a banged up front seven in New Orleans. On the other side, the Saints are very inconsistent running the football. New Orleans is league average in rushing yardage, but 21st in yards per carry at just 3.8. The Falcons hold the league’s best run defense, allowing the fewest rushing yards, yards per carry, and zero rushing TDs allowed. The Saints also just lost major free agent addition Travis Etienne Jr. to IR, putting everything on the plate of an aging Alvin Kamara. I wouldn’t rule out Kamara having one last big game against Atlanta, but it’s a very tough matchup. The Saints might be forced into a very one-dimensional game script on offense, which could lead to futher issues. Those issues start with the offensive line, which lost left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. for the season last week. The Raiders took advantage of his replacement, Asim Richards, particularly late in the game. Atlanta somehow possesses one of the league’s best pass rushes, and could feast on an undermanned Saints line—particularly if the run game is nonexistent. This is a key matchup for both sides: the Saints have thrived throwing the ball with Tyler Shough, and Atlanta is a bit undermanned in the secondary. There could be big play opportunities for New Orleans if they can protect the QB, but that might be a difficult task. I do expect New Orleans to put up quite a fight, but I think the culmination of injuries and a one-dimensional offense ultimately lead to more turnovers for Tyler Shough and the Saints offense. The Falcons manage to steal a hard-fought divisional matchup on Monday Night Football, thanks to dominance from Bijan Robinson and some clutch plays by the defense. I’m predicting the Falcons to emerge victorious, 27-24. Rise up with Falcons fans on the SB Nation app! title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 4: Mounting injuries force lineup shuffling
summary: Offense Jackson played all 33 snaps in the first half but did not return after halftime with an ankle injury. Backup quarterback Tyler Huntley (31 snaps) played the final two quarters. The Ravens suffered another offensive line injury as Andrew Vorhees exited after 28 snaps with a foot ailment and did not return. That forced […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens throws a pass during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Offense QB: Lamar Jackson 33, Tyler Huntley 31 RB: Derrick Henry 40, Justice Hill 24 WR: Zay Flowers 47, Devontez Walker 44, Rashod Bateman 30, Elijah Sarratt 23, LaJohntay Wester 2 TE: Mark Andrews 37, Matthew Hibner 37, Durham Smythe 18, Josh Cuevas 18 OL: John Simpson 64, Vega Ioane 64, Roger Rosengarten 64, Ronnie Stanley 62, Emery Jones Jr. 36, Andrew Vorhees 28, Carson Vinson 2 Jackson played all 33 snaps in the first half but did not return after halftime with an ankle injury. Backup quarterback Tyler Huntley (31 snaps) played the final two quarters. The Ravens suffered another offensive line injury as Andrew Vorhees exited after 28 snaps with a foot ailment and did not return. That forced Emery Jones to plug in at right guard, where he played 36 snaps. Carson Vinson played two snaps as an extra blocker upon Ronnie Stanley’s return to the starting lineup. After playing limited snaps in Week 3, Zay Flowers’ workload increased as he led all wide receivers in playing time (47 snaps). Devontez Walker saw a big jump in playing time with 44 snaps, 14 more than Rashod Bateman (30 snaps). Bateman got shaken up at one point in the game. Rookie Elijah Sarratt played a season-high 23 snaps and made his first NFL catch for 13 yards. Chris Moore was inactive for this game. Matthew Hibner’s 37 snaps were a season-high at tight end and he matched Mark Andrews in playing time. The latter caught five passes with a touchdown grab, while Hibner recorded 34 receiving yards. Durham Smythe suffered an achilles injury after 18 snaps and did not return. If Smythe is out long-term, expect Hibner and Josh Cuevas to quickly take on larger roles. Defense DL: Nnamdi Madubuike 46, Travis Jones 33, Calais Campbell 31, Broderick Washington Jr. 19, John Jenkins 9 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 46, Mike Green 41, Zion Young 25, Ethan Burke 16 ILB: Roquan Smith 64, Trenton Simpson 36, Teddye Buchanan 11 CB: Nate Wiggins 64, Chidobe Awuzie 56, Chandler Rivers 29, Marlon Humphrey 8 S: Kyle Hamilton 64, Malaki Starks 59, Jaylinn Hawks 45, K’Von Wallace 2 In his second game back from injury, Madubuike again led the defensive line group in snaps (46). He had four tackles and two quarterback hits. Travis Jones and Calais Campbell were near-even in playing time, while Broderick Washington and John Jenkins combined for 28 snaps. Aeneas Peebles was a healthy scratch. With Trey Hendrickson (finger) inactive, Mike Green saw a significant role expansion (41 snaps). He had a team-high six pressures and three quarterback hits. Tavius Robinson led the edge rushers with 46 snaps and Zion Young played 25 defensive reps. Undrafted rookie Ethan Burke saw his first defensive action of the season and recorded a sack. Roquan Smith went the distance as usual with 64 snaps at linebacker, followed by Trenton Simpson (36) and Teddye Buchanan (11). Simpson had a team-high nine tackles and logged an interception, continuing his strong start to the season. Buchanan saw a few more snaps than last week in his second game back from injury. At cornerback, Marlon Humphrey suffered a calf injury after just eight snaps and did not return. That forced Chidobe Awuzie to start the remainder of the game (56 snaps) alongside Nate Wiggins, who played all 64 snaps. Rookie Chandler Rivers played 29 snaps in the slot. The Ravens continue to opt for four cornerbacks and four safeties in the secondary rotation. Jaylinn Hawkins saw his snap share decrease as the No. 3 safety (45 snaps) and K’Von Wallace received two defensive snaps in the mix.

title: Winners and Losers from the Ravens’ Week 4 win over the Titans
summary: The Baltimore Ravens defeated the Tennessee Titans in Week 4, 24-18, but face a litany of injury questions in the aftermath of the game. There was far more good than bad for the Ravens in their win on Sunday, including a solid performance from a reshuffled offensive line. Winners Lamar Jackson: Jackson’s stellar game was […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Mark Andrews #89 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Tennessee Titans during the first half at M&T Bank Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens defeated the Tennessee Titans in Week 4, 24-18, but face a litany of injury questions in the aftermath of the game. There was far more good than bad for the Ravens in their win on Sunday, including a solid performance from a reshuffled offensive line. Winners Lamar Jackson: Jackson’s stellar game was ended early when an ankle injury sidelined him for the second half. Jackson completed 15 of 20 pass attempts for 222 yards and two touchdowns through the first two quarters. Zay Flowers: Flowers’ ascendance into the top tier of NFL receivers continued this week with another monstrous first half prior to Jackson’s injury. Flowers finished the game with 118 receiving yards and a touchdown on eight catches, including a 52-yard reception. Mark Andrews: Jackson’s old reliable tight end was just that on Sunday. Andrews finished the game with just 27 yards on five catches, but one of those was a touchdown catch, while another one came on a third down earlier in that same drive. Vega Ioane: The rookie first-rounder made his first start at center after desperation forced him there from right guard a week ago. Ioane was solid in the middle of the offensive line, helping to hold superstar defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to a quiet day. According to PFF, Ioane allowed zero pressures on the day. Mike Green : The Ravens entered the game without Trey Hendrickson to rush the passer. Mike Green stepped up in his absence with six pressures on Cam Ward, according to PFF. While Green did not record a sack, he was close on several occasions, and a quick pressure on the first drive of the game led to a Trenton Simpson interception. Trenton Simpson: Simpson had one of two turnovers forced by Baltimore’s defense when he picked off Ward on the opening drive of the game. He also led the team in total tackles with nine. The fourth-year linebacker is earning himself a nice contract with his play so far this season. Nnamdi Madubuike: Madubuike looked like his old self in just his second game back, recording five pressures and two quarterback hits, according to PFF. Madubuike also had a drive-ending tackle on a fourth-down run at the goal line. Ethan Burke : The undrafted rookie got his first NFL start on Sunday and made the most of it with the team’s only sack of Ward. Malaki Starks: Starks has been a polarizing subject to start the season, but a strong game against Tennessee will hopefully quiet some of the noise. Starks recovered a forced fumble by Kyle Hamilton and recovered the Titans’ onside kick to end the game. He finished with six total tackles. Kyle Hamilton: After being on the receiving end of a questionable unnecessary roughness penalty, Hamilton bounced back to force a fumble on rookie first-round receiver Carnell Tate after a 33-yard catch-and-run. The do-it-all safety continues to be the best player on the Ravens’ defense. Tyler Loop: Loop followed up his late-game heroics in Brazil with the longest field goal of his career in Week 4, nailing a 64-yarder before halftime to give Baltimore a 24-7 lead. Loop later missed a field goal from 40 yards, but the main culprit seemed to be the hold by Ryan Eckley. The second-year kicker appears to have his confidence back after a difficult end to last season and a shaky preseason. Losers Elijah Sarratt: The rookie fourth-round receiver got his first catch of the regular season on Sunday with a 13-yard reception, but a handful of mistakes brought his day down. First, Sarratt was flagged for holding, wiping out a 29-yard scramble for Jackson. Next, Sarratt attempted and failed to catch a pass that was intended for Flowers on a route behind him in the two-minute drill before halftime. Lastly, Sarratt was involved in an illegal shift penalty as both he and Justice Hill were moving at the time of the snap. Devontez Walker: Walker had a holding penalty that brought back a successful third-down run by Derrick Henry. He also failed to haul in a catchable pass earlier in the game. Walker finished with one catch for 19 yards.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 4: Imperfect performance in a gritty win
summary: The Baltimore Ravens improved to 3-1 with a six-point win over the Tennessee Titans in Week 4. After leading by 17 points at halftime, the Ravens were outscored 11-0 in the second half without their starting quarterback but hung on to emerge victorious for a second straight week. Here are report card grades for each […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Zay Flowers #4 of the Baltimore Ravens rushes for a second quarter touchdown during the game against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens improved to 3-1 with a six-point win over the Tennessee Titans in Week 4. After leading by 17 points at halftime, the Ravens were outscored 11-0 in the second half without their starting quarterback but hung on to emerge victorious for a second straight week. Here are report card grades for each position group from yesterday’s game. Quarterback: A- Lamar Jackson was in the midst of another heater in the first half of this game, completing 15-of-20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns. His completions and attempts were the exact same as last week, which he matched in just two quarters, and his passer rating was 144.2. In relief of Jackson after his ankle injury, Tyler Huntley completed eight passes for 63 yards. Huntley had one long first down pass to Rashod Bateman but otherwise his throws were screen-heavy and mostly around the line of scrimmage. Jackson’s performance before leaving the game was good enough to carry the grade for this group. Running Back: C+ The Ravens found running room hard to come by against the Titans’ defensive front. Derrick Henry was featured heavily against his former team with 23 carries but mustered only 73 rushing yards (3.2 yards per carry). His longest run went for 14 yards, and it was Henry’s second straight game averaging 3.4 yards per carry or less. The Ravens were able to convert some short yardage rushes with better efficiency in this game than last week. Justice Hill had two catches for 22 yards out of the backfield as a dump-off screen option. Wide Receiver: B + Zay Flowers had another dynamic performance with 118 receiving yards and a touchdown, reeling in a season-high eight catches. Flowers had a long reception of 52 yards on a sideline grab from Jackson. His effort carries the grade for this group, as has been the case so far this year. Rashod Bateman caught two passes for 46 yards but no other wideout made a substantial impact. Devontez Walker and Elijah Sarratt each had one first-down catch but also a miscue. Walker dropped a would-be long catch that was nearly intercepted as a result, and Sarratt committed a costly holding penalty that negated a big first-down scramble by Jackson scramble. Tight End: B- Mark Andrews had the second most catches of any Raven pass-catcher with five. While he gained only 27 yards, he made some nice short grabs over the middle of the field and also had a touchdown grab. Andrews appears to be in better athletic form than he was last year. Matthew Hibner recorded a season-high 34 receiving yards on two catches with a long gain of 25 yards. Veteran Durham Smythe exited the game early with an achilles injury that appeared to be serious and did not return. Offensive Line: C+ The Ravens’ mixed-and-matched offensive line had their best pass protection performance of the season. While the Titans did record a couple sacks and five quarterback hits, the impact of star defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons was limited. Vega Ioane held up well in his first start at center. The unit overall was not able to replicate a successful run blocking showing to match an improved pass blocking game. The Ravens were stuffed for minimal gain on rushing attempts repeatedly and weren’t able to open up significant holes for Henry. False starts and other penalties continue to be an issue from the offensive line as well. Defensive Line: B Nnamdi Madubuike had four tackles, two quarterback hits and a handful of pressures in his second game back, making strong plays at the line of scrimmage. Madubuike had one of the defensive plays of the game with a fourth-down run stuff at the team’s own goal line. Travis Jones surprisingly was blanked in the box score and Calais Campbell had just one tackle. The Ravens were stout against the run after the first couple drives of the game. They allowed just 85 rushing yards and 3.3 yards per carry. Edge Rusher: B He may not have finished plays with sacks, but Mike Green had an impactful performance. Green led the team with three quarterback hits and was charted for the most pressures as well. He flushed Cam Ward out of the pocket on multiple occasions and came up just short of bringing him down. Tavius Robinson and Zion Young had quiet showings, but undrafted rookie Ethan Burke picked up the slack. Burke recorded a sack, quarterback hit and tackle for loss. Linebacker: B+ A breakout season for Trenton Simpson continued in this game, as he recorded a team-high nine tackles and his first career interception. Simpson picked off an errant shovel pass on the opening drive of the game and returned it 24 yards. Roquan Smith had six total tackles but only one of which was solo. The Ravens’ linebackers were strong against the run, stuffing most attempts by Tony Pollard for minimal gain. Cornerback: C+ Marlon Humphrey exited the game early, on the second drive in the first quarter, with a calf injury and did not return. That left Chidobe Awuzie to slide into his starting role. Awuzie and nickel corner Chandler Rivers each had a pass breakup. The Ravens had some challenges defending rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate, who had a a career-best performance with nine catches for 145 yards. No other Titans’ wideout made a significant impact but Wan’Dale Robinson caught a late touchdown in the fourth quarter. Safety: B- Kyle Hamilton had another impactful all-around game with six solo tackles, one tackle for loss and a pass breakup. Hamilton forced a fumble against Tate to prevent a long reception and give the Ravens the chance to add three more points before halftime. Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins were more sturdy with open-field tackling, although Starks did have one notable whiff late in the fourth quarter. The Titans were not successful generating explosive plays for most of the game. Special Teams: C+ Tyler Loop’s confidence carried over from Brazil last week, nailing a career-best 64-yard field goal at the end of the second quarter. It was the longest field goal ever made at M&T Bank Stadium. Unfortunately, Loop later badly missed a 40-yard attempt in the fourth quarter that would have given the Ravens’ a 27-10 lead. Ryan Eckley had a busy day with six punts, four of which landed inside the 20 yard line with a longest punt of 56 yards.
author: Frank Platko

title: Roundtable Reactions: Ravens grind out a win over Titans in Week 4
summary: The Baltimore Ravens battled through injuries and penalties to hang on for a 24-18 win over the Tennessee Titans in Week 4. The Ravens did not score in the second half after Lamar Jackson exited but they managed to hang on for their third victory of the season. Here are the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reactions […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Zay Flowers #4 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens battled through injuries and penalties to hang on for a 24-18 win over the Tennessee Titans in Week 4. The Ravens did not score in the second half after Lamar Jackson exited but they managed to hang on for their third victory of the season. Here are the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reactions to the winning result. Time to exhale. That was UGLY. The game ends up in the win column for the Ravens, but as we’ve seen so often, it was a lot more stressful than it needed to be. The injuries stacked up, including being without Lamar Jackson for the second half, and sub-par officiating contributed to a heap of penalties that put Baltimore behind the eight-ball. Combine that with a second half defense that was woefully insufficient in the secondary and another missed kick by Tyler Loop, and you had a perfect storm of a game that almost got away. I’ll give credit where it’s due: Loop hit a massive kick at the end of the half to give the Ravens some breathing room, LJ and Zay put together a couple of really nice plays, and the defense did generate a couple of turnovers and some decent pressure on Cam Ward (even with the officials missing holds on every other play). They’ve got to have their fingers and toes crossed that the injuries they suffered today aren’t long-term and that they can shore up defense before taking a road trip to Atlanta next week. Offensive MVP: Zay Flowers Defensive MVP: Kyle Hamilton — Kevin McNeils What was shaping up to be a blowout victory turned into an ugly second-half slugfest following Lamar Jackson’s injury. The Titans were able to key in on Derrick Henry and make life difficult for Baltimore in the run game. Zay Flowers was once again putting on a show before Jackson left the game, proving every week now that he was worth every penny of his new contract. The Ravens’ defense had a strong day outside of a couple of drives, but it was disappointing to see the unit only sack Cam Ward once despite effective pressure throughout the game. Penalties were yet again a massive issue for the Ravens and is something that threatens to hold them back every week. Obviously the biggest talking point following this game will be injuries, the most notable being Jackson, but also to Marlon Humphrey, Andrew Vorhees, and Durham Smythe as Baltimore looks toward Atlanta now. Offensive MVP: Lamar Jackson Defensive MVP: Kyle Hamilton — Dustin Cox While it wasn’t a pretty win, it was won handily by the Ravens. An incredible first half from Lamar Jackson and the Ravens offense gave them 24 points and that was all they needed as the defense had their best performance of the season, holding the Titans to 18. The win was heavily marred by a Lamar Jackson injury that held him out of the second half and a massive amount of penalties. But overall, I was happy with the performance. The offense was unstoppable outside of penalties when Lamar Jackson was on the field and the defense was incredibly solid outside of the first drive of the game. Outside of Carnell Tate’s catch and run at the end, the tackling was massively improved and they were in Cam Wards face all day. Big home win that was much needed to get rid of some bad voodoo. For as close as it felt, it’s important to remember this game would have been a 20+ point blowout if Lamar Jackson played the whole time. Offensive MVP: Lamar Jackson Defensive MVP: Mike Green — Zach Canter This felt like a game we all just wanted to end. The Ravens established a 17-point cushion in the first half due to a red-hot offense and opportunistic defense. However, on the final offensive play of the half, Lamar Jackson appeared to twist his ankle and did not return. Unfortunately, it didn’t stop there as Andrew Vorheees, Durham Smythe, and Marlon Humphrey all exited with injuries. The Ravens did what they needed to do and beat the lowly Titans but the main topic moving forward will be the status of Jackson and some of the other injured Ravens. It goes without saying that any meaningful injury to Jackson would eliminate any chance of real success this year. The penalty issues continue to be a major thorn in their side, and while there are some procedural things they need to get worked out, it’d be nice for some of the 50/50 type calls to go their way every once in a while. All-in-all, the Titans are so bad, it’s difficult to take anything meaningful away from this game but I’d consider myself disappointed in the Ravens performance. — Stephen Bopst The Ravens were in the driver’s seat to secure a 20+ point win in the first half before Lamar Jackson exited the game. Nevertheless, it was still disappointing that they couldn’t put any points on the board over the final two quarters with Tyler Huntley under center. They seemed content with avoiding any risks and allowing their defense to close out the game, which they managed to do with multiple three-and-outs forced. Jackson was the cherry on top of an injury-slewed matchup in which the Ravens also lost Marlon Humphrey, Andrew Vorhees, Durham Smythe, etc. While the Ravens’ offensive system is different than years past, they clearly are a drastically less potent offense when Jackson is not on the field. Offensive MVP: Zay Flowers Defensive MVP: Kyle Hamilton — Frank Platko

title: Instant takeaways from the Ravens’ win over the Titans
summary: The Baltimore Ravens limped out of Week 4 with a 24-18 victory over the Tennessee Titans and injuries to several key players, including Lamar Jackson. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant takeaways: All eyes on Lamar Jackson’s ankle It’s hard to come away from this game with any other takeaway than how important Lamar Jackson is […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers (4)at M&T Bank Stadium. Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson (8) and Baltimore Ravens offensive tackle Roger Rosengarten (70) react after a play during the second quarter against the Tennessee Titans. Mandatory Credit: Mitch Stringer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens limped out of Week 4 with a 24-18 victory over the Tennessee Titans and injuries to several key players, including Lamar Jackson. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant takeaways: All eyes on Lamar Jackson’s ankle It’s hard to come away from this game with any other takeaway than how important Lamar Jackson is to this offense. Jackson was having his way against the Titans in the first half before leaving the game with an ankle injury. Tyler Huntley was unable to keep the offense moving at a similar pace in the second half, scoring zero points in the final two quarters. Zay Flowers seemed to disappear after a monster first half as well once Jackson left the game. Hopefully Jackson’s injury is not one that will linger and affect him much going forward or cause him to miss any games. – Dustin Cox Kyle Hamilton should be in the DPOY conversation The NFL’s year-end awards tend to be driven by stats, and Kyle Hamilton’s unique role will keep him from racking up the kind of sack and interception numbers that typically lead to hardware. But I’m not sure any single defender in the league is as impactful on a play-to-play basis and capable of moments of such individual brilliance. Watching him chase down and strip Carnell Tate from behind was a thing of football beauty. In that way (and a few others), Hamilton is a defensive Lamar Jackson – but he’ll never get recognized as one. – Nikhil Mehta Vega Ioane held up at center One of my main takeaways from this game was how prepared Vega Ioane seemed to be making his first start at center. Jeffery Simmons was a major worry against Baltimore’s interior offensive line entering the game, but the unit kept the superstar defensive tackle from taking over the game. I did not notice any obvious issues with snaps either from Vega. The Ravens may have found something with their first-round pick moving to a new position. – Dustin Cox Minter owns money downs Jesse Minter’s defense has not been the world-beating unit most expected to start the year. They have especially struggled against opposing scripted drives and gave up a touchdown on Tennessee’s opening drive. On that possession, the Titans did not face a third down until they got to the three yard-line. They faced nine more over the course of the game, plus two fourth downs, and only moved the chains twice. Baltimore’s pass rush was not as effective without Trey Hendrickson, but Cam Ward struggled to sort through Minter’s coverages and find open receivers. The first-year head coach also dialed up some creative pressure packages that forced Ward to throw the ball out of bounds several times, though he was only sacked once. – Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens QB Lamar Jackson exits game vs. Titans with ankle injury
summary: Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson is questionable to return to Sunday’s matchup with the Tennessee Titans due to an ankle injury suffered on a sack at the end of the first half. Jackson had been playing brilliantly up to that point, completing 15 of his 20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns. Right after […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on from the sideline during the third quarter of the game against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson is questionable to return to Sunday’s matchup with the Tennessee Titans due to an ankle injury suffered on a sack at the end of the first half. Jackson had been playing brilliantly up to that point, completing 15 of his 20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns. Right after his injury, second-year kicker Tyler Loop drilled a career-long 64-yard field goal to give Baltimore a 24-7 lead going into halftime. Backup Tyler ‘Snoop’ Huntley entered the game and led the offense to just 38 yards on three drives in the third quarter. The Ravens lost three other key players by the end of the game – cornerback Marlon Humphrey (calf), tight end Durham Smythe (Achilles), right guard Andrew Vorhees (foot) – with outside linebacker Trey Hendrickson and centers Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic already hurt entering the week. Ravens head coach Jesse Minter projected cautious optimism about Jackson’s status in his post-game press conference and even indicated that the team considered putting him back in the game. Huntley also said ( via Jonas Shaffer of The Baltimore Banner ) that he did not know he was playing in the second half until shortly before kickoff. With a sizable lead against the Titans on an increasingly slippery playing surface, it made sense to put the franchise’s most important player on ice for the second half in the hopes of avoiding a more severe injury and a longer absence. Jackson left M&T Bank Stadium with a boot on his left ankle, per Jeff Zrebiec of The Athletic . He is “believed to be day-to-day,” NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport adds . Minter will provide a status update on Monday and the Ravens’ first Week 5 injury report will provide more concrete information on Thursday.

title: Breaking down Buffalo Bills problems after Week 4; concern or overreaction?
summary: The Bills have the most regular-season wins in the NFL since the start of 2020, and that means a few things. It establishes how profoundly consistent the team has been during the Josh Allen era. It also quite obviously means there haven’t been many losses over the past six seasons. There is a negative byproduct […]
full_text: The Bills have the most regular-season wins in the NFL since the start of 2020, and that means a few things. It establishes how profoundly consistent the team has been during the Josh Allen era. It also quite obviously means there haven’t been many losses over the past six seasons. There is a negative byproduct of that winning, though, particularly when to date it hasn’t amounted to a Super Bowl victory. When a relatively rare loss does occur, the sky-is-falling phenomenon tends to arise more often than not. Because Buffalo’s Week 4 loss happened immediately following a shaky performance in a win over the Chargers in Week 3, a lot of concerns have materialized among the fan base and the media. Or are they overreactions? Here’s how I’d categorize these takes: Overreaction: Josh Allen isn’t running enough This was the first takeaway I had from the loss to the Patriots . Is it a situation worth monitoring? Yes. Am I super concerned about it? Not really. In fact, I won’t be surprised if we see an especially run-happy Allen against the Rams and Raiders the next two weeks. Concern: DJ Moore’s shoulder An AC joint sprain then an aggravation of that injury in the span of four games for the 29 year old who has been incredibly tough and durable throughout his NFL career. I am starting to wonder if this will be a lingering problem given that this is Year 9 as a professional. Overreaction: James Cook isn’t getting enough carries This is one of the most obvious overreactions. The Bills could’ve given the ball to Cook on the ground more than 12 times against the Patriots. Absolutely. I wrote as such in my takeaways article that published this morning. But he’s seventh in carries through four weeks — pending MNF — and went over 20 carries in back-to-back contests in Weeks 2 and 3. Cook will get his in this Joe Brady offense. Don’t you worry about that. Overreaction: Dion Dawkins struggling The past two weeks have represented an unproductive stretch for Dawkins, as he’s allowed nine total pressures. He did lock it down against Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter in Week 1 and held his own against Aidan Hutchinson and Co. against the Lions. Is Dawkins in the peak prime of his career? No. Can he still play quality football at left tackle for the Bills? Definitely. He’s only 32. Healthy, high-caliber tackles can be valuable assets well into their mid-30s. We’ve seen this little lulls from Dawkins throughout his career. But he doesn’t look slower, or less powerful. He’ll be fine. Concern: Alec Anderson’s overall play I have not seen “it” from Anderson through four games. I thought his best performance came against the Lions, but it was mostly when blocking for the run game. That certainly carries its importance. Pass protection is king in the NFL, and the fifth-year pro has been a liability in that area in every contest. He has found work well — helping out a teammate when he’s left without a defender to block — and laid some devastating blocks in those scenarios. In true one-on-one situations, Anderson has mostly struggled. The former UCLA Bruin has allowed eight pressures on 152 pass-blocking snaps through four contests. David Edwards allowed four in the first month of the season a year ago. With Austin Corbett, a nine-year vet with a stable game, waiting in the wings, I wonder how much longer of a leash Anderson has as a full-time starter. Overreaction: Dalton Kincaid’s sudden drop in production Three catches for 45 yards including a one-snag, seven-yard performance against the Patriots. A shocking downturn in production from what we saw from Kincaid in the first two weeks of the season. I don’t think the lacking productivity continues. The sample is large enough to realize that when Kincaid is healthy and on the field, he’s one of the most productive receiving tight ends in football. Now, does Joe Brady need to dig a little deeper in the playbook or get more creative with how he deploys Kincaid? Absolutely. And I believe he will. No reality check hits harder this time of year for a coach than a loss in the division at home. He’ll start implementing Kincaid as a 1A or 1B option sooner than later, and Kincaid will make plays. Concern: Max Hairston’s demeanor and post-game reaction Hairston allowed two touchdowns and four total catches on seven targets in his coverage area. The nonchalance he showed on the game-sealing first down was downright stunning. I am not nor will ever be an analyst who takes it personally when a player doesn’t feel like talking to the media after the game. I do think it can give us an indicator of where a player’s head is at. Apparently Hairston “stormed out” of the locker room after what was clearly a bad performance. He’s allowed to be upset. Of course. The still very young cornerback needs to understand his job is very much a snap-to-snap gig. He needs to have amnesia out there. Prime example of this came in this contest when Hairston stayed stride for stride with a Patriots receiver on a deep ball and registered a pass breakup before allowing a first down on a dig the very next play. He needs to forget whatever happened on the last play, good or bad, and move forward to his next opportunity in coverage. Or to make a tackle in space. And it’s almost if he’s playing too tentatively even if off-coverage. Hairston has freaky physical talent. Twitchy as it gets at the cornerback spot. But for as much as he could rely on that explosion in the SEC to make plays on the football when planting and driving on a comeback route toward the sideline, or in-breaker… he can’t regularly do that in the NFL. He has to be more situationally aware and mentally strong to accentuate all his robust skills. Those two elements are more concerning to me than his actual play, believe it or not. If he can get right mentally, I truly believe Hairston will be fine. Overreaction: Josh Allen’s decision-making Contrary to popular belief in and around Western New York, among Bills Mafia, and, really, the entire football-watching population, Allen is not a flawless football player. He’s not going to make the perfect decision 100% of the time. And Allen did not become the superstar he is today because of his decision-making specialty anyway. Much more often than not, the Bills quarterback makes the right decision. The enormous sample size of his career tells us that. I’m not concerned about his clearly bad decision on the interception on Buffalo’s final drive of the Week 4 loss. Concern: Terrel Bernard’s lack of explosiveness Bernard is first on the team in tackles and third in stops (tackles that constitute a “loss” for the defense based on down and distance). But I can’t shake some of the reps I saw live — and on the in-stadium replay — from Bernard the past two weeks. What were those reps exactly? Outside runs or quick throws to tight ends or receivers in which Bernard had a free run to the ball-carrier and simply couldn’t get to the football in time before the offensive player could turn upfield for a solid gain. Sure, it could be Bernard still learning the intricacies of Jim Leonhard’s defense which is slowing the speed at which he reads and reacts to his keys. But he doesn’t appear as explosive or fast as he was even a few years ago. In coverage too. Overreaction: WR screens are back! Entering this Week 4 game, the Bills offense was below the league average in screen rate . Sure, the few thrown against the Patriots could conceivably move Buffalo closer to league average. But Allen isn’t utilizing screens at an alarmingly predictable frequency. And a screen — to a RB or WR — is a very viable play every team should have in its playbook and probably utilize every week. Plus, Connor McGovern confirmed on WGR 550 this was not the called play in the huddle. It was an audible based on the look the Patriots defense gave the Bills. Do the Bills want to have something other than a quick screen to a WR dialed up if they see a max pressure look from the defense on third down? Yes.

title: No game ball from Buffalo Bills Week 4 loss to Patriots; in fact, we may need a few back
summary: Generally speaking, we don’t hand out Game Balls after a loss. And after what we watched from the Buffalo Bills against the New England Patriots on Sunday, handing one out would feel a little ridiculous. Actually, forget handing them out. I’d consider taking a few back. If anyone from the secondary, our inside linebackers, offensive […]
full_text: Generally speaking, we don’t hand out Game Balls after a loss. And after what we watched from the Buffalo Bills against the New England Patriots on Sunday, handing one out would feel a little ridiculous. Actually, forget handing them out. I’d consider taking a few back. If anyone from the secondary, our inside linebackers, offensive line or several other position groups, still has a game ball sitting on the mantle from the first three weeks, please return it at your earliest convenience. We’ll keep the receipt and reconsider your eligibility next week. Because this was ugly. Josh Allen is one of the biggest offenders here. He doesn’t get to escape criticism just because he’s usually a unicorn. One of one. Yesterday not only didn’t he looking uncomfortable, he was sloppy with the football again. Not just protecting the football but uncharacteristic decision making for someone of his caliber I’m year nine. The Bills had plenty of opportunities to put New England away and couldn’t do it. There were breakdowns all over the field, and when Buffalo needed someone to make the play that finally swung the game, too often it was the Patriots making it instead. So no Game Ball this week. But there were a few players who deserve to escape the repossession department and my scathing remarks. Honorable Mention: Keon Coleman If there was one Bills receiver Josh Allen could consistently count on Sunday, it was Keon Coleman. Coleman finished with six catches for 116 yards, but this was one of those performances where the numbers don’t completely explain how good he was. During Buffalo’s fourth-quarter scoring drive, Coleman somehow came down with an incredible catch off a deflection on third down to keep the possession alive. Then, with Buffalo desperately trying to take control late, Allen went right back to him. Coleman caught back-to-back passes for a combined 58 yards, with the second going for the go-ahead touchdown with less than five minutes remaining. Big catches. Big situations. Big response. Coleman has started to find a groove in his third season, and on a day when Buffalo desperately needed someone in the receiving corps to step forward, he did. Honorable Mention: James Cook James Cook averaged more than six yards per carry for the second consecutive game. So naturally, the Bills gave him the ball…12 times. I’m just as confused as you are. Cook continued to look dangerous when Buffalo actually put the football in his hands. Unfortunately, somebody apparently decided the best way to capitalize on that was to stop putting the football in his hands. There are games where the running game simply isn’t working and an offense has to move away from it. This wasn’t one of them. Cook was effective. Buffalo needed offensive consistency. And somehow he finished the afternoon with only a dozen carries. Make it make sense. Honorable Mention: Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb This one goes to the EDGE tandem because Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb spent a significant portion of Sunday making Drake Maye uncomfortable. Unfortunately, Maye eventually discovered the cheat code: Survive the pass rush long enough and somebody will be open. And all too frequently, somebody was. Rousseau’s streak of recording two sacks in every game finally came to an end, but don’t mistake the lack of sacks for a quiet afternoon. He had eight quarterback pressures and at least four hits on Maye, and Rousseau was equally disruptive against the run. He also appeared to have a strip-sack before the play was overturned. Which (at the very least), I still feel like it should have been called intentional grounding. Chubb had a strong afternoon of his own, particularly against the run. He also generated a huge third-down pressure late in the first half that helped get the football back to Buffalo’s offense and got his hands on Maye several times throughout the game. The sack numbers haven’t arrived yet, but watching Chubb play, you get the feeling they’re coming. The problem for Buffalo wasn’t getting pressure. It was what happened behind it. When Maye had just enough time to look downfield, Buffalo’s secondary repeatedly gave him somewhere to go with the football. Keep Yours. Everyone Else, Check Your Mailbox Buffalo is 3-1. One bad Sunday doesn’t erase what this team accomplished during the first three weeks of the season. But there were enough problems against New England that simply chalking this up as “one of those games” would be a mistake especially after a pretty bad offensive performance a week ago vs a struggling Los Angeles Chargers team. No game ball this week. Just a few honorable mentions. And maybe a couple prepaid shipping labels for some game ball returns.
author: Sara Larson

title: Bills news: What went wrong in loss to New England?
summary: The Buffalo Bills (3-1) entered Sunday’s home game against the New England Patriots (2-2) with a chance to create some serious separation in the AFC East, but instead, Josh Allen threw a late interception, Buffalo’s depleted secondary allowed Drake Maye to regain his passing form and the Bills suffered yet another agonizing loss to the […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills (3-1) entered Sunday’s home game against the New England Patriots (2-2) with a chance to create some serious separation in the AFC East, but instead, Josh Allen threw a late interception, Buffalo’s depleted secondary allowed Drake Maye to regain his passing form and the Bills suffered yet another agonizing loss to the Patriots. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks recaps the good, the bad, and the ugly from Buffalo’s 29-26 setback. Patriots. Check out the assessments below and then let us know how concerned you are about the Bills in the comments section. What happened in the Bills loss to Patriots? Time and time again on Sunday, Buffalo’s defense came up short in its matchup with Drake Maye and the struggling Patriots’ offense, which came into the game having scored 29 points on 30 possessions but was able to equal that output in a 29-26 victory. Maxwell Hairston was easily the worst defender on the field on Sunday, allowing Romeo Dobbs to come away with two touchdown catches, and Josh Allen made a terrible decision with the Bills potentially driving for the tying score late, throwing an ill-advised pass into double coverage that was picked off. The game then ended when Buffalo’s defense couldn’t come up with a stop on the ensuing possession. We recap the first loss of the Joe Brady era, discuss what has gone so horribly wrong for Buffalo’s secondary, reflect on what defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard can do to shake up his struggling defense and offer up observations and key takeaways as the Bills drop a home game they had every right to win. title: DJ Moore injury update: Adam Schefter provides report on shoulder of Buffalo Bills receiver
summary: For the second time in the first month of the season, Buffalo Bills receiver DJ Moore left a game early after suffering a shoulder injury, and we now have some idea of its severity thanks to an Adam Schefter report. Against the Patriots in Week 4, Moore left in the first half after aggravating the […]
full_text: For the second time in the first month of the season, Buffalo Bills receiver DJ Moore left a game early after suffering a shoulder injury, and we now have some idea of its severity thanks to an Adam Schefter report. Against the Patriots in Week 4, Moore left in the first half after aggravating the shoulder injury from Week 2’s win over the Lions. He initially was listed as questionable to return but later was downgraded to doubtful and did play in the second half. This was Schefter’s report on where Moore apparently stands health-wise: Bills WR D.J. Moore aggravated his shoulder injury during today’s loss to the Patriots, per source. It is not considered “a long term issue as of right now.” pic.twitter.com/EB6897w4bp — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 5, 2026 The thought that it’s not a long-term issue is clearly huge for the Bills, especially given the original circumstances. The initial reaction from many when Moore hurt his shoulder against the Lions was that he broke his collarbone which would’ve likely been a multi-month injury. It ultimately was an AC joint sprain. Without a medical degree and using Schefter’s report as context, I’m assuming the aggravation was of the same variety. It wouldn’t appear Moore broke anything. As you can see here from Thigh Doctor on Twitter/X, this aggravation was almost identical to how he initially sprained that left AC joint in Week 2: #billsmafia DJ Moore Left AC joint aggravated. Will be tough to get back in for second half, but just might! Here is today vs original injury, identical 🤯 pic.twitter.com/EqY1Lgia8J — Thigh Doctor (@ThighDoctor) October 4, 2026 Moore had one carry for six yards and one reception for 11 yards on two targets against New England. His catch went for a first down on a 3rd and 8 early in Buffalo’s opening touchdown drive that tied the game 7-7 in the first quarter. He’s vital to Buffalo’s offense as a the true X who can separate against man-to-man coverage and find the football down the field. This will, of course, be a situation we’ll closely monitor as the Bills prepare for Monday Night Football in Los Angeles against the Rams in Week 5.

title: 4 takeaways from Buffalo Bills home loss to Patriots
summary: The Buffalo Bills couldn’t mount a game-winning drive in the final two minutes against the Patriots and fell to their AFC East foe 29-26 inside the new Highmark Stadium on Sunday. They’re still sitting atop the division at 3-1, but the Patriots climbed back into the race at 2-2. These were my takeaways from Buffalo’s […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills couldn’t mount a game-winning drive in the final two minutes against the Patriots and fell to their AFC East foe 29-26 inside the new Highmark Stadium on Sunday. They’re still sitting atop the division at 3-1, but the Patriots climbed back into the race at 2-2. These were my takeaways from Buffalo’s Week 4 loss. Something is up with Josh Allen as a scrambler… I think The Bills have squashed any speculation about a Josh Allen injury hindering his propensity to run with the football and effectiveness doing so. And that’s all this is — speculation. We all noticed Allen pass up some easy running lanes against the Chargers in Week 3. He ran for four yards on five carries against the Patriots and most of those yards came on tush pushes. Now, of course, I’m not advocating for Allen to take punishment when scrambling or on designed runs. But Drake Maye reminded the Bills how impactful a nimble quarterback can be throughout the course of the game, particularly when the defense feels like it has called and executed the perfect counter to what the offense throws at it. And at least when Allen is scrambling, he’s seeing defenders as they approach him, is larger than all of the second and third-level defenders, and can brace for contact. More quarterbacks are actually injured inside the pocket than when scrambling outside it. Allen is the most dangerous and productive rushing quarterback in the NFL. In his career, Allen has run for three more first downs on 196 fewer rushing attempts than Lamar Jackson. Think about that. It’s a huge, borderline unstoppable element of what Allen brings to the Bills offense. And it’s been mostly missing the past few weeks when we know it’s not in Allen’s DNA to be timid rushing the football. It’s definitely something to continue to monitor closely in the coming weeks before the bye. Jim Leonhard’s blitzes aren’t regularly getting home Entering Week 4’s game against the Patriots, the Bills were 23rd in blitz rate at just 24.2%. Hardly a clear uptick from the Sean McDermott defense that was mostly blitzing-averse from an original game plan perspective. Then, Leonhard cranked the blitz dial against Maye, and it hardly worked. He blitzed the Patriots quarterback on 47.6% of his dropbacks. Against it, the third-year quarterback went 11-of-18 for 156 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions. It’s actually been the individual play of Greg Rousseau and Deone Walker —sprinkled in with some Ed Oliver and Bradley Chubb — that has generated the most regular pressure, not Leonhard’s blitzes. And the Patriots blitzes felt significantly more effective — even blitzes of the delayed variety. They more regularly got a free rusher to Josh Allen. Part of the problem with the Bills defense through the first month of the season is that it’s a “pressure-package” based philosophy, and beyond the first half against the Lions, those pressure packages haven’t confused quarterbacks to the level we all expected. In a game like that, James Cook needs more carries I am the biggest advocate of throwing the football, especially when Allen is your quarterback. I’m also in awe of Cook’s development as a runner and certainly remember his rushing title from a season ago. I do need to remind myself of it at times. In a tightly contested game, Cook needs to get handed the football more than 12 times. Do I think he needs it 28 times? No. Hardly. But 12 felt like not enough when the margin was within one score the entire game. I don’t want the Bills to be one of the run-heaviest teams in the NFL. Far from. Buffalo’s field-goal drive that started late in the third quarter was a prime example of how the Bills can lean on the opponent with the run game, even if it’s not effective early, and where Joe Brady made a mistake That drive started with runs of 8, 17, and 10 yards from Cook on consecutive plays. Keon Coleman made a ridiculous tip-to-himself catch to convert a third down later in the drive, but Buffalo’s star running back never touched the ball after gaining those 35 yards on the opening three plays of the possession. Cook is an elite back and needs to be treated like one every game, particularly the tightly contested battles. Sometimes opposing players just make spectacular plays A week ago, Chargers wideout Quentin Johnston dropped what would’ve been a first-down in the second half on a third down, which of course led to a Los Angeles punt. Against the Patriots, Romeo Doubs and Efton Chism both reeled in one-handed touchdowns in the corner of the end zone against tight coverage. DeMario Douglas had an exquisite toe-tap excruciatingly close to the sideline. Doubs had a few of those snags as well. Sometimes in the NFL, with how naturally talented and positionally skilled players are today, you simply have to tip your cap to your opponent in those key moments. From my vantage point, I thought Maye overthrew Chism. And the second-year pro from Eastern Washington I loved during the 2025 pre-draft process simply made a spectacular grab. There’s really no blame to be assigned to anyone employed by the Bills on that play. Davison Igbinosun was a quarter-step behind Chism on a double move. The throw actually had to be slightly overthrown for it to have any chance to be completed. Maye regularly stepped away from pressure and either ran or made a pinpoint accurate throw, typically near the sideline, to move the chains. All of which was very similar to how he played in New England’s win against the Bills a season ago. Buffalo is accustomed to their players like Allen, Cook, Rousseau, Walker, Khalil Shakir, Christian Benford and Co. making those plays. In Week 4, the Patriots got a few more spectacular efforts from their players, and that’s why they won. Hat tip.

title: Bills vs. Rams odds: Opening lines for Week 5 matchup
summary: After a three-game home stand at the brand-new Highmark Stadium, the Buffalo Bills hit the road to take on the Los Angeles Rams in primetime for Week 5 of NFL action. The Bills and Rams meet under the brightest football lights of Monday Night Football, and it’s a matchup with odds that currently favor the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - DECEMBER 08: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) scrambles in the second half of an NFL football game between the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium, December 8, 2024, in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Tony Ding/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After a three-game home stand at the brand-new Highmark Stadium, the Buffalo Bills hit the road to take on the Los Angeles Rams in primetime for Week 5 of NFL action. The Bills and Rams meet under the brightest football lights of Monday Night Football , and it’s a matchup with odds that currently favor the home team. For the first time this season, Buffalo enters play as underdogs against their opponent. As of publishing, FanDuel Sportsbook lists the Bills as 2.5-point underdogs (+2.5 / -104) against the Rams (-2.5 / -118) in Week 5 . The money line opened at +126 for Buffalo and -148 for Los Angeles, with an over/under of O/U 53.5 (-110). Given the way both teams have played to begin the season, it’s anyone’s guess as to what sort of game is in store in Week 5. The Rams were flat out of the gate, perhaps due largely to the way they prepared for a Week 1 game in Australia. Since that point, they’ve alternated between winning and losing toward a 2-2 record through four games. The Bills stormed out of the gate on offense and a 2-0 record. They then sputtered to victory in Week 3 before a Week 4 collapse against the New England Patriots handed Buffalo its first loss of the season. The injury reports for both teams will be of utmost importance during the week. Notably for the Rams is the injury to defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who missed Week 4. The Bills suffered a litany of injuries in Week 4, with wide receiver DJ Moore re-aggravating his AC-joint sprain. Additionally, defensive tackle Ed Oliver had his ankle rolled up on by former teammate and Patriots fullback Reggie Gilliam, while defensive back Dee Alford picked up an ankle injury. Additional defenders in defensive back Te’Cory Couch and defensive lineman Landon Jackson also suffered injuries in Week 4. Buffalo was also without top cornerback Christian Benford, who missed the game due to a toe injury. The last game between the Bills and Rams was an epic shootout. Buffalo ultimately lost 44-42 to Los Angeles during the 2024 NFL season, which ended their seven-game winning streak. Quarterback Josh Allen became the first player in NFL history to throw for three touchdowns and rush for three scores in a single game — a feat accompanied by his 342 passing yards and 82 rushing yards. Allen and Matthew Stafford combined for 662 yards through the air. Allen is 2-1 against the Rams since entering the NFL. Will we see similar fireworks in the latest matchup? Don’t bet against it!
