title: Bills vs. Patriots Week 4 game analysis: Buffalo dealt major setback by AFC rivals
summary: The Buffalo Bills lost 29-26 to the New England Patriots in their first visit to the new Highmark Stadium, allowing the struggling divisional rival to resurrect itself early in the 2026 NFL season, and losing a great opportunity to open up a bigger advantage in the divisional race. It’s the kind of loss that severely […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 4: Efton Chism III #86 of the New England Patriots makes a one-handed touchdown catch during the fourth quarter against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills lost 29-26 to the New England Patriots in their first visit to the new Highmark Stadium, allowing the struggling divisional rival to resurrect itself early in the 2026 NFL season, and losing a great opportunity to open up a bigger advantage in the divisional race. It’s the kind of loss that severely impacts the Bills’ hopes for a number-one seed and playoffs seeding in general. Here are my notes about this loss, as I wrote them during the game. 1st Half Patriots’ defense all over Bills’ offense during the first drive. Josh Allen’s gotta throw that screen better, and their secondary was ready for all the in-routes on third down. Great punt by the rookie. Drake Maye hasn’t been able to do anything but run recently , and the Bills’ D obviously allowed him to escape for a 15-yard run. Can’t allow a struggling QB to gain confidence. Bills’ run D keeps getting better each past week. Pass rush starts slow, though, and Maye is gaining confidence. Three good throws on this 1st drive already. Bradley Chubb really is an underrated signing. He’s been very good. Bills’ D forces 4th & 3, Pats go for it and convert against soft zone coverage. TD pass on the very next play. Both catches were Romeo Doubs on Maxwell Hairston. Awful start for the Bills, 3 and out (just the 2nd this yr), followed by TD drive by Pats. Gotta answer it quickly, can’t allow a struggling team to like the game. (Doubs: 2 TD catches, 14 and 2 yards) Dion Dawkins gets beat one-on-one way too often for a franchise LT, IMO. Allen to DJ Moore to convert a 3rd and long. This connection will be key today. Another James Cook fumble , this time on a weird exchange with Allen. C’mon now. Run game struggling early. NE has been able to keep the Bills behind the sticks and force obvious passing downs. Josh was awesome on this 3rd down pre-snap. Simply knew what the Pats D was sending at him and changed protections, allowing time for a good completion to Khalil Shakir. 1st down set up the TD run by Cook. Impressive drive by the passing offense. (Cook: 8-yard rushing TD) Tyler Bass kicks it short of the landing zone and gives NE a possession starting at the 40. Incredible. Now Pats’ run game comes to life. NE is executing at a very good level, minimizing mistakes overall. Speaking of mistakes, Maye makes his 1st one of the day — pocket closed on him, Landon Jackson using his length to (kinda) force a fumble (sack credited to Ed Oliver), recovered by Greg Gaines. Great to see the “dirty work” guys getting rewarded with a game-changing play. Time for the offense to keep the momentum going. Ray Davis getting involved on offense for the 1st time this season. I like it, Cook is awesome, but it’s good to give defenses a different look sometimes + also good to have Ray happy and confident. We’re one play away from having him as the bell cow in the run game. Joshua Palmer drops a big play. The guy simply can’t be trusted. For every good play there’s one like this. Greg Rousseau was an inch away from making that a fumble and not a forward pass. Way too much time for Maye in the pocket. He finds Mack Hollins for a big play. D lets Maye scramble for another big play , setting up a NE 1-yard TD run by Rhamondre Stevenson. Frustrating day by this defense, especially the front 7. They should be dominating this matchup but it hasn’t been the case. Josh Allen magic on the very next drive to put the Bills in the red zone. Avoids the rusher and throws a laser to Shakir on an in route. Amazing play by 17. Another Cook 1st-down run stuffed. I’d like to see Joe Brady spread it out on 1st down a bit for a change. Throw early, even run from shotgun a bit. Try different stuff to open up the run game that hasn’t worked so far. 2nd down, flag on Dawkins. It wouldn’t matter because of the penalty, but Josh gotta take the yards on Cook there, he was completely free on the checkdown. Give him a chance. Moore looked hurt , and it looked like the same injured shoulder. Josh makes history with another tush push TD. Most TDs from scrimmage in Bills history, surpassing Thurman Thomas and Andre Reed. (Allen: 2-yard rushing TD) Now they kick it to a touchback , giving NE the ball at the 35-yard line and 1 min left. Why? Make them return it and milk that clock a bit. Good game by Davison Igbinosun so far. Great defensive series and now the O gets the ball back with 29 seconds and 2 timeouts left. Closing the 1st half with a lead would be awesome here. Tough game so far. Keon Coleman has done nothing but take advantage of his opportunities this season. Another great catch to start the drive. Shakir fumbles the checkdown pass. Bills would be in FG range. Those have happened way too often. What a sequence, Doubs with an awesome effort to gift Dee Alford with an interception. Bills in the red zone, 5 secs left. Bass FG makes it 17-14 Bills. NE ball to start the 2nd half. (Bass: 27-yard FG) Bills O couldn’t run the ball and insisted on it and the heavy formations, especially on 1st down. I’m not asking them to move completely away from it and the insistence might be justified as the game progresses, but I’d like to see a different approach here and there for a change. Bills D hasn’t played well. DL should be dominating this struggling Patriots’ interior DL. LBs have been invisible, I expect way more from Terrel Bernard, especially. The secondary couldn’t do much with the amount of time Maye has had. Adjustments needed for the 2nd half. 2nd Half Bills keep allowing Maye to escape for big gains with his legs. Hairston beat by Doubs on another 4th down conversion. Max has been too conservative on those, playing way too off the receiver. Very soft call on Hairston hold on 3rd down. On the other hand, no reason for him to hold on Doubs’ undershirt and let it stretch that way, you’re giving the refs a chance to throw that flag. Shortly after, Doubs beats Hairston on a fade for a TD. Rough game for the former 1st round pick. Next Bills offensive drive starts with another stuffed run from under center in a heavy formation, and Milton Williams killing Alec Anderson and hitting Josh’s hand just after he released the ball. The downgrade from Moore to Palmer is brutal. NE’s best players are simply winning their matchups against Bills players right now. Doubs on offense and Williams on defense. Mike Vrabel has been extremely aggressive on 4th downs , and Brady has been conservative with his offensive and defensive game plans. Fans are clearly frustrated in the stands. Damar Hamlin in as the nickel CB and promptly exploited in coverage on 3rd down. Can’t use him there, it eliminates man coverage possibilities completely. Ed Oliver also out injured with a knee. Frustrating season from him. Rousseau has been on fire this year. He rushes Maye and D gets out of the field. Important stop, can’t allow the Pats to make it a two-possession game. Josh Allen with a crazy play to save a safety. Could’ve been the dumbest INT ever, but it worked. Dawkins was beaten so badly he ended up sitting on his butt. Holy moly. Another incompletion on 3rd down as Shakir couldn’t hold a ball thrown behind him. Patriots have taken Dalton Kincaid away from the game. With no Moore anymore, Shakir has been Josh’s go-to guy, but he hasn’t been able to win consistently enough. Bad game by the offense, Vrabel’s owning Brady here. Another injury, Landon Jackson this time. Very frustrated, seems like he knows something bad happened. With the injuries he’s been through, an awful sign. I feel really bad for the young man. Despite the rough game overall, back-to-back great defensive drives, again, giving the offense a chance to rebound. End of the 3rd and the Bills have 30 rushing yards…
author: Fernando Schmude

title: Buffalo Bills’ struggles magnified in mistake-filled loss vs. Patriots in Week 4
summary: The Buffalo Bills weren’t going to finish undefeated this season. It’s an impossibly difficult task that, ironically enough, has only been duplicated twice before by AFC East foes in the Miami Dolphins (1972) and New England Patriots (2007). The key, however, is winning the right games on the schedule. To that end, the Bills dropped […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 04: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills scrambles with the ball under pressure from Christian Elliss #53 and Dre'mont Jones #5 of the New England Patriots during the second quarter at Highmark Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills weren’t going to finish undefeated this season. It’s an impossibly difficult task that, ironically enough, has only been duplicated twice before by AFC East foes in the Miami Dolphins (1972) and New England Patriots (2007). The key, however, is winning the right games on the schedule. To that end, the Bills dropped a ball they could ill-afford to lose control of in Week 4. Yes, every game counts, but not every game holds equal value. Buffalo picked a really bad weekend to play terrible football, where a loss against an AFC opponent — and their division rivals — far outweighs any loss to NFC darlings like the Los Angeles Rams. The reigning AFC Champions were reeling at 1-2, and ripe for another loss against what had been a prolific Bills offense. Buffalo couldn’t afford to give up another home game to New England, and once more they did just that early in the season. However flawed the Patriots may prove to be, their defense entered Week 4 ranked sixth overall. That, alone, should have served up a warning sign for anyone looking at buckable trends. When you add in the fact that often enough in recent games Allen and the Bills have looked ordinary against the Patriots’ defense thanks to brilliantly called games, it seems the one ripe for something was Buffalo’s rookie head coach Joe Brady. The season couldn’t have started better for Brady and the Bills, but it did place an early target on their backs. One of football’s ultimate litmus tests, Allen will always carry the sort of gravitas that encourages teams to knock Buffalo swiftly to the ground at every turn. It’s an especially tough situation to defend when you’re one of the teams still searching for your first Super Bowl win. Anyone who thought the Patriots were going to highlight their visit to Orchard Park, NY with a stay at that other Brady’s favorite hotel should now better understand the situation. There will be zero rolling over to play dead against Allen and the Bills in 2026 because nothing deserves to be written in stone after three weeks of play. In truth, it’s fair to hold Josh Allen to account for his play in the last two games. He’s not infallible, and his boneheaded play in the closing minutes of regulation handed the Patriots a win. To Allen’s credit, he immediately took responsibility for the throw, saying he “ should’ve thrown the ball out of bounds and live to fight another day ,” stating several times that he “shouldn’t have thrown it,” per Matt Bové. That’s also true of the absurd backwards pass. Buffalo is going nowhere quick without Josh Allen at quarterback. But they’ll find themselves in a similar situation if Allen continues asking a struggling defense to pick up his slack in the biggest moments. If you can’t trust the defense to hold up, then you can’t force them back out onto the field. Allen’s done so much to win an incredible amount of games for the franchise and by no means is this criticism meant to minimize what he means to the team, community, and beyond. But there have been too many mistakes to the extent that Weeks 3 and 4 stand out. It’s a team game, but Allen shouldn’t feel forced into such decisions at this point in his career. That interception wasn’t the final play of the game, but anyone watching knew the game was over in that moment simply due to Buffalo’s troubles on defense. Perhaps this was the brand of loss Brady and the team needed. It’s clear that defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard has a massive uphill battle in front of him. Outside linebacker Greg Rousseau has blossomed in Leonhard’s scheme and the pass rush in general is promising, but there are far too many other defenders who just aren’t doing enough of the 1/11th required each down. If you didn’t understand how important wide receiver DJ Moore is to the offense, consider the team’s play without him. The pass-catching unit looks eerily similar to the one that lined up in 2025, and you should well understand how difficult it was for them to accomplish much of anything downfield. Yes, wide receiver Keon Coleman has made huge strides at all levels of the field, but it’s clear that Moore is key to the passing attack and that tight end Dalton Kincaid is the one person defenses key in on down the field. It’s also true that Brady was vastly out-coached in Week 4. Despite his familiarity with the organization and the offense, Brady is a rookie himself. That said, the team’s two-point offense belongs on a milk carton. It’s often far less than a 50/50 proposition that the Bills successfully convert a two-point try. That leaves them chasing points instead of taking the near-given one. Had more fruitful pushes came to shove, that failed attempt left Buffalo staring at a game-tying field goal try for overtime instead of lining up for a game-winning boot. It’s early enough in the season that Allen and the Bills should be able to make needed adjustments. There will be a lot to unpack in the coming days, which includes a large amount of injuries. Now is when One Bills Drive must look itself in the mirror and find what’s needed to rise above the talk and stand tall at the end of the season. Right now, the Bills need flawless play by Josh Allen in order to win.
author: Matt Byham

title: Bills winners and losers: Keon Coleman shines, Maxwell Hairston struggles vs. Patriots
summary: The Buffalo Bills battled throughout the afternoon against the New England Patriots, but ultimately, it was the previously 1-2 Patriots coming into Highmark Stadium to earn the victory against the previously 3-0 Bills. The Bills had a lead in the fourth quarter, but a porous defense combined with a bad decision on offense from Josh […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 04: Keon Coleman #0 of the Buffalo Bills reacts after a play against the New England Patriots during the fourth quarter at Highmark Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills battled throughout the afternoon against the New England Patriots, but ultimately, it was the previously 1-2 Patriots coming into Highmark Stadium to earn the victory against the previously 3-0 Bills. The Bills had a lead in the fourth quarter, but a porous defense combined with a bad decision on offense from Josh Allen was all it took to give the Patriots a 29-26 victory. Buffalo’s first defeat was a frustrating one, as for the second straight week, the Bills played an AFC opponent with a poor record. And, for the second straight week, the Bills played down to their opponent’s record, giving a team life when they had plenty of chances to win. As with anything, there is definitely some up-and-down to today’s stock report. Some of our horns up players made bad plays. Some of our horns down players had a decent moment or two. There was good to go with the bad, and vice versa. Here are our horns up and horns down for today’s 29-26 loss to New England. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Up and Down: Josh Allen After the Bills began the day with a quick three-and-out, Allen went to work. He was patient, accurate, and poised, leading a long touchdown drive to tie the game at seven early in the second quarter. Then, after New England stretched their lead to 14-7, Allen led another long drive that ended with his 88th career touchdown from scrimmage. That surpassed both Andre Reed and Thurman Thomas for the most in Bills history. Buffalo’s receivers had a hard time finding space, and Allen found himself hemmed into the pocket throughout the afternoon. There were some chances for big plays downfield, but Joshua Palmer dropped one — a play that would not have counted thanks to a penalty — and failed to adjust to one along the sideline. Allen did find Keon Coleman on a few shots downfield, including a gorgeous touchdown pass, but with DJ Moore missing more of the contest thanks to an aggravation of his shoulder injury, Buffalo’s receivers struggled to find separation. Ultimately, it was a horrendous force downfield that erased any chance Buffalo had at coming back to win, as Allen eluded a sack and then fired a meatball sub into double-coverage. He was trying to give Joshua Palmer a chance, but he had little. Allen was 23-of-33 for 253 yards with one passing touchdown, and one back-breaking interception. He ran five times for just four yards and a touchdown. Horns Down: Pass Defense Drake Maye hasn’t looked this comfortable or this competent at any other time during this season. Buffalo’s pass defense, which looked better last week against the Los Angeles Chargers, was back to its porous ways this weekend. The Patriots’ offense came into the contest averaging just 12 points per game; New England surpassed that total in the first half. Pass rush lanes were vacant, giving Maye plenty of room to scramble. He also spent most of the day in clean pockets throwing to open receivers. It’s difficult to cover players for five seconds, and Buffalo’s inability to generate a consistent pass rush allowed those Patriots wideouts to find plenty of room. The pass defense was an issue again, and it’s beginning to appear like it will continue to be one. On New England’s first three drives, Maye was 8-for-11 for 111 yards with a passing touchdown. He also gained big chunks on a pair of scrambles, totaling 42 yards on three carries. In the second half, it wasn’t much better, and injuries in the secondary made things that much more difficult. Dee Alford and Te’Cory Couch were both injured at some point, so Buffalo had to use safety Damar Hamlin as a nickel corner. All told, they allowed Maye, who entered play completing just 58% of his passes with a 1:6 TD-to-INT ratio, to complete 22-of-37 passes for three touchdowns with just one fluke interception. Maye killed the Bills with his legs, as well, totaling 54 rushing yards on eight carries. Horns Up: Khalil Shakir After seeming like the forgotten man over the first three weeks, Shakir finally found some targets. Head coach Joe Brady made a concerted effort to involve Shakir early, as they called everyone’s favorite pass play, the bubble screen for the first pass of the game. He caught all six of his first-half targets for 75 yards, including a big 50-yard catch and run to set up Buffalo’s second touchdown. Shakir derailed a scoring drive at the end of the first half, fumbling after making a catch that would have put Buffalo in scoring position. Fortunately for the Bills, New England turned over the ball on the next set of downs. Overall, it was good to see Shakir as a focal point of the passing game. He totaled a team-high seven catches on a team-high eight targets for 82 yards. That total was second only to Keon Coleman. Horns Down: Dion Dawkins Dawkins committed a bad hands-to-the-face penalty to knock the Bills outside of the 10-yard line in a goal-to-go situation. He also allowed a pressure and a sack in the first quarter, as he was beaten badly by Elijah Ponder. In the third quarter, rookie Gabe Jacas bulldozed Dawkins and nearly caused a safety — and likely should have caused one given that Josh Allen fired a backwards, underhanded pass towards the middle of the field, which did not seem to have any receivers in the area. Playing left tackle is often thankless, and Dawkins has been better than most left tackles in the NFL for quite a while now. Sunday wasn’t his best day. Horns Up: Dee Alford After struggling the first two games, Alford looked better last week against the Chargers. This weekend, he made a couple of good plays in coverage. Alford intercepted Maye on a fluke play late in the first half, returning the interception to the nine-yard line to set up a short Tyler Bass field goal, which gave the Bills a 17-14 lead at halftime. On New England’s first drive of the second half, Alford was able to stick with DeMario Douglas on a slot fade, preventing a touchdown with solid coverage. Alford had to leave the game with an ankle injury, but he was able to walk off under his own power. He did not return, though, leaving some questions for an already-thin and under-performing defensive secondary moving forward. Horns Down: Maxwell Hairston After a solid start to the season, it was a day to forget for the second-year corner. Hairston was burned repeatedly by Romeo Doubs, allowing two touchdowns to No. 87 while Hairston was lined up against him in man coverage. Hairston also extended a drive by playing way too far off Doubs on a fourth-down play, giving New England’s top wideout on this Sunday far too much space. Later on in that same drive, Hairston was called for a pretty brutal holding penalty in the end zone, which extended the drive one more time and led to Doubs’ second touchdown reception. Hairston made up for it with good coverage on Doubs in the fourth quarter, preventing what could have been a back-breaking grab. Overall, though, he was not good in Week 4. Horns Up: Greg Dortch Dortch has done a nice job returning punts and kicks all season, but Sunday, he even looked good as a gunner on punt coverage. Dortch made a nice tackle on one of Tommy Doman Jr.’s punts, and it’s the first time I noticed someone other than Sam Franklin Jr. coming down hard on a punt. Dortch continues to prove himself useful on special teams, even when he doesn’t touch the football. He’s quite adept at the deke, coming up and pretending to field a punt that ends up going over his head and bouncing into the end zone. Will Dortch see more time on offense at some point this season? Horns Up: Keon Coleman With DJ Moore out for most of the afternoon, Buffalo needed players to step up, and Coleman delivered.…

title: The Optimist: A statement win and a much needed rest
summary: The Carolina Panthers have had a long, heavy hangover since their triumphant, 15-1 2015 season. The 11 years since then have seen some of the most pitiful play, coaching, and management that this franchise has ever known. A lot of us were holding our breath entering the 2026 season, waiting to see if the career […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 4: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers looks to pass against the Detroit Lions prior to an NFL football game at Bank of America Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have had a long, heavy hangover since their triumphant, 15-1 2015 season. The 11 years since then have seen some of the most pitiful play, coaching, and management that this franchise has ever known. A lot of us were holding our breath entering the 2026 season, waiting to see if the career of Bryce Young was going to take an incremental step forward—as he had managed each of the past two season—or if Young was simply going to take his place as one more sad chapter of the last decade. Instead, he may finally have found the first steps on the path to being the Panthers’ next franchise quarterback. 2026 may be the year of putting to rest all the sad streaks and facts of the last decade. January saw the first playoff game in over a decade. Last night was Charlotte’s first time hosting Sunday Night Football in over a decade. Now, after four games, Young leads the league with 1,268 yards passing, nine touchdowns, and only two interceptions. He is one of the top passers in the league right now and will, for the first time in over a decade for a Panthers quarterback, legitimately be in MVP conversations for at least the next two weeks. As we have said with every benchmark he has met thusfar in his career, what happens next is on him. Beating the Lions to pull up to 2-2 feels like a season-saving moment. 1-3 with more holes due to injury than a screen porch—even in light of three stellar offensive performances—would have felt defeating. Instead, Ejiro Evero’s defense used a preseason roster to hold off one of the best offenses in the NFL. They held the Lions to just 19 points before losing Jaelan Phillips to a concussion. The offense put up 22 points before 2026 first round pick and second string right tackle Monroe Freeling went down with an unspecified knee injury, leaving third stringer Stone Forsythe to match up against one of the best defensive linemen in the NFL in Aidan Hutchinson. They gutted out the rest of the game with a 10-7 margin to keep the win. In a game where they came in with two hands behind their backs, they lost another leg, shot themselves in the remaining foot with two missed extra points, and still won. What’s not to be optimistic about? There is no break down of what I did and didn’t like this week. Let’s just celebrate. We’ll dig into injury timelines and updates more during the bye, but the bottom line is that the Panthers are poised to get healthier and be a stronger team when they come back to face the Eagles in Week 6 and the rest of their schedule beyond. Almost all of us predicted the team would be 2-2 heading into the bye, but I guarantee that none of you predicted it would look like this—or that it would feel so promising.

title: Panthers vs Lions: Final Score and Recap
summary: Bryce Young and Tetairoa McMillan dominated all game long as the Carolina Panthers marked their return to Sunday Night Football with an electrifying win over the Detroit Lions, 32-26. First Quarter The Lions leaned on their stars in the first drive. Jahmyr Gibbs picked up a few nice gains and Amon-Ra St. Brown had a […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Tetairoa McMillan #4 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates a second quarter touchdown against the Detroit Lions at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bryce Young and Tetairoa McMillan dominated all game long as the Carolina Panthers marked their return to Sunday Night Football with an electrifying win over the Detroit Lions, 32-26. First Quarter The Lions leaned on their stars in the first drive. Jahmyr Gibbs picked up a few nice gains and Amon-Ra St. Brown had a big catch over the middle to take the Lions across midfield. The defense was able to deflect a Jared Goff third down to force a long field goal for the game’s first points. Bryce Young hit a couple of quick completions in the middle of the field to John Metchie and Tetairoa McMillan on RPOs, though the former was called back for a penalty. The Panthers ended up in a third and short and elected to air it out since the run hadn’t worked to that point, and full-in left guard Corey Bullock was walked back to Young by Alim McNeil for a sack. A Lions penalty backed them up near their own goal line after the punt, and the Panthers defense took advantage to force a punt right back. Young picked apart the Lions defense with a handful of quick completions along with some good runs from Chuba Hubbard. Hubbard capped off by breaking free on an off tackle run to the left for a 15 yard run to put the Panthers up 7-3. A Trevis Gipson personal foul for hitting Jared Goff low helped the Lions out to midfield as the first quarter came to a close. Second Quarter Devin Lloyd blew up a Gibbs run on the second play of the second quarter, but the Lions back answered with a long run off the left side on the next play. Goff hit Gibbs in the middle of the field for what looked like a first down completion, but Latham Ransom jarred the ball free with a big hit to the back of Gibbs. Dan Campbell challenged the call but did not get his way. Jake Bates hit his second field goal to make it 7-6. Alim McNeil was allowed to blow up another play, this time a second down run by Hubbard, to put the Panthers behind the sticks. No matter. Bryce Young climbed the pocket and Tetairoa McMillan with a little jump pass for a big gain and a first down. A few plays later, on fourth down, Young hit John Metchie on a crosser to pick up another first and his 11th straight completion to start the game. A throwaway on the next play marked his first incompletion, but he rebounded from that to hit McMillan over the top for a 32 yard touchdown. Ryan Fitzgerald shtoinked the extra point, so the Panthers took a 13-7 lead. The Lions finally found some offensive rhythm on their ensuing drive. They picked up a few third downs on passes to Jameson Williams. The Panthers tried to heat up Goff with pressure, but he got the ball out quick to his play makers. Akayleb Evans was called for pass interference in the end zone with the Lions threatening from inside the ten. On the next play, Gibbs slipped through the line for his team’s first touchdown of the game. Young and the offense took possession with the game tied and just over two minutes left in the half. McMillan took a bubble screen for a quick first down to start the drive and take the game to the two minute warning. Young continued to spam McMillan all the way into field goal range. The offense stalled there, and a questionable non-call on what should have been an intentional grounding kept the Panthers in field goal range. Ryan Fitzgerald just snuck it through the left upright to put the Panthers up 16-13 in the final seconds of the half. Young finished the half with 178 passing yards, and 147 of those were to McMillan. Goff took a shot down field on the first play after the kickoff and Jameson Williams was able to pull it while taking a hit for a 49 yard gain that immediately put the Lions on the edge of the red zone. Akayleb Evans made amends for his earlier pass interference with a very good pass breakup in the end zone. The Lions ultimately settled for a field goal to tie the game at 16 heading into the half. Third Quarter Young hit McMillan with a swing pass to start the second half and keep the good times rolling. Some strong runs by Hubbard and completions to Brycen Tremayne and John Metchie earned a couple more first downs. The Lions resorted to interfering with McMillan to stop him, and that moved the Carolina offense to just outside the red zone. A completion to Darren Waller set the Panthers up around the ten, and that set up yet another touchdown to McMillan, this time on a slant to the middle. Ryan Fitzgerald missed the extra point again though. The Panthers caught a break with a personal foul on the Lions offense after they picked up a first down. Moment after Cris Collinsworth said the Panthers defense cannot give up a first down when set up with a 1st and 25, they let Isaac TeSlaa run wide open behind the defense for a 57 yard completion that was very reminiscent of the play they gave up late in the first half. Fortunately they were bailed out by Derrick Brown, who swatted away a third down pass to force a Lions field goal. Young found Waller and Tremayne across the middle for some more nice gains. The throw to Tremayne was on a dime despite Young taking a hit while delivering the ball. Two plays later, it was Metchie’s turn to catch a ball across the middle. Unfortunately, in between those plays, Monroe Freeling left the game after having his leg fallen on. Stone Forsythe stepped in and held up. Chuba Hubbard broke free from a few tackle attempts run the ball all the way down to the two. He was rewarded for his efforts and given the ball again on the next play to punch it in for another touchdown. This time Fitzgerald was true on the extra point to put Carolina up 29-19. The third quarter ended with the Lions driving into Panthers territory. The defense almost got a stop from another Derrick Brown tip, but Amon-Ra St. Brown was able to reel in the pass anyway for a first down. Fourth Quarter Will Lee kinda broke up a pass to Jameson Williams on second down and then Goff sailed a ball on third down to force the Lions to actually punt the ball. Chuba Hubbard broke free down the left sideline for a 32 yard gain on the first play of the ensuing drive. Two plays later, he pounded forward for another 12 yards and a first down. He had to step out, and AJ Dillon struggled to find space. The offense was faced with a 4th and 4 on the 37 yard line after one of the stuffs. Dave Canales kept his foot on the gas and left the offense on the field. Young found Waller across the middle for the conversion. A few incompletions forced a field goal attempt, and Fitzgerald made that to put the Panthers up 32-19 with 8:59 to play. The Panthers defense left Sam LaPorta uncovered in the middle of the field for a big gain on the first play after the touchdown. Jaelan Phillips joined the injury party looking like he was pointing at his hamstring. Goff continued to pick apart the Panthers ailing defense with little resistance. The Lions worked into the red zone, and that’s where the defense finally put up a fight. Goff missed a couple of throws into tight-ish coverage and then some pressure resulted in a batted ball at the line of scrimmage. The Lions were called for back to back penalties on 4th and 10, a delay of game and a false start, to make it 4th and 20. The Lions tried a hook and ladder, but the defense snuffed it out and forced the turnover on downs. The offense went three and out with two incompletions, which was not an ideal way to try to put the game away. The Lions knocked over Sam Martin on the punt but were fortunately (for them) called for running into the kicker. The Panthers declined the penalty since Martin did get a good punt away anyway. The Lions took possession on their own 32 and immediately went back to dicing up the defense with intermediate…

title: 10 Bears Takes: Ben Johnson beats Aaron Glenn, Soldier Field Domination, and More
summary: Following another dominant win at Soldier Field, the Chicago Bears exit the first quarter of their regular season at 3-1. Although many will look at the box score and see a 23-12 final score, make no mistake: the Bears dominated this game from start to finish. If anything, they were their own worst enemy on […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following another dominant win at Soldier Field, the Chicago Bears exit the first quarter of their regular season at 3-1. Although many will look at the box score and see a 23-12 final score, make no mistake: the Bears dominated this game from start to finish. If anything, they were their own worst enemy on Sunday. With a quality start to the season locked in, all eyes will turn to the health of their starting quarterback heading into a big Week 5 matchup against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. Before we turn the page on their second-straight win, let’s take a deeper dive into Sunday’s game and what to expect next in Week 4’s edition of 10 Bears Takes. 1. After coaching on the same staff for four years in Detroit, the first matchup goes to Ben Johnson, and it wasn’t really that close. It’s always hard to label an 11-point win as “dominant,” but that’s exactly what this team did on Sunday. From the opening whistle until the final kneel-down, the Bears dominated this game, and despite the score, it never felt relatively close. Much was made about this matchup coming into the weekend, especially on a short week for Chicago. Conventional wisdom would have said that two head coaches who spent four years together on the same team would have made for a much closer matchup. Even if these two teams are in different spots at this juncture of this season, Johnson owned the matchup of his offense versus Glenn’s defense. Still, Dennis Allen also schooled Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich, despite some advantageous field position for the Jets coming off their two takeaways. As I wrote about last week, it’s time for fans to ignore past troubles and embrace the fact that this is a very good football team. Even more encouraging, they’ve yet to come close to reaching their ceiling. Penalties, self-inflicted mistakes, and injuries have held this group back from playing their best football. All things considered, that’s pretty impressive considering they are 3-1 and exit Week 4 with a +47 point differential. Maybe that’s why many, including myself, came away from Sunday’s game wanting more. Despite having more rush attempts (54) than the Jets had plays run (32), an 11-point margin of victory feels light. It took the Jets until the third quarter to break the 100-yard threshold, and outside of Geno Smith’s 58-yard bomb to Isaiah Williams late in the fourth quarter, the Jets offense managed just 109 yards on 31 plays. Let that sink in for a minute- the Bears had 153 yards over their first two possessions in the first quarter. Simply put, the Bears controlled every aspect of this game (outside of the turnover margin), including 345 more yards and 57 more plays, to go with a heavily lopsided 25:30 time of possession advantage. Considering the dominance displayed on Sunday, it’s only a matter of time before the scores start reflecting it. For now, Johnson will gladly take Round 1 against his former coaching mate. Now, we wait to see if there will ever be a Round 2. 2. With Caleb Williams’ status still up in the air for the next few games, Ben Johnson might want to reevaluate the quarterbacking situation heading into a crucial Week 5 matchup in Green Bay. If you look at the box score, you might have come away impressed with Tyson Bagent’s overall numbers. After all, he finished the game 25-of-34 (73.5%) for 268 passing yards, a 7.9 yards-per-attempt average, and the lone interception. That said, what didn’t show up on the stat sheet might warrant a more extensive conversation about who should start in Week 5, assuming Williams isn’t ready to go. I don’t want this to sound like I’m dumping on Bagent, but evaluating his overall performance needs nuance. On the plus side, when Bagent was accurate and on time, he was responsible for multiple big plays downfield. Aside from the one sack he took earlier in the game, his protection was fantastic, and for the most part, Bagent’s footwork and overall mechanics looked good. The bigger issue is that because of his lack of arm strength, when he doesn’t play on time or isn’t pinpoint accurate with his throws, the margin for error is much thinner than it would be with most starting-caliber quarterbacks in the league. Bagent had three interceptions that penalties would have wiped out, though one came on a “free play”. The issue is that he had a few other close throws that could have gone the other way, too. Now, don’t get me wrong- Case Keenum was far from perfect last Monday night, and had a few passes that should have gone for interceptions as well. The difference is that, for the rest of the time, Keenum was extremely accurate and rarely late to his reads. Aside from age, Bagent and Keenum play similarly. They must have good protection, must play on time, and must be more accurate than most quarterbacks because of their lack of natural arm strength. If the Bears decide to give Bagent another look in Green Bay, it’s best to trust the head coach. So far, he’s 2-0 in games started with backups, which is something he had yet to experience coming into the season. That said, it’s worth wondering if a veteran like Keenum would give them a better chance to win, especially in a big game on the road against their most-hated rival. My hunch is it’ll be Bagent again (assuming Williams still isn’t ready), but I hope there are at least some honest conversations at Halas Hall this week before they decide. 3. After back-to-back games without a consistent run game, Johnson made a concerted effort to get things back on track. I’d say- mission successful. Unlike Week 3, Johnson leaned on his run game early and often on Sunday afternoon. In fact, they ended up with a 54-36 run-pass split when the clock struck zero. Since 2025, the Bears have four games with 230-plus rushing yards, according to an NFL Researcher on X. No other team has more than two in that same time span. Last week, it felt like the Eagles were able to key in on their run game without a mobile quarterback under center. This week, Bagent’s athleticism and early success allowed Johnson more freedom to grind the clock and bludgeon the opposing defense. In total, four runners combined for 232 yards on the ground, two touchdowns, and a 4.3-yard-per-carry average. Even with D’Andre Swift being benched for his second-half fumble, the Bears’ two-headed monster combined for 204 yards and a quality 4.5 yards per carry average. Heck, even Roschon Johnson factored in on the 232-yard total. Both Swift and Monangai have proven to be very good players, but this scheme lends itself to maximizing opportunities, which is promising for this season’s prospects. Even once Williams is back under center, expect this team to keep establishing the run and not get away from it. That’s not something we have been able to say in the past, but as we’re learning, Ben Johnson isn’t your typical offensive mind. 4. Despite dominating all but one series, their goal-line struggles and turnovers made this game look a whole lot closer than it was. The “record” numbers have kept pouring in since the game ended, and they all heavily favor the Bears. Some of those examples: The Bears didn’t punt in a game for the first time since 2014. The play differential (+57) was the fourth biggest in a game since 1970. Their 89 plays were the most in a single game since 199,7 when they ran 90 plays against… You guessed it- the Jets. The Jets’ 32-play run was the fourth-fewest run by a team, according to Pro-Football-Reference. The Bears had more first downs (34) than the Jets had plays (32). This is just the second time this has happened in the Super Bowl era. The Jets had just 45 seconds of time of possession in the fourth quarter. Although I’m…

title: Bears vs. Jets: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and Chasing Records
summary: The Chicago Bears entered Week 3 against the New York Jets as the NFL’s number one ranked rushing team, averaging 184.3 yards per game. Chicago’s offensive line paved the way for 232 yards on the ground, bringing their average up to 196 this year. They still have a long way to go in the 2026 […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears running back Kyle Monangai (25) runs with the ball against the New York Jets during the second half at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Mike Dinovo-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Chicago Bears entered Week 3 against the New York Jets as the NFL’s number one ranked rushing team, averaging 184.3 yards per game. Chicago’s offensive line paved the way for 232 yards on the ground, bringing their average up to 196 this year. They still have a long way to go in the 2026 season, but they are on pace to break the franchise record for rushing yards in a season set in 2022: 3,014 yards (177 per game). I’ll have more on this tonight on Bear & Balanced, so join us at 6 ! Speaking of records, the Bears set a franchise record with 34 first downs. Those 34 first downs were more than the 32 total offensive plays the Jets ran, making this the second game in the Super Bowl era (since 1966) in which a team had more first downs than its opponent had offensive plays. The Bears may have won by only 11 (23 to 12), but it was a dominant performance by the Navy and Orange. They had more yards (492 to 157), more plays (89 to 32), and had the time-of-possession edge (42:45 to 17:15), while holding the Jets to only 7 first downs. The 7 first downs are the fewest a Bears team has allowed since December 14, 1991, when they allowed 7 to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Jets only had the ball in the fourth quarter for 45 seconds. Chicago had fewer penalties, with just 4 for 29 yards (both season lows), compared to New York’s 12 for 76. The Bears were 7 for 15 (46.7%) on third downs, and 2 of 3 on fourth downs. The only place the Jets had the edge was the turnover margin, which they won 2-0. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing time breakdowns and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE This was Tyson Bagent’s first *start in over a thousand days, but unlike Case Keenum, who also went over a thousand days between starts, Bagent didn’t have over a decade and 81 games of experience to pull from. This was just Bagent’s fifth career start, so I’ll judge his performance accordingly. Bagent was fine, but he was also lucky he didn’t throw multiple interceptions. One of his could-have-been-interceptions came off a free play that he went deep on, and the other was a direct result of a defensive penalty that let the defender get in position. But he had two others that were awful decisions, negated by penalties. His actual pick was on a throw he was a bit late and behind on. But he also had some really nice moments working his progressions. The throw down the seam to Rome Odunze got them points before the half. The aforementioned deep shot on a free play is a veteran move. He worked his cadence well. His timing on screens was good. All in all, this game is a good learning experience for him and the Bears. The running game was brilliant, led by Kyle Monangai’s career-high 30 carries, which came after Swift was seemingly pulled after his fumble. When asked if Swift was shaken up on the play he fumbled on — he seemed to get up slowly, and he had a knee issue earlier in the week — head coach Ben Johnson said, “No, no, nothing, nothing like that.” *The record books will technically list Case Keenum as the starter at quarterback for this game, unless they asterisk it at some point because Bagent also started the game. Also, how great is it that Ben Johnson basically started Keenum just to troll the insiders who reported that Bagent would start? DEFENSE Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman has either led or tied for the team lead in total tackles in every game of his young NFL career. That’s not necessarily a good stat for a safety, but he’s been used up close to the line of scrimmage plenty, and he’s flying up in run support while rallying to the ball in the secondary. I’ve been pleasantly surprised at Dayo Odeyingbo this season. While his sack was a gift this week because Geno Smith ran out of bounds, Dayo was in hot pursuit. It also gives him a team-leading 3 sacks in 4 games. Chicago held the Jets to 0-8 on third-down tries, and The Athletic’s Kevin Fishbain shared that this was the first time since October 5, 1997, that they didn’t allow a single third-down conversion. They held Jets QB Geno Smith to just 8 of 15 (53.3%) passing for 119 yards. Before Sunday, he was leading the NFL with a 75.5% completion percentage. Marcus Davenport got a stat in his season debut! I wasn’t expecting much, but I thought he looked decent out there. SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos hit 3 field goals and both extra points. Tory Taylor did nothing but hold for field goals and extra points. The Chicago Tribune’s Brad Biggs had this interesting nugget: This is just the fourth time in the Super Bowl era that the Bears have gone through a game without punting, and the first time since September 28, 2014, against the Green Bay Packers. Zavion Thomas had 4 kickoff returns for 70 yards, and Kalif Raymond had 16 yards on 2 punt returns. Daniel Hardy had 2 special teams tackles. Rookie tight end Sam Roush had a holding penalty on a kickoff, and he had a tackle on the Bagent interception. To check out the complete Bears vs. Jets box score, I find ESPN’s site is easy to navigate. All statistics and snap counts, as well as the accompanying pictures, are taken directly from the NFL’s Game Statistic and Information System.

title: Bears lay the smack down on Jets, take control on both sides of the ball
summary: Coming out of Week 4, the Chicago Bears have a 3-1 record in the 2026 season. Each of those three wins has come with a different quarterback at the helm. On Sunday, Tyson Bagent was the one who got the job done in their 23-12 victory over the New York Jets. The Bears utterly dominated […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball during the second quarter against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming out of Week 4, the Chicago Bears have a 3-1 record in the 2026 season. Each of those three wins has come with a different quarterback at the helm. On Sunday, Tyson Bagent was the one who got the job done in their 23-12 victory over the New York Jets. The Bears utterly dominated the time-of-possession battle, squeezing out 42 minutes and 45 seconds of the 60-minute period to give the Jets very little time to get anything going on offense. It helped that Chicago’s defense held New York to just 157 yards and stopped the offense on each of its seven third-down conversion opportunities. Though the offense had its flaws, there was still more than enough firepower to make up for the absence of Caleb Williams in the lineup. As of this writing, the Bears ranked No. 4 among 28 NFL offenses in PFN Offense Impact grading in Week 4, and they ranked No. 6 in PFN Defense Impact grading. These are some of my takeaways from Sunday’s win, which match up with what the analytics have to say. Ben Johnson is a wizard, and Tyson Bagent is good enough The efficiency of the Bears’ offense on Sunday was commendable. The team certainly took a run-heavy approach against the Jets, rushing the ball 54 times against 35 dropbacks to pass. Ben Johnson did a fantastic job of realizing where he had the leverage, and utilizing his athletic offensive line and impressive running back tandem to run it down New York’s throats. That helped Chicago dominate the time of possession battle, but when Bagent did drop back to pass, he was effective in moving the ball down the field. Bagent completed 73.5% of his passing attempts on Sunday, throwing for 268 yards in the process. Of his 34 passing attempts, ten of them went more than 10 air yards past the line of scrimmage, and he completed seven of them. I’d argue that Case Keenum’s performance in Week 3 was slightly better from a decision-making perspective, but Bagent was tested with more opportunities to move the ball down the field, especially in the first half of the game. In all, Bagent was perfectly serviceable. He wasn’t great, as made evident by his lack of passing touchdowns and his interception (a total which would have been four if three of them hadn’t been called back for penalties). There is no quarterback controversy in Chicago, and Bagent is a backup-caliber quarterback. And that’s perfectly fine. There’s a lot of value in a solid backup, especially one who understands Ben Johnson’s offense like Bagent does. The Kyle Monangai showcase Kyle Monangai out-carried D’Andre Swift 30 carries to 15 on Sunday, which is the largest gap Monangai has ever taken ahead of Swift in a single game. Once Swift coughed up a fumble in the third quarter — his second in three weeks — he didn’t touch the ball once for the remainder of the game. Monangai handled the load as the running back chosen to wind the clock down for the Bears, and he executed. On his 30 carries, Monangai finished with 146 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns, and an average of 4.9 yards per carry. He was decisive running in between the tackles, he was powerful bouncing off of defenders, and he showed off his trademark determination to battle for every yard he got. He already had an impressive performance before the Bears pulled Swift from the game, but from that point on, his consistency helped Chicago squeeze out the clock and put the game on ice. Rome Odunze makes a statement There’s admittedly very little to take away from the Bears’ defensive performance compared to most weeks, though credit belongs to the secondary for shutting down the Jets’ passing attack for much of the afternoon. Instead, I wanted to give a shoutout to Rome Odunze, who put together one of his best career performances to date on Sunday. Odunze finished the game with six catches for 94 yards, hauling in all but one of his seven targets and averaging 15.7 yards per reception. His fluidity shined across the middle of the field, and he demonstrated his underrated ability to create separation pretty consistently. The big difference was his hands, as he’s had issues with drops over the course of his NFL career. Drops were not an issue for him on Sunday, and he put up legitimate WR1 production as a result. With how many mouths the Bears have to feed in their offense, it can be easy to overlook Odunze sometimes, but do so at your own risk. He showed improvement in his biggest weakness this week, which allowed him to maximize his existing strengths.

full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - DECEMBER 07: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears and Carrington Valentine #24 of the Green Bay Packers react after the play during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on December 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers play in Week 5 at Lambeau Field, and our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook just dropped their early odds for the game, and this one surprised me. This will likely change over the coming days, but right now the Bears are a 1.5-point road favorite. Sure, Chicago has been playing better over the last four weeks, but Green Bay was favored by 3.5 points on the look-ahead line. I figured the line would tighten up a bit after today’s performances by each team, but that’s a big shift. The (3-1) Bears dominated the New York Jets earlier today, winning 23 to 12, while the (2-2) Packers held on to beat the winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers 17 to 14. Both teams are trying to keep pace with the (4-0) Minnesota Vikings, who just beat the winless Miami Dolphins, 15 to 10, behind five field goals. But back to the fiercest rivalry in sports. The Bears have won three of their last four games against the Packers, including last season’s Wildcard game. Chicago will no doubt lean on their league-leading rushing attack no matter who starts at quarterback, but it does seem like Tyson Bagent will get his second consecutive start. Okay, so technically since Bagent didn’t take the first quarterback-center exchange, he doesn’t get credit as the starting QB, but he started and went 25 of 34 (73.5%) for 268 yards, an interception, with a passer rating of 83.9. Green Bay’s starting quarterback Jordan Love completed 22 of 30 (73.3%), for 197 yards, 2 touchdowns, an interception, and a passer rating of 98.9. This was the first game this season that Love completed better than 55.2% of his passes. All three games these two teams played against each other last year were one-score games, so I’d expect another close one. What are your thoughts on the early line? title: Bears Dominate on Ground & D as that Guy and Bagent lead the Beloved to Victory
summary: CHICAGO, IL — With Caleb Williams watching in street clothes, and Case Keenum, the hero of Monday Night, watching from the sidelines, the Bears routed the Jets behind Kyle Monangai and Tyson Bagent, combined with a stiff defensive game plan from Dennis Allen. Bagent managed the game, Monangai pounded the Jets for 146 yards and […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 04: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears reacts after rushing for yards during the fourth quarter of the game against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jessie Alcheh/Getty Images) | Getty Images CHICAGO, IL — With Caleb Williams watching in street clothes, and Case Keenum, the hero of Monday Night, watching from the sidelines, the Bears routed the Jets behind Kyle Monangai and Tyson Bagent, combined with a stiff defensive game plan from Dennis Allen. Bagent managed the game, Monangai pounded the Jets for 146 yards and two touchdowns, and Chicago’s defense spent most of a sunny Sunday at Soldier Field pinning Aaron Glenn’s offense in place. The result was a 23-12 win that was never really in doubt. Chicago led 13-3 at the half, pushed it to 23-6 in the 4th quarter, and managed to absorb New York’s only real punch: a 58-yard Geno Smith touchdown to Isaiah Williams, with the extra point no good. Monangai’s 1-yard score late in the first and his 5-yard run in the third did the heavy lifting, Rome Odunze (six catches, 94 yards) kept the chains moving, and Cairo Santos cleaned up the rest. For a team already 2-1 coming in, it was the kind of ground-and-control afternoon Ben Johnson has been trying to install — and a reminder that the run game can carry a Sunday when the starting quarterback is out with a hamstring. ESPN’s Game Box Score My HOT TAKES and game summary for each quarter of this game: 1st Quarter: Bears 7, Jets 0 The Bears, with Tyson Bagent under center, were super efficient on offense. I actually thought that the Jets did a good job of anticipating Ben’s inverse strategy – ie play-action rather than run when the defense is expecting a run – but the Bears offense is just too varied, with weapons at too many positions for the Jets to match play-for-play. It’s the difference between a chess master playing a grand master. So the striped ones took two Swift touchdowns off the board after both were called touchdowns on the field. I think we have thoroughly lost the entire concept of “clear and obvious,” as in the preference for the call on the field – as neither of the replays were clear that Swift didn’t cross the goal line before he was down. The NFL simply has to address this. No one is entertained by this kind of nonsensical, picayune review. The Bears turned it over on downs at the goal line. The Jets took over at their own 1, went nowhere, and Austin McNamara punted them out of immediate trouble. The next possession was the one that counted. Bagent hit Luther Burden III for 22 yards down the right sideline, Swift bounced outside for 13, and the drive finished the way most of this game would: Monangai, right guard, one yard, touchdown. Cairo Santos made the kick. Twelve plays, 57 yards, and a 7-0 lead with 23 seconds left in the quarter. Geno Smith, in his second stint with New York, had barely been allowed to throw the ball – take that, Jets! Second quarter: Bears 13, Jets 3 Austin Booker opened the quarter by dropping Smith for a 9-yard sack and a three-and-out. Then came the play the Jets had been waiting on for a year and a half. Bagent looked deep middle for Colston Loveland, and Minkah Fitzpatrick stepped in front of it and returned it 27 yards to the Chicago 34. It was New York’s first interception since Jan. 6, 2025 — 643 pass attempts and a league-record 20 games between picks. Bagent had the right read – he just needed more zip on the pass and a better target; had he led Loveland, it’s a big gainer. But for all of the Jets’ celebration, they got a total of 16 yards out of it. Motivated Odeyingbo sacked Smith on the drive, and Jason Sanders bailed them out with a field goal from 36. The Jets were on the board, 7-3, and that was the high-water mark of their first half. Chicago answered with the methodical approach Ben Johnson has taken with his backups on the field. The Bears marched off an 11-play, 59-yard march that ended in a Santos 30-yard field goal. Another 11-play, 68-yard drive ran the clock out, and Santos hit from 30 again as the half expired. Halftime was 13-3. Smith had five passing yards. The Bears had the ball, the line of scrimmage, and the only touchdown. Halftime Thoughts The refs were waaaaaaay too involved in the first half, frankly, for both teams. Bagent illustrated he can run BJ’s efficient and forward-thinking offense. And Dennis Allen did what I thought he would do to the Jets – keep Geno Smith guessing and force tough down-and-distance situations. One concern: Swift might have a fumbling problem. You know who doesn’t? Kyle Monangai. Third quarter: Bears 20, Jets 6 New York’s best chance arrived on a gift. Jamien Sherwood jarred the ball loose from Swift, and Brandon Stephens recovered at the Chicago 28. Smith found Isaiah Williams for 15 to the 13, then the drive died. Sanders made it from 30, and the Jets were within a score at 13-6. It lasted all of one possession. Chicago went 72 yards in nine plays, Monangai carrying the load, and he walked in from the 5 with 2:26 left in the quarter. Santos’s kick made it 20-6. The turnover had bought New York three points – not enough against the Chicago Bears today. Fourth quarter: Bears 23, Jets 12 The Bears kept to the same script. Pound. The. Rock. Eleven plays, 77 yards, and Santos from 21 pushed it to 23-6 with 10:01 left. Smith finally got behind the defense. On second down, he hit Williams in stride for 58 yards and New York’s only touchdown – it was a busted play by Stephenson, who had dropped a sure interception in the first half. He continues to be a boom-and-bust player. The extra point was no good, however, so it was 23-12. That one throw was more than half of what the Jets had managed to that point — 99 yards on their first 31 plays. Chicago then took the ball and kept it. The final possession ran 9:16. Stephens intercepted Bagent on third-and-3 from the Chicago 15, but Demario Davis had jumped offside – Jets fans (and my nephew is one) may complain – but that was a classic recognition by the QB that he had a free play and Bagent threw it up. D’Angelo Ponds appeared to pick off a pass to Kalif Raymond on third-and-8, and that one came back for a hold (again – pretty clear it was picked because of the hold). On fourth-and-1 from the Jets’ 30, T’Vondre Sweat jumped, as Bagent channeled early career Aaron Rodgers, and the first down was free. Four plays later, the Bears were in victory formation. Monangai finished with 30 carries for 146 yards and both Chicago touchdowns. Bagent was efficient enough. Smith went 8 of 15 for 119 yards, a touchdown and three sacks. Chicago outgained New York 492-157, and the Jets finished with 12 penalties, several of them on the drive that ended the afternoon. The scoreboard said 11 points. The field said it was never that close. I predicted a Rome breakout game, and we saw it. Also – Loveland has finally been so consistent; he has added key receptions after reception. The Bears defense continues to defy expectations, and Kyle Monangai made his case as a co-equal partner in the Bears backfield. Bring on the Pack.

title: 3 things we learned from the Bengals’ wild loss to the Jaguars
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals (2-2) are nowhere near a finished product, but they might not have enough time to figure out some of their persistent problems. Here’s what we learned from their second straight loss, a wild 22-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The lack of a running game has made this team rely on hero […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 04: Chase Brown #30 of the Cincinnati Bengals is tackled by Rayuan Lane III #25 and Branson Combs #50 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the game at Paycor Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals (2-2) are nowhere near a finished product, but they might not have enough time to figure out some of their persistent problems. Here’s what we learned from their second straight loss, a wild 22-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The lack of a running game has made this team rely on hero ball At first, it was fun to watch Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins make toe-dragging sideline grabs. But then, after watching the Bengals rely on similarly athletic sideline catches from Higgins, Mike Gesicki, and Mitch Tinsley just to create any semblance of an offense against the Jaguars, something became clear: that’s the only way they know how to score points. Whether you want to blame Chase Brown, his blocking, or both, the running game is doing next to nothing. Brown got just 10 yards on nine carries against Jacksonville. Though he’s known as a speedy, dual-threat back, his longest run of the year is 13 yards and his longest catch is 12 yards. There is no way you’re going to consistently be able to score points with such a lack of explosion at the RB position. Turnovers at the worst possible moments are tanking the season In Week 3, it was the muffed punt and the Joe Burrow fumble that ended the game. In Week 4, it was a bizarre fourth-quarter Burrow interception. Yes, mistakes happen, and even the best quarterbacks misfire on occasion. But these seem to be an indication of a sort of nervousness or lack of preparation for the moment. Something is going on with the Bengals mentally, and they need to get more confident in what they’re doing on the field so that they can make level-headed decisions in the clutch. The tackling issue isn’t going away The Bengals’ front office did a nice job of fixing the defensive line. Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe, and others are consistently getting into the backfield to make plays and create pressure. The problem is everything after that. Dax Hill and DJ Turner are doing their part, but outside of them, the Bengals can’t seem to stop pass catchers. The strength of the Bengals' defensive back 7 is DJ Turner and Dax Hill, right? They got targeted 3 times in this game. The Jags just threw the ball at everyone else. Linebackers: 8 targets Safeties: 6 targets Edges dropping into Cov: 3 targets The other CBs: 2 targets — Goodberry (@JoeGoodberry) October 5, 2026 Most significantly, the Bengals still can’t stop tight ends or get guys down on the first attempt. Tight ends, in particular, have posed a problem. Dalton Schultz had 140 yards against Cincinnati in Week 2. Darnell Washington had a 47 yard catch and run down the sideline where he evaded four tacklers to set up the game-winning field goal in Week 3. And then Brenton Strange put up 95 yards for the Jaguars in Week 4. Giving up easy yards to opponents while not being able to get them for yourself is a bad recipe in the NFL. Zac Taylor and the coaches have to figure out how to make things easier on their players quickly for this team to stay in contention.

title: Bengals News: Mike Gesicki owns up to late mistake
summary: One of the big things to happen at the end of the end of the Cincinnati Bengals loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was what appeared to be a miscommunication between Joe Burrow and tight end Mike Gesicki on the final series of downs. Gesicki owned up to the mistake after the game: “It was a […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) and tight end Mike Gesicki (88) celebrate a Burrow touchdown rush in the fourth quarter of the NFL Week 4 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Jacksonville Jaguars at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. The Bengals fell to 2-2 on the season with a 22-17 loss at home. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co One of the big things to happen at the end of the end of the Cincinnati Bengals loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was what appeared to be a miscommunication between Joe Burrow and tight end Mike Gesicki on the final series of downs. Gesicki owned up to the mistake after the game : “It was a play that, because of personnel shuffling, normally that’s Tee (Higgins) running that. So then, I went we moved to Tee’s spot. I felt the corner heavy inside. I’m supposed to cross his face. I didn’t. I learned that one on the sideline. It just is what it is. There’s no excuse for things like that. I was just trying to make a play.” Unfortunately, these are the kinds of things that can happen when you are shuffling so much due to injuries. It is bad enough to be without Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, but when they both go down in a game things can be hectic. Bengals News Postgame Quick Hits | Ja’Marr’s Injury, Jags Defense Beat Joe Burrow’s Big Passing Day The Bengals may have an issue at wide receiver next week against the Miami Dolphins. We will have to see how Ja’Marr Chase progresses through concussion protocol over the week. We will also have to monitor an injury to Tee Higgins (adductor) as well. Burrow could be without his top two wide receivers on a week that seems crucial going into their Bye Week after. Bengals Big Betting Favorites Against Dolphins in Latest AFC Battle During 2026 Season Cincinnati opens as a full touchdown favorite on the road against Miami. That is pretty significant amount of points for a team to be spotted on the road. It really feels like the odds makers are expecting a bounce back game a la what college teams get. Joe Burrow on lack of offensive balance: My response is “throw it more” On a day when the running game clearly had issues and the team fell behind while also having troubles stopping the Jaguars, it made sense to let Burrow do his thing a bit more throwing the ball. Chase Brown also ended up with 11 receptions, and the team had several wide receiver screens to keep the defense on its toes. NFL News Jim Harbaugh backs Mike McDaniel after Chargers fall to 0-4: ‘His job is not in jeopardy’ The Los Angeles Chargers were expected to take a big step forward with McDaniel’s offense, but that hasn’t exactly transpired on their way to 0-4. This past week was their first time crossing 20 points in a game. Not a good look for the Justin Herbert truthers Jets end 20-game interceptionless streak with Minkah Fitzpatrick’s pick vs. Bears One of the crazier stats in the NFL was the Jets not having an interception since the 2024 season. Seems almost impossible with things like tipped balls and such. Yet here we are. Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson exits win over Titans early due to ankle injury Jackson left the stadium in a walking boot after the game. Things are sounding positive, but it is definitely worth monitoring as Baltimore goes as Jackson does.

title: Best available NFL free agent wide receivers the Bengals could target following injuries
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals came into their Week 4 game against the Jaguars boasting the best wide receiver duo in the NFL. They finished the game with both of those wide receivers injured and on the sidelines. Ja’Marr Chase was lost in the first half after a brutal helmet-to-helmet hit from linebacker Ventrell Miller while the […]
full_text: Sep 29, 2025; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Miami Dolphins wide receiver Tyreek Hill (10) practices before the game against the New York Jets at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rich Storry-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Cincinnati Bengals came into their Week 4 game against the Jaguars boasting the best wide receiver duo in the NFL. They finished the game with both of those wide receivers injured and on the sidelines. Ja’Marr Chase was lost in the first half after a brutal helmet-to-helmet hit from linebacker Ventrell Miller while the wide receiver’s facemask was being held by cornerback Jarrian Jones. Then, in the second half, Higgins was lost to an adductor injury. He tried to come back but eventually was forced to turn over his helmet. That left the Bengals with Dohnte Meyers and Mitchell Tinsley, who was signed off the Texans’ practice squad earlier this week. It’s currently unclear as to how much time Chase and Higgins will miss, if they miss any time at all, but the Bengals are going to at least need to kick the tires on bringing in help at the wide receiver position. If they do, they’re most likely to pluck someone from one of the league’s practice squads, but here’s who’s available if they decide to bring a free agent in. Curtis Samuel Samuel suffered an elbow injury that ended his 2025 season, but he has since recovered and is an unrestricted free agent after being cut from the Bills in March. The former second-round pick and Buckeye could find himself in need as injuries mount up this season. DeAndre Hopkins Hopkins is 34 years old, and he may be an assistant wide receivers coach for Georgia Tech, but he’s not retired. He played in 17 games for the Ravens in 2025. Even though he didn’t do too much with Baltimore, the future Hall of Fame wide receiver should still command enough respect that it could open things up for others. Zay Jones Jones suffered a torn Achilles in Week 10 of the 2025 season and was placed on IR, but has since recovered. He was signed by the Houston Texans before the 2026 season. He was cut in August and is still awaiting a phone call from a receiver-needy team. Tyreek Hill Hill has been around the league for a long time. He suffered a nasty knee injury in Week 4 of the 2025 season, and he’s not completely cleared for action, but his team is eyeing a possible November return. Considering the injury and the fact that he’s lost a step, this one’s not realistic. Trenton Irwin Hey, here’s a guy you may remember. Irwin was signed off the Dolphins’ practice squad in 2019 and stayed on the team until December of the 2024 season when he was waived. Since then, he bounced around the league. He was most recently with the 49ers, where he was cut at the end of August. Hopefully both Higgins and Chase don’t miss any time, and the Bengals won’t need to bring in any outside help at wide receiver. If they have to, though, who would you like them to sign? Would you take someone from this list or someone else not mentioned? Sound off!

full_text: The goodwill the Cincinnati Bengals bought with their 2-0 start has been wasted on the two losses that see them going into Week 5 with a 2-2 record. After such a great start to the season, the Bengals dropped a winnable game in Pittsburgh in Week 3 and then did everything they could to ensure they’d lose in Week 4. Now the Bengals travel to Miami to face the 0-4 Dolphins before they head into their Week 5 bye. According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Bengals are opening as 7.5-point favorites for their game in Hard Rock Stadium. The Bengals will definitely want to head into their bye week with a winning record because they travel to Baltimore for their first of two division games against the Ravens. The Bengals are definitely banged up as they head into Week 5. They came into Week 4 missing safeties Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger, and they came out of their loss to the Jaguars without wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase (concussion) and Tee Higgins (adductor). It’s currently unclear as to what the status of the best wide receiver duo in the league will be, but their impact on a defense can’t be overstated. full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals have lost largely because of their defense over the past couple of years. Against the Jacksonville Jaguars , that wasn’t the case, though, as the Bengals’ defense kept them in the game. The offense was what let down the team today, and it has a lot to do with Ja’Marr Chase going out early in the game. The wide receiver room, already missing Andrei Iosivas and rookie Colbie Young, became very thin with Chase being ruled out following a concussion. With that, Joe Burrow struggled, throwing multiple interceptions, and the Jaguars were able to key in on the run defense, keeping that entirely shut down. Burrow and the Bengals made a valiant effort, but were a yard short on offense. They will have to figure out an answer at wide receiver after finishing the day with only Dohnte Meyers and Mitch Tinsley still healthy. With that said, let’s take a look at the Twitter reactions to the Bengals’ loss. 4th and the ballgame, and you throw the ball 5 yards short of the sticks — Let Joe Cook (@burrow_time) October 4, 2026 Wow.
