title: Instant reaction: Broncos falter in Week 4 loss to 49ers
summary: The Denver Broncos battled the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday afternoon. It was a close matchup through three quarters, but eventually the 49ers were able to pull away and prevail 24-14 to deliver the Broncos their second loss of the season. Here are several instant reactions from this afternoon’s game. Once again, the Broncos show […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Santa Clara, California, USA; San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. (19) and Denver Broncos running back RJ Harvey (12) shake hands prior to a game at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Denver Broncos battled the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday afternoon. It was a close matchup through three quarters, but eventually the 49ers were able to pull away and prevail 24-14 to deliver the Broncos their second loss of the season. Here are several instant reactions from this afternoon’s game. Final. pic.twitter.com/MNUrCdkOAm — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) October 4, 2026 Once again, the Broncos show no dedication to the run early in games The 49ers entered this game giving up a lot of yards on the ground last week to the Arizona Cardinals. Despite being one of the best scoring defenses in the league, they have had issues stopping the run to start their season. This was one avenue I hoped the Broncos would try and exploit with their offensive game plan. Unfortunately, it didn’t appear that Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb took note of that during his weekly preparations. The Broncos ran the ball just nine times in the first half for 32 yards. Meanwhile, quarterback Bo Nix threw the ball 24 times and had just 14 completions for 93 yards. That’s far too unbalanced. This is simply inexcusable. While Denver was able to edge out the 49ers in the time of possession battle in the first half, not committing to the run on the road was yet another disastrous decision for Webb and the Broncos’ coaching staff. They waited until late in the fourth quarter on their late touchdown drive to do so. How many more weeks will it be before they realize establishing the run early is something you have to do in order to be a successful offense in the NFL? This continues to be absolutely baffling to me. Defense fought hard, but couldn’t hold of 49ers in second half I’ll give credit to the defense for playing hard for most of the game. They did a good job of limiting the 49ers opportunities in the first half. The only big issues for me were some missed tackles and failing to sack Brock Purdy. However, after thirty minutes of play, the Broncos held one of the league’s best offenses to just three points. I’d call that a success. Alas, with the offense failing to pull their weight and Marvin Mims Jr.’s fumble on a punt return in the second half, they had their backs up against trying to defend Kyle Shanahan’s offensive attack on short fields. As the game went on, the Broncos’ defense began to wear down. They never registered a sack on Purdy for the entire game. In the final minutes of the game, George Kittle cemented the 49ers victory with a big 56-yard catch-and-run for a touchdown. It was a great call by Shanahan, who dialed up the perfect play to combat Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph sending everything and the kitchen sink at Purdy to try and get the ball back. Injuries pile up for Broncos in loss to 49ers As if the result of the game wasn’t bad enough, the Broncos lost three key players due to injury Sunday afternoon against the 49ers. Their top-ranked cornerback duo of Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss exited the game late in the first half. I’m not too optimistic about the timetable for Surtain’s return. The defense will definitely struggle without him in the lineup. Hopefully neither is too serious, but I won’t hold my breath. Late in the third quarter, second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant was carted off the field after a leg injury on a chain-moving first down grab. An emerging player in the Broncos’ offense, Bryant’s made some big plays for them this season. It was officially ruled as an ankle injury. Without #13, the Broncos will have to turn to Mims Jr., Troy Franklin, and hope to get more out of Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton moving forward. I’ve been less than impressed with their aerial attack thus far and it just took a big hit with Bryant’s injury. At 2-2, the Broncos have a lot of work to do Quite honestly, there aren’t many positives to write about with respect today’s game. Three big injuries, terrible play on offense, too many penalties, and far too many mistakes across the board. It’s a surprise the game was as close as it was through three quarters. This team has a lot of soul-searching and work to do. I don’t want to think about worst-case scenarios, but if Surtain and Moss are out for an extended time period, there will be some growing pains on defense. So much of what Joseph is able to call and do is predicated on Surtain being able erase one side of the field with his coverage prowess. It’s been lacking through four weeks, but Denver needs its pass rush to step up more than ever moving forward. While I was critical of Webb’s lack of commitment to the run, the performance Denver had through the air was also troublesome. Far too many pre-snap penalties, way too many drops, and absolutely nothing was working over the middle of the field. For a third straight season, the offense is starting off slow, and the offensive line certainly didn’t pass the eye test versus the 49ers. This may have been one of their worst performances over the past few seasons.
author: Christopher Hart

title: Broncos played with fire one too many times; burned by 49ers in second half
summary: It would appear the injury bug doesn’t just affect the San Francisco 49ers, but also the teams that play in their stadium. The Denver Broncos lost three very integral part of their starting units in this game and two appear to be serious with Pat Surtain (ankle) and Pat Bryant (leg) exiting the game. Riley […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: RJ Harvey #12 of the Denver Broncos gets tackled by Upton Stout #20 and Dre Greenlaw #57 of the San Francisco 49ers in the first quarter at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It would appear the injury bug doesn’t just affect the San Francisco 49ers, but also the teams that play in their stadium. The Denver Broncos lost three very integral part of their starting units in this game and two appear to be serious with Pat Surtain (ankle) and Pat Bryant (leg) exiting the game. Riley Moss (ribs) also never returned after halftime. The injuries mounted and Brock Purdy and the 49ers began finding openings in the defense after those two starters exited. All it took was one very questionable call to turn the tide. A call that even non-Broncos fans considered highly suspect. Now we need to figure out where the forearm begins and the wrist ends… NFL rules are currently trying to tell you there's a difference between the wrist and the forearm, and that difference is the difference between a fumble or not. — Sam Monson (@SamMonsonNFL) October 4, 2026 It is what it is. They had their chances and couldn’t figure out a way to capitalize. At 2-2, they have a must-win game against the Los Angeles Chargers next week. Broncos vs. 49ers final score Team 1st 2nd 3rd 4th Final Denver Broncos 3 0 0 11 14 San Francisco 49ers 0 3 7 14 24 First Quarter Denver got the ball first and predictably went three-and-out. In fact, they didn’t even perform a run play until the seventh play of the game. Fortunately, the Broncos defense came to play and stymied Brock Purdy and the 49ers offense in that first quarter. The first big play came from Bo Nix and Tyler Badie who connected on third down to get their second drive going. Great play by Bo Nix and Tyler Badien for a 25 yard gain pic.twitter.com/fk5BRFto9v — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 4, 2026 They would get into field goal range, but a Mike McGlinchey holding penalty would knock them back and they’d settle for a 52-yard Wil Lutz field goal after struggling just get those 10 yards back. That would be the only score of the quarter by either team. Broncos 3, 49ers 0. Full first quarter recap . Second Quarter The story of the first half was how Denver’s offense couldn’t get out of his own way. The good news for the team is that the defense was handling the 49ers offense pretty well too. They’d pick up a field goal late to tie it up and had a chance to take a lead over the Broncos at the end of the half, but Zach Allen would block the field goal attempt. ZACH ALLEN BLOCKS THE FG ATTEMPT pic.twitter.com/cRlLCDymBp — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 4, 2026 The big story is that Pat Surtain II went down with a non-contact injury on that same drive. The non-contact nature of the injury is very concerning. Losing him for an period of time would be a devastating loss to both the defense and the entire team. Broncos 3, 49ers 3. Full second quarter recap . Third Quarter The entire third quarter was a bad dream for fans. First, this was called a fumble despite Marvin Mims’ forearm being clearly down. Marvin Mims's ENTIRE forearm is down and the ball is still in his possession. pic.twitter.com/989BYpHEiI — Swipa (@SwipaCam) October 4, 2026 That would give the 49ers the ball at the Broncos’ 28 yard line where they would convert it into a touchdown with both Riley Moss and Pat Surtain ruled out of this game with an injury. Then on the next drive for Denver they would be driving only to have Pat Bryant make a huge 30 yard catch and run suffer a serious injury and have to be carted off the field . The Broncos would be in field goal range when the quarter ended and would at least get that field goal attempt in early in the fourth quarter. 49ers 10, Broncos 3. Full third quarter recap . Fourth Quarter The tide had turned and the 49ers had the momentum to keep grinding away in the fourth quarter. They would get a few no-call holds while the Broncos stacked more and more penalties. It was what it was. I didn’t really expect Denver to win this game, but they had chances. Down 17-6 with just under nine minutes in the game, there would be no Bo Nix magic left in the tank after the last two weeks. They found their run game on the drive and ate up a lot of time with it, but a dart from Nix to Jaylen Waddle would put the Broncos on the board in the touchdown column with four minutes left in the game. JAYLEN WADDLE'S FIRST TOUCHDOWN AS A BRONCO!! pic.twitter.com/HtdlvOhYPp — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 4, 2026 The two-point conversion was successful to close the game to just three points. Denver sold out on defense to try to stop the run, and the 49ers called a screen to George Kittle who would house it to ice the game and the win for San Francisco. 49ers 24, Broncos 14.

Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 62 (83%) — 6 (20%) DT Tyleik Williams: 50 (67%) — 6 (20%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 32 (43%) — 6 (20%) — 1 offensive snap (1%) DL Levi Onwuzurike: 10 (13%) 3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP ( INACTIVE ) The Lions defensive line was the bright spot of the defense, and even they took a step back from previous week’s production. title: Detroit Lions grades: Defense is beyond embarrassing vs. Panthers
summary: The Detroit Lions fell to the Carolina Panthers 32-26 on Sunday night in a particularly disheartening game. The team does not look like it has evolved or improved from week to week. The offense, while still a clear strength, is dealing with bouts of self-inflicted mistakes, leading to consistenetly inconsistent play. The defense is a […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Carolina Panthers wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan (4) makes a catch defended by Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4) during the second quarter at Bank of America Stadium. McMillan scored a touchdown on the play. Mandatory Credit: Bob Donnan-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions fell to the Carolina Panthers 32-26 on Sunday night in a particularly disheartening game. The team does not look like it has evolved or improved from week to week. The offense, while still a clear strength, is dealing with bouts of self-inflicted mistakes, leading to consistenetly inconsistent play. The defense is a complete disaster with no end in sight. Here are my positional grades for the Lions’ Week 4 report card. Quarterback: B Jared Goff was fine for most of the night. There was obviously a lot of pressure on his shoulders for most of the second half with the Lions down two scores, and he kept them competitive with steady plays and a couple of deep shots. However, his operation on the final drive was a disaster. He can’t take a coverage sack, he can’t miss Sam LaPorta by five feet, and it wasn’t much help to throw short of the sticks on fourth down either. Unfortunately, Goff is in a position where he needs to play near-perfect ball to win the game, and on Sunday night, he didn’t. Running backs: C- Jahmyr Gibbs had his least effective game of the season, rushing for just 46 yards on 15 carries. He also had a critical drop on third down forced Detroit to settle for a field goal—something they just couldn’t afford to do in the middle of a shootout. Gibbs did find the end zone once, but he was more of a non-factor than expected against a Panthers defense that had struggled to stop the run. Wide receivers: B- Jameson Williams and Isaac TeSlaa had some huge plays in this game to help the Lions keep it close. However, Williams had a weird drop(?) early in the game, then had another critical drop that could’ve gotten the Lions out of a second-and-14 situation. It felt like a night of two steps forward, one step back for this unit. More good than bad, but some critical mistakes in critical moments. Tight ends: B Sam LaPorta was one of Detroit’s most potent weapons in this game, finishing with eight catches, 84 yards and a touchdown. Unfortunately, Brock Wright brings the unit’s grade down for his two penalties—a personal foul leg whip and a false start. Offensive line: C Pass protection was pretty solid, in general. Although, I thought the Lions could’ve handled blitzes a little better. What was more concerning was Detroit’s run blocking, which provided almost zero daylight for Gibbs. On top of that, the line was called for three false starts and two holding penalties (one declined). Defensive line: B Perhaps the most frustrating part of Sunday night’s defensive performance is that the defensive front didn’t let Bryce Young get comfortable all night. In total, they tallied 11 quarterback hits (all but one from the DL), three sacks, and a handful of TFLs. When it comes to the pass game, they held up their part of the bargain and more, but Bryce Young had the back seven in the palm of his hand. The Lions defense produced a 40.0% pressure rate (ninth best of the week) despite only blitzing 26.7% of the time (21st). Unfortunately, I can’t even give the defensive line an A because the run defense completely fell apart in the second half. In the final two quarters alone, the Panthers tallied 93 rushing yards on just 18 carries (5.2 YPC). Linebackers: F Young’s use of RPO concepts had the Lions’ linebacker room in a tizzy all night. Their zone discipline was a disaster, their tackling was not on point, and the amount of wide open field over the middle was significantly the fault of poor depth from the linebackers. Just look at how much Young attacked the middle of the field: Per @NextGenStats : Bryce Young’s 14 completions on in-breakers tied his career-high, and he totaled 160 yards and a touchdown on such throws. pic.twitter.com/7eOkEq6VxJ — John Ellis (@1PantherPlace) October 5, 2026 Detroit tried to switch up personnel again, using rookie Jimmy Rolder a few times early in the game before realizing he wasn’t ready. But no one else stepped up, either. Defensive backs: F When the Lions play zone, the safeties are too late to break on the ball and the corners aren’t playing disciplined ball. When the Lions play man-coverage, the cornerbacks are getting toasted. Detroit is shuffling through schemes, personnel, and trying several different things, but when it comes to the question: what does this Lions secondary do well? I’m afraid the answer right now is nothing. Special teams: B Jake Bates was a perfect 4-for-4 on field goals and 2-for-2 on extra points. He was also excellent on kickoffs, landing every single one of them inside the 8-yard line and none in the end zone. However, the Lions coverage and return units weren’t particularly good. Both Tom Kennedy and Jacob Saylors averaged less than 22 yards per kick return. Meanwhile, the Panthers averaged 25.5 on theirs. Coaching: F Let’s start with in-game management. Detroit had to burn a timeout early in the game after having too many men on the field. Then they burned a second timeout on a challenge that had little chance of succeeding. Late in the game, a delay of game (then false start) doomed a fourth down attempt. Not a terrible list of transgressions, but not great, either. No, the coaching gets an ‘F’ this week for preparation and game-planning. On defense, I don’t know if there’s anything left to say. The team is far, far, far less than the sum of their parts on that side of the ball, and that falls directly on Kelvin Sheppard’s shoulders. And what’s particularly concerning is that coach Dan Campbell openly admitted they weren’t prepared for all the RPO looks they got early. “To start the game, we didn’t do well enough in the coverage aspect. They had a couple of things in there, the RPOs that got us,” Campbell said. “They put your run-pass-hook defender in conflict there a little bit and he’s got such a quick release. That got us a little bit early.” Detroit’s adjustment there was far too late, and as Campbell then pointed out, once they settled that down, the run defense levee broke. By now, the Lions defense should have an identity, an area of strength, or some sort of “bread and butter” concept they can fall back on. Instead, Lions defenders look as lost as ever, and I can’t point to a single thing the back seven is doing well consistently. Then there’s the discipline on offense. Detroit racked up another nine penalties on Sunday night, most of which were of the pre-snap variety. Campbell took complete ownership of those mistakes after the game. “The bottom line is I’m not getting that across. I’m not getting it done right now because it’s still happening, so I put that squarely on my shoulders—that I’m not getting it coached properly,” Campbell said. “I’m the one who’s going to get this fixed. I’m the one who is going to fix this whole discipline thing, whatever it takes.” And if I can get a little nitpicky, offensive coordinator Drew Petzing deserves some heat for the final drive of the game. Detroit had plenty of time to mount a game-winning drive, but he got greedy. On second-and-7, Petzing dialed up a long-developing double-move to Jameson Williams—hoping to get a big chunk play. Instead, the Lions got the one thing they couldn’t afford: a sack. I know the Lions had hit on some deep shots earlier in the game, but that play reeked of desperation when they didn’t need to be in desperation mode. Detroit had plenty of time for some easier, shorter passes to methodically move down the field and get their late shots at the end zone.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit’s defense comes face-to-face with its ugly past selves
summary: The sports teams in the city of Detroit had a weekend. The Detroit Red Wings kicked things off on Friday, and before the season even started, the fans voiced their frustration with Dylan Larkin, mercilessly booing the former captain. Within five minutes of the puck dropping, the Hockeytown faithful summed up their thoughts on ownership […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches a play against Kansas City Chiefs next to defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard during the second half at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Sunday, Oct. 12, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The sports teams in the city of Detroit had a weekend . The Detroit Red Wings kicked things off on Friday, and before the season even started, the fans voiced their frustration with Dylan Larkin, mercilessly booing the former captain. Within five minutes of the puck dropping, the Hockeytown faithful summed up their thoughts on ownership in just three words . Less than 24 hours later, Simon Edvinsson, the team’s young and promising defenseman—think Year 2 Jack Campbell—informed the team he’d prefer to be traded than sign another contract. Signs sat outside on the porch of one condo on Woodward facing LCA: “Sell the team, Chris.” “Red Wings fans deserve better.” The scene in Detroit Sunday, when I went down there for the Red Wings game against the Winnipeg Jets, it reminded me of that era of Lions football. The “Millen Man March” in December of 2005 came after the Lions went an abysmal 20-57 over a stretch of football games from 2001 to 2005. It was the lowest of lows for Lions fans both young and old. “Sunday Night Football” was an opportunity to wipe away the bewilderment brought on by the 2026 Detroit Red Wings. Their season was over before it began because of poor direction from leadership. Here’s to hoping this 2026 Detroit Lions team doesn’t fall victim to the same pitfalls. Because point blank, Detroit needs to do something to improve their secondary. Additional help at safety and a cornerback could both be used back there, but it isn’t going to mean a single thing if the person pulling the levers and pushing the buttons wants to spam Cover 0. Carolina ran the RPO so effective because Bryce Young could identify the pressure and get the ball into the space the defender had vacated. The Panthers ran the football on the Lions: Chuba Hubbard averaged 6.1 yards per carry across 20 carries but had a long of just 32. Sunday night’s takeaway is that the leadership on the defensive ball needs to be better. It needs to be built to cater and accentuate the strengths of its current personnel, not who they want to be when they’re at “full health.” The former linebackers coach has got to get those guys back on track. Jack Campbell looks like he’s playing not to make a mistake—and in turn, making mistakes. The vibes are way off. This defense is historically bad through four games . Detroit has allowed the third-most points per game (31.8) in the last 40 years, only outdone by… the Lions in 2008 (32.3) and 2020 (32.4). It’s hard on a weekend like this to see this defensive performance and not think about some of the other dysfunctional moments when this defense was absolutely dreadful. To think this team could be 3-1, maybe even 4-0 if they had a defense that wouldn’t let a team score 21-unanswered points on three straight drives to start a game, it’s remarkable. Not world beaters. Not Brian Flores and what he’s doing with much, much less—they rank 28th in spending on defensive players in the NFL, and only one player makes north of $10 million (Andrew Van Ginkel). If Kelvin Sheppard could even get this defense to be slightly below average , it’d help me forget about the territory this defense is headed toward. And after missing out on Joey Porter Jr., is Brad Holmes going to keep checking in with teams ahead of November’s trade deadline? Do the Lions have that much time to wait around and see if Brian Branch makes the difference? What’s going to happen during that upcoming bye week after the team travels to the desert to play a beatable Arizona Cardinals team? Do the Lions have time to wait around and see if the defense can avoid being as porous as its been? Only two people could answer these questions, and they’re the two leaders of this football team in Holmes and Dan Campbell. It’s more than just cleaning up and fixing a few things here or there for Campbell. He isn’t worried about being 2-2 with a 17-game schedule, and he isn’t going into “panic mode,” but I’d be lying if I think Brian Branch is going to make all the difference. It’s going to take Holmes digging into his draft day bag and getting talent in the building. It’s going to take Campbell entrusting the right person to lead that defense. If that person is indeed Kelvin Sheppard, it better happen soon. Another performance like this against the Arizona Cardinals could have the boo birds fly back north for a long Week 6 of restlessness.
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Dan Campbell refuses to talk about Kelvin Sheppard’s job security
summary: The Detroit Lions are four games into the 2026 season, and the defensive performance is reaching historically bad levels. Through four games, the Lions have allowed a league-high 1,695 yards (423.75 per game)—which is the second-most the Lions have ever given up through Week 4. Their 127 points allowed (31.75 per game) is, again, league-high, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, left, shakes hands with Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young (9) after 32-26 loss to Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions are four games into the 2026 season, and the defensive performance is reaching historically bad levels. Through four games, the Lions have allowed a league-high 1,695 yards (423.75 per game)— which is the second-most the Lions have ever given up through Week 4 . Their 127 points allowed (31.75 per game) is, again, league-high, and it’s fourth-worst in franchise history . Naturally, the topic of firing defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has come up publicly. Given the perceived talent on the team and the pretty significant spending on that side of the ball , the performance of the defense has been less than acceptable. It’s been atrocious, particularly with a back-seven of the defense that leaves acres of open grass for the opposing quarterbacks to attack. After Sunday night’s 32-26 loss to the Carolina Panthers, Lions coach Dan Campbell was not ready to talk about the future of Sheppard’s employment. He was asked how many of these bad performances he needs to see before he considers a change at defensive coordinator. His answer: “Yeah, I’m not talking about all that, man,” Campbell said. “I’m talking about getting better right now with what we got, and that’s what we’re going to do. We’re going to find a way to get better with what we got.” No one should expect Campbell to talk publicly about the job security of someone on his coaching staff, particularly in the minutes after a particularly humiliating loss. And Campbell was at least cognizant enough to point out that significant changes need to be made on that side of the ball. Campbell said he believes they have players who can play. They just need to start putting them in better positions to win. “We’ve got guys on the back end that can cover. We’ve got guys that can hit. We got to pull this thing together and find the right combination of coverage versus pressure and job responsibility, putting guys in the right spot to do what they do,” Campbell said. “And so this is a work in progress. We’re four games in. There again, we just have to find a way to get better. I thought we would play better than we did last week, and as a whole, we didn’t.” But at the same time, Campbell warned about overreacting too early. The team is still 2-2 with everything in front of them. The last thing he wants to do is go into “panic mode” with 13 games left. And he believes there are still plenty of things the team can try to pull themselves out of this defensive rut. “There’s some things we can mix in here that we haven’t done a ton of this year, and that’s next step. Let’s see what we can do,” Campbell said. “I want to exhaust everything here. Let’s exhaust everything we have.” While Campbell didn’t say it, “exhausting everything they have” should certainly involve entertaining the idea of some coaching changes. Whether it means shifting responsibilities or making some tough staff decisions, the Lions truly need to have everything on the table, because they won’t go far with the worst defense in football.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions vs. Cardinals odds: Opening lines for Week 5 matchup
summary: The Detroit Lions (2-2) will stay on the road in Week 5, traveling to the desert to take on the Arizona Cardinals (1-3), and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -4.5 points. The Cardinals fired head coach Jonathan Gannon and his staff after the conclusion of the […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 22: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions looks to pass during an NFL football game between the Arizona Cardinals and the Detroit Lions at State Farm Stadium on September 22, 2024 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (2-2) will stay on the road in Week 5, traveling to the desert to take on the Arizona Cardinals (1-3), and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -4.5 points . The Cardinals fired head coach Jonathan Gannon and his staff after the conclusion of the 2025 season—creating an opportunity for the Lions to hire offensive coordinator Drew Petzing—and hired former Rams offensive coordinator Mike LaFleur (brother of Packers HC Matt LaFleur). LaFleur retained Nick Rallis as defensive coordinator, brought in veteran playcaller Nathaniel Hackett as offensive coordinator, and went to work overhauling the roster. The Cardinals kicked their offseason off by releasing QB Kyler Murray and promoting Jacoby Brissett to their starting role, then drafted RB Jeremiyah Love with the third overall pick and signed Tyler Allgeier to bolster their running backs room while James Conner recovers from a 2025 foot injury on injured reserve. Additionally, they also signed WR Kendrick Bourne, LG Isaac Seumalo, and RT Elijah Wilkinson to starting roles. On defense, they re-signed DT Roy Lopez (who spent last season in Detroit) and gave him a starting role, then added LB Jack Gibbens and S Andrew Wingard as additional starters. As with most new regimes, things have started off bumpy. While the Cardinals pulled off a Week 1 win, it was over the 0-4 Chargers, who have struggled all season. Since then, the Cardinals have given up at least 31 points in all three games, losing 31-7 to the Seahawks, 36-30 to the 49ers, and 36-24 to a Jameis Winston-led Giants this past Sunday. Against New York, it was a back-and-forth game that came down to the wire, as the Cardinals got themselves in position to win the game, but Brissett threw his third interception of the contest, a pick-six that put the game out of reach. With all the problems the Lions are having on the defensive side of the ball right now, they’ll likely need to continue the trend of putting up 31+ points against the Cardinals if they want to win this game. title: Discussion: Is the 2026 Detroit Lions defense fixable?
summary: If it weren’t for Ford Field being indoors, you could easily see the sky falling on the Detroit Lions. Although the team sits at 2-2 on the season, things feel far more grim. The Lions defensive ineptitudes once again stole the spotlight for the wrong reasons. Because the defense is struggling to stop any opponent, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard walks off the field after 32-26 loss to Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co If it weren’t for Ford Field being indoors, you could easily see the sky falling on the Detroit Lions. Although the team sits at 2-2 on the season, things feel far more grim. The Lions defensive ineptitudes once again stole the spotlight for the wrong reasons. Because the defense is struggling to stop any opponent, it is leading to the offense having to muster a perfect game. The Lions managed to stay alive against the New Orleans Saints in Week 1 and the New York Jets in Week 3, but things came crashing down against the Carolina Panthers. The Lions offense has some issues to work through, but not only is there a blueprint for success there, we have seen enough flashes through four weeks to instill some faith and confidence. The same cannot be said about the defense, a unit that has sunk the Lions early in the season. The question going forward is whether the Lions can bail their way out of this shipwreck, or if the defense will continue to drag them to the depths of the NFL. Today’s Question of the Day is: Is the 2026 Detroit Lions defense fixable? My answer: No. I want to be optimistic about the defense—I really do. Aidan Hutchinson is making an impact on every snap. Alim McNeill has rebounded phenomenally in 2026 and looks like the player that deserved a $97 million contract. Jack Campbell is coming off an All-Pro season. Tyleik Williams has taken a big step in his second season. D.J. Wonnum has been a solid addition to the defensive line. Derrick Barnes looks much-improved after a rough 2025 campaign. Brian Branch is seemingly close to returning . For all the faults in the secondary, the defense has enough pieces that it should at least look competent. We are not asking for the prime Baltimore Ravens or Seattle Seahawks that led their team to a Super Bowl. This Lions team could suffice with even an average or below-average defense. Instead, we are facing one of the worst starts to a season in history: Most points per game allowed in a season in the last 40 years: 2020 Lions – 32.4 2008 Lions – 32.3 2026 Lions – 31.8 (through 4 games) — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) October 5, 2026 The 2020 Lions team went 5-11 and was the dying corpse of the Matt Patricia era. The 2008 team was the infamous 0-16 team in contention for worst team in history. The fact that the 2026 Lions are meant to be in their Super Bowl window and are trotting out a defense like this is inexcusable. Worse yet, I think that the Lions have made their bed with the 2026 roster. They will live and likely die by their defense playing incapable football. No amount of in-season adjustments can fix it. I do not think that firing Kelvin Sheppard will solve the issue. Whether his replacement came from inside or outside the organization, the team would have to undergo a significant identity change within the span of a few weeks. This is something that can happen over the course of a training camp. I do not see this happening midseason, especially with an early Week 6 bye. One argument in favor of firing Sheppard is justifiable: it’s not like the Lions can get much worse, right? For how chaotic a midseason schematic change could be, the Lions clearly cannot continue with the status quo . However, I think too many things would have to go right to course correct the defense. At this point, there is no singular solution. Unfortunately, the Lions simply do not have time to correct most of their mistakes. Let us examine a best-case scenario. Not only do the Lions need Brian Branch to return to the lineup soon, but they would also need him to return at a high level—looking at McNeill’s 2025 campaign, you can see how that is far from guarantee. Perhaps even Kerby Joseph returns, although it presently feels like Santa Claus could return before Joseph. If the Lions do make a coaching change, that coordinator would have to overhaul a playbook months in the making in a matter of weeks, all while improving communication and execution. Finally, the Lions would have to add more talent to the secondary via trade, moves that would surely cost them capital and cap space and threaten their ability to restock in 2027—something that might be necessary at this rate. On top of all that, the Lions need the current roster to stay healthy. I am not trying to have a knee-jerk reaction, but four games is enough of a sample size to be concerned. For the Lions to turn around this defense, they need a lot to go in their favor.
author: John Whiticar

title: 5 winners, 5 losers from Detroit Lions’ loss to the Carolina Panthers
summary: For all of the Detroit Lions’ failures through three weeks, they were still 2-1 on the season. A date with the Carolina Panthers could have been an opportunity to win back-to-back games and, with the Arizona Cardinals on deck, potentially go into the bye week with positivity. Instead, the Lions looked like a kitten in […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions looks on during the first quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images For all of the Detroit Lions’ failures through three weeks, they were still 2-1 on the season. A date with the Carolina Panthers could have been an opportunity to win back-to-back games and, with the Arizona Cardinals on deck, potentially go into the bye week with positivity. Instead, the Lions looked like a kitten in this catfight. The Panthers were in control of this game from the start, and the final score of 32-26 does not illustrate Detroit’s struggles. The offense was failing with execution. The defense continues to be a calamity. From players to coaches, it was a failure for the entire Lions team. A team with playoff aspirations cannot put together many performances like these before a systematic change needs to happen. The Lions have yet to hit the iceberg, but it is visible in the horizon. Suddenly, next week’s game against the Cardinals looks daunting. Can this team even stop an offense like Arizona’s? Can the offense stop shooting themselves in the foot and actually dominate a game like they are capable of? Before we go too far into the future, let us examine the Winners and Losers from this Sunday night tilt. Note: The label of “loser” is used to evaluate and contrast in-game performance and is not an indictment of a player’s ability, value, or character. The term is not intended to be disrespectful in nature. Loser: Kelvin Sheppard, DC Patience with Sheppard is wearing thin. The Lions have personnel issues on defense, without question, but the growing thought in my mind is that this is a poorly coached unit more than anything else. In a game where the Panthers had essentially one weapon in the passing game, Tetairoa McMillan, that should make for an easier game plan, even with a depleted secondary. Instead, McMillan went off, totaling 193 yards on 14 catches and two touchdowns. Worse yet, the next-leading receiver for Carolina was John Metchie with just three catches for 37 yards. The Panthers, as expected, were feeding McMillan, yet the Lions defense continually had no answer for him. Bryce Young, meanwhile, was essentially perfect, going 29-of-41 for 329 yards and two touchdowns. The defensive line actually looked good on Sunday night, which makes the failures of the secondary and Sheppard an even tougher pill to swallow. If the Lions could cover for a split second longer, they would have had multiple impactful plays—sacks, pass breakups, perhaps even interceptions. Instead, the Lions were consistently getting beat within seconds of the snap. When the Lions were calling blitzes, they were ill-timed and forced the defensive backs into 1-on-1s that they promptly lost. Jeremy eloquently voices my frustration with the play calling: STOP SENDING COVER 0 BLITZES YOU DO NOT HAVE THE DEFENSIVE BACKS — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) October 5, 2026 To add insult to injury, the run defense fell apart in the second half. Chuba Hubbard ran wild down the stretch, finishing with 122 yards on the ground and a pair of touchdowns. The Lions linebackers and secondary were missing assignments frequently, giving lanes for Hubbard to coast through. A few misplays over the course of the game is expected. Constant misplays are an indictment of a poorly coached team. The Lions are not putting their players in positions to succeed, and they are naturally failing because of a lack of talent to overcome stacked odds. This teams incapability to stop explosive plays is mindboggling. I want the Lions to add a cornerback before the trade deadline, but that alone is not the solution to the secondary woes—it starts at the top with Sheppard. Loser: D.J. Reed, CB Failing to trade for Joey Porter Jr. could haunt the Lions if Reed continues to struggle. While Reed started off as a rare bright spot in the secondary, his play over the last two weeks has fallen off a cliff. McMillan in particular was giving Reed fits, outright bullying him with both size and speed. On McMillan’s 32-yard touchdown, Reed got burnt for an easy catch. He did not record a single pass breakup on the night—in fact, he was rarely in position to even make a play. Reed is simply not a CB1, yet the Lions are forced to rely on him to be their top dog. Loser: Dan Campbell, HC This was a sloppy, sloppy game. I have already gone over the defensive struggles, but the Lions were struggling with fundamentals in every aspect. The offense tried its best to play catch up, but too many instances of self-inflicted wounds neutered any chance of a comeback. Early on, the Lions had to burn a timeout because they were missing a player on a field goal attempt (an attempt that was thankfully converted). I was okay with his challenge of a potential catch-fumble-touchdown that was not overturned, but Detroit looked discombobulated on a fair number of snaps, either racing to beat the play clock or running players on and off the field. The worst example of poor execution came late in the game. On fourth-and-10 with the game essentially on the line, the Lions got called for a delay of game despite holding three timeouts. On the subsequent fourth-and-15, the Lions got called for false start. On the ensuing fourth-and-20, the Lions tried to run a hook and ladder that only managed 13 yards. My frustration really boils down to one thing: I am tired of the Lions needing to fix things. It has sadly been a common comment after Lions games that they have a few things to clean up. We are in Week 4 of the 2026 season. The Lions have had things to clean up since 2023. After a certain point, that line means nothing. Winners: Alim McNeill and Aidan Hutchinson, DL For as bad as the Lions secondary was, their work in the trenches was impressive. No players stood out as much as McNeill and Hutchinson. McNeill was a menace up the interior, recording two tackles for loss and numerous pressures. He turned one of those into a 10-yard sack of a backpedaling Young. As for Hutchinson, he was his usual game-wrecking self, even if a sack eluded him. What he lacked in sacks he brought in pressure, many of which came on his patented spin move. If anything, the Lions could have had at least three more sacks if the coverage could have held for even a second. The Lions were bringing pressure up front but Carolina was countering with quick hits all night long. The front seven is doing its part to attack the passing game. Loser: Brock Wright, TE Wright had a pair of brutal penalties, an inexcusable performance for a backup tight end. The first drive was stalled by a false start penalty on Wright on first down, which eventually led to a 54-yard Jake Bates field goal. His second was an unnecessary roughness call that set the team back 15 yards, although he was promptly bailed out by a massive 57-yard shot to Isaac TeSlaa. Considering that Wright is neither shining as a blocker or receiver, these types of mistakes stand out for wrong reasons. Winner: Isaac TeSlaa, WR Jameson Williams finished as the leading receiver, but a couple of drops keep him off the winners list. Instead, I will give a nod to TeSlaa, who has returned to relevance after a quiet start to the season. He only added four catches on the night, but one of which was a 57-yarder that set up the Lions deep in Panthers’ territory (a drive that stalled for a field goal, unfortunately). That led to his receiving total of 95 yards, a career-high. He can be a big-play receiver like Williams when called upon, even if those instances are somewhat limited. Given the Lions red zone woes this season, I would like to see him more involved—we know he can use his size to make acrobatic catches. Winner: Sam LaPorta, TE With LaPorta’s contract extension talks stagnating , he is proving why the Lions need to pay him. LaPorta was vacuuming up…
author: John Whiticar

title: 7 takeaways from Detroit Lions’ 32-26 loss against Carolina Panthers
summary: After waiting all day for “Sunday Night Football,” the Detroit Lions took on and lost to the Carolina Panthers 32-26. These games are always worse when you wait all day for your team to put out a difficult performance. Detroit falls to 2-2 and faces a whole lot of questions after just a month of […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Chuba Hubbard #30 of the Carolina Panthers runs for a first quarter touchdown against the Detroit Lions at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images After waiting all day for “Sunday Night Football,” the Detroit Lions took on and lost to the Carolina Panthers 32-26. These games are always worse when you wait all day for your team to put out a difficult performance. Detroit falls to 2-2 and faces a whole lot of questions after just a month of football. Here are my seven takeaways from the Lions’ Week 4 loss to the Panthers. Detroit’s (lack of) discipline is disturbing Penalties have been a problem for the Lions this season, mostly on offense, as they continue to kill successful drives. Of the nine penalties Detroit was called for, seven were on offense. While the defense struggles to make a stop, the offense backs things up and makes life harder on itself. The defense had an almost clean game with only one penalty, and special teams took one for a better punt opportunity, but the offense can’t seem to get out of its own way. With the defense playing as poorly as they have, the offense can’t make life harder for themselves and go backward. I get the offense shouldn’t be expected to play perfect, but some of these are simple and come at the worst time. On the drive with just over seven minutes left in the fourth quarter on fourth-and-10, Detroit got called for a delay of game and false start penalty. So now, down by 13 and needing a touchdown, it takes 20 yards to move the chains and keep hope alive. Detroit failed on that attempt on a hook-and-ladder play. If neither, or maybe only one, of those penalties are called, Detroit has a better chance at getting a first down and scoring. Same stuff, different week for the Lions secondary It’s not a good thing when Panthers quarterback Bryce Young starts the game 11-for-11, the most consecutive completions to start a game in his career. The Panthers were without their leading receiver, Jalen Coker, and their third wide receiver, Xavier Legettue. Despite being down two of the three starters, Young and the passing game had their way with the Lions’ secondary. Young was on fire, finding wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan for 14 catches, 192 yards, and two touchdowns. Detroit’s secondary couldn’t keep up as Young threw for 329 yards, with a 70.7 percent completion percentage. The RPO and quick passing game killed them over and over again. I’m not sure the return of safety Brian Branch will fix all the secondary woes, since he won’t instantly play every snap or be the same player right away. It will take a few weeks for him to return as a full-time starter, so if the Lions stand pat and think he’ll be the saving grace, it could be another rough season for the defense. The trade deadline is November 10, so time’s ticking. At least the tight ends were slowed down While the Panthers receivers had their way, the tight ends weren’t as dangerous as expected. Tommy Tremble had four catches for 12 yards, while Darren Waller was the better tight end with three catches for 36 yards, and even third-string Mitchell Evans caught one for 8 yards. The Lions were struggling against tight ends entering Sunday night, so not having them be a factor helped the defense. Detroit better take this good film against the tight ends and prepare for Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride next week. Gibbs not used as much as he should have been Entering the game, the Panthers’ run defense ranked dead last in yards allowed and yards per carry allowed, and tied for most touchdowns allowed. So, Detroit ran the ball a lot, right? How about 15 carries while throwing the ball 52 times? Sure, the Panthers’ secondary is missing both starting cornerbacks, but how do you not attack the run more? The game was a shootout, and with Detroit trailing by double digits in the second half, I understand why you have to ease up on the running game, but abandoning it completely just didn’t feel right. Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs is one of the best running backs in the NFL; he needs to be used more. While the offense didn’t do itself any favors with some drives stalling due to penalties, it seemed to want to focus more on the passing attack in the end. I get why, but when you have someone as good as Gibbs, you can’t put him on the shelf. Goff threw for over 400 yards and in the end, it wasn’t enough. Chuba Hubbard has Detroit’s number It seems some players have the best games of their careers against Detroit. Panthers running back Chuba Hubbard is one of them. He ran for 125 yards against Detroit in 2022, his third-best game ever. On Sunday night, Hubbard ran for 122 yards, the fourth-best game of his career, scoring twice and averaging 6.1 yards per carry. Hubbard is a solid running back, but it’s troubling that he keeps having these types of games against the Lions, who are known for stopping the run. The secondary is already dealing with problems, so if teams can run and throw on Detroit, every game is about to be a shootout. When do changes happen for the defense? The team is a week away from the bye week; do they wait until then to address anything, or should they be aggressive and make changes immediately? I think if you sign or trade for a player, you do it as soon as possible. That gives them a week to learn a few things and a bye week to study and prepare for more playing time. For coaching, I say you make those changes at the bye week. There’s no point in changing everything a week before you have a week off, and players gotta come back trying to remember what changed. I think it’d be better to present the team with new changes post-bye week to show what is going to change and start fresh. Does someone need to be fired? Maybe. Who? I couldn’t tell you, but I don’t think firing defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard instantly fixes all the woes this defense has. I think it’s too early to make such a drastic change, and Lions coach Dan Campbell has never fired a coordinator midseason. Could Sheppard lose defensive playcalling duties? Possibly, but I don’t know who would get the nod to take over that part of his job, as Campbell is more of an offensive mind. That kind of shift could also hurt the culture and the locker room, so whatever needs to happen needs to be done carefully. Shoutout Jake Bates While the Lions offense couldn’t find the end zone often, kicker Jake Bates did his job when asked to. He made all four field goals, including the longest from 54 yards out, and made his extra point attempt. Unlike Carolina, Detroit doesn’t have that problem.
author: Brandon Knapp

title: Lions vs. Panthers recap: Detroit can’t overcome defensive disaster, lose 32-26
summary: The Detroit Lions defensive problems are starting to reach a fever pitch. In Week 4 against the Carolina Panthers, they allowed nearly 450 yards of offense and six straight scoring drives, including four touchdowns. While the defense did come up with a couple of fourth quarter stops to give the offense a chance to make […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Tetairoa McMillan #4 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates a second quarter touchdown against the Detroit Lions at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions defensive problems are starting to reach a fever pitch. In Week 4 against the Carolina Panthers, they allowed nearly 450 yards of offense and six straight scoring drives, including four touchdowns. While the defense did come up with a couple of fourth quarter stops to give the offense a chance to make a miraculous comeback, it was too late and the Lions were out of gas. Detroit’s defensive problems have not been even close to fixed through four games, and the pressure is starting to mount on defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. Time is running out to fix that side of the ball, or at least show signs of progress. Detroit ultimately fell 32-26 to the Panthers, dropping their overall record to 2-2. Here’s how the game played out. First quarter The Panthers won the toss and deferred, putting the Lions offense up first. Detroit’s offense finally came out looking strong, with gains of 7 to Jahmyr Gibbs, 6 to Jameson Williams, and 18 for Amon-Ra St. Brown. That man strong @amonra_stbrown pic.twitter.com/mNGKWLNyUP — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 5, 2026 But after a false start on Brock Wright, the Lions fell behind the sticks. On third-and-12, Jared Goff turfed it under pressure. Jake Bates drilled a 54-yard field goal to take an early 3-0 Lions lead. The Lions defense forced a third-and-9 after a nice tackle for loss by rookie Jimmy Rolder. However, Bryce Young found Tetairoa McMillan, who broke a tackle attempt from Jack Campbell to gain 10 yards and a first down. Carolina quickly faced another third down—third-and-2—but this time Detroit got off the field thanks to Alim McNeill’s bull rush-turned-sack. Bully ball @AlimMcneill pic.twitter.com/Gx172krR6P — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 5, 2026 The Lions offense tried to build on their lead, starting at their own 11-yard line. However, they couldn’t overcome another penalty. After a first-down hold from Juice Scruggs, Detroit went three-and-out thanks to a missed deep shot to Williams that just barely missed the Lions receiver. The Panthers methodically drove down the field to take the lead. Carolina, using a lot of RPO concepts, dinked and dunked their way down the field, until Young found a wide-open McMillen for 21 yards. Young ➡️ McMillan for 22 and the Panthers enter the red zone @DETvsCAR on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/RSOboBCcJ8 — NFL (@NFL) October 5, 2026 On the next play, Chuba Hubbard took a toss play for a 16-yard touchdown. 7-3 Panthers. Primetime tuddy ‼️ 📺 NBC #DETvsCAR pic.twitter.com/nW9xo45AZU — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) October 5, 2026 The Lions looked to respond, and an 11-yard pass to Sam LaPorta with a roughing the passer call tacked on pushed Detroit to midfield almost immediately. A 4-yard run from Gibbs closed out the first quarter. Second quarter A Gibbs 13-yard run got the Lions into field goal range, but the Lions running back dropped a third-and-7 conversion after absorbing a big hit. Detroit challenged the play, but the call was upheld, and Detroit had to settle for a 43-yard field goal attempt. 7-6 Panthers. For the second time, the Lions defense forced an initial third-and-9, and for the second time, the Lions blew it. An Alim McNeill tackle for loss set up the play, but Detroit’s blitz on third down didn’t get home and Young found a wide-open McMillan for a 26-yard gain. Another 25 yards for Tetairoa McMillan! @DETvsCAR on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/T1KePyLdzP — NFL (@NFL) October 5, 2026 Detroit did get a third-down stop, however, the Panthers opted to go for it on fourth-and-4, and they converted on a pass to John Metchie. Two plays later, Young connected with McMillan—who beat D.J. Reed for a 32-yard touchdown. The extra point was missed. 13-6 Panthers. Beautiful ball 📺 NBC #DETvsCAR pic.twitter.com/8zCzIdhA6s — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) October 5, 2026 Detroit managed to avoid a three-and-out, with Goff finding Sione Vaki for 17 yards on a third-and-10. Williams managed to keep the drive alive with an 8-yard catch on third-and-5. Then Goff found St. Brown for another 14. Now in the red zone, the Lions faced a critical third-and-3. Goff checked at the line and tossed a wideout screen to Williams for an 11-yard gain and a first-and-goal situation. A pass interference against the Panthers put Detroit at the 1-yard line. From there, Gibbs rushed it in, and the Lions tied it with 2:14 left in the half. 13-13 tie. Sonic Six @DETvsCAR on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/gyQoW2PuRC — NFL (@NFL) October 5, 2026 Carolina was able to take the lead before the end of the half. They were gifted a no-call on a very obvious intentional grounding, but Detroit was at least able to keep the Panthers out of the end zone with three straight forced incompletions. Ryan Fitzgerald drilled a 47-yard attempt to give the Panthers a 16-13 lead with 28 seconds left. That turned out to be too much time, because Goff hit Williams for a 49-yard bomb on the very first play of the drive. Go get it, Waymo pic.twitter.com/Sq11q0qoS0 — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 5, 2026 Detroit tried to take a couple shots in the end zone, but ultimately just settled for a 41-yard field goal attempt, and Bates tied it up. 16-16 tie. Third quarter The Panthers got the ball first and went right back to work against a Lions defense that had no answers. They converted a third-and-1 with a run, then converted a third-and-2 with an easy wide receiver screen to Metchie. A pass interference on McCreary pushed the Panthers into field goal range. An 11-yard pass to Darren Waller set Carolina up in the red zone. Then McMillan continued his ridiculous night by juking Christian Izien out of his shoes for a 10-yard touchdown (and another missed extra point). 22-16 Panthers. TMAC x2 📺 NBC #DETvsCAR pic.twitter.com/PMH5eRpusE — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) October 5, 2026 Detroit appeared to be in trouble after a personal foul penalty on Brock Wright, however Goff was able to connect on another bomb. This time, Isaac TeSlaa got behind the Panthers secondary for a 57-yard gain. TESLAAAAAA pic.twitter.com/M6v5FVisdI — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 5, 2026 Unfortunately, Detroit was stopped in the red zone when Goff’s third-down pass was batted down at the line of scrimmage. The Lions opted to kick the field goal and make it a three-point game. 22-19 Panthers. A special teams penalty put the Panthers deep in their own zone—their own 15-yard line—but it didn’t matter this night. Young completed passes to Darren Waller for 16, then Brycen Tremayne for 22, then Metchie for 18 yards. Then the run defense fell apart and allowed Hubbard to get 25 yards down to the 2-yard line. Chuba takes off 💨 📺 NBC #DETvsCAR pic.twitter.com/FFrqGN6jiw — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) October 5, 2026 Then Hubbard plunged in for the score. 29-19 Panthers. Chuba bulldozes his way in 📺 NBC #DETvsCAR pic.twitter.com/bmmWJU1a2t — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) October 5, 2026 The Lions offense tried to keep the game from spiraling out of control. Completions to Williams (14) and St. Brown (19) moved them comfortably into Panthers territory, but they faced a second-and-14 after a false start from Blake Miller. Fourth quarter Williams dropped a potential first down on the first play of the final quarter, setting up a third-and-14. Goff’s next throw was too high for St. Brown, and Detroit punted. The Panthers took over, having scored points on five consecutive drives, and put the game away. They started on their own 14-yard line, but on the very first play, Hubbard reversed field and picked up 31 yards. Chuba Hubbard breaks free for 31 yards! @DETvsCAR on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus…

full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - NOVEMBER 06: An aerial view of Bank of America Stadium and the downtown Charlotte skyline ahead of the NFL game between the New England Patriots and Carolina Panthers on November 6, 2021 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Lance King/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions look to keep pace with a competitive NFC North in Week 4 by facing off against the Carolina Panthers on “Sunday Night Football.” The Lions have looked a little uneven through the first three weeks of the season. While the offense has been pretty solid, producing 31 points in each game, the defense has been extremely worrisome. They got blown out by the Bills offense, and the defensive struggles allowed both the Saints and Jets to climb back into a game, despite the fact that they were trailing by two scores in the fourth quarter. The Panthers could prove to be a significant challenge to Detroit’s defense. Bryce Young and the Panthers are averaging 29.7 points per game and have one of the most aggressive passing attacks in football. Against Detroit’s struggling secondary, that could be a mismatch, even with Carolina receiver Jalen Coker likely out for this game. That said, it’s also a mismatch in favor of Detroit’s offense. The Panthers are allowing 27.7 points per game (26th), and they currently hold the worst rushing defense in football by yards per game and yards per carry. Could this be another week in which Jahmyr Gibbs eats? Come watch with us to find out. This page will be our live game chat for all four quarters of the game. title: The Packers’ easy portion of the schedule is over
summary: According to ESPN’s Football Power Index, which has now been updated for Week 4’s action, the Green Bay Packers have played the 31st schedule in the NFL through four games — the second-easiest schedule in the league so far, only behind the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Moving forward, they’ll have the second-hardest schedule in the […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Football Power Index , which has now been updated for Week 4’s action, the Green Bay Packers have played the 31st schedule in the NFL through four games — the second-easiest schedule in the league so far, only behind the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Moving forward, they’ll have the second-hardest schedule in the league from Weeks 5 to 18 — per FPI. Here is how ESPN explains FPI: The Football Power Index (FPI) is a measure of team strength that is meant to be the best predictor of a team’s performance going forward for the rest of the season. FPI represents how many points above or below average a team is. Projected results are based on 10,000 simulations of the rest of the season using FPI, results to date, and the remaining schedule. Ratings and projections update daily. Below are the games the Packers have played so far: Week 1: @ MIN (4-0) Week 2: @ NYJ (1-3) Week 3: vs. ATL (1-2) Week 4: @ TB (0-4) The only team with a winning record that they’ve played so far is Minnesota, the first NFL team to start 4-0 without scoring a touchdown in two of those games since the 1934 Detroit Lions. (With that being said, I do think the Jets are a little underrated , and there was a noticeable difference for the Falcons when Michael Penix Jr. was under center for the team.) Moving forward, here is the Packers’ schedule: Week 5: vs. CHI (3-1) Week 6: vs. DAL (2-2) Week 7: @ DET (2-2) Week 8: vs. CAR (2-2) Week 9: @ NE (2-2) Week 10: vs. MIN (4-0) Week 11: BYE week Week 12: @ LAR (2-2) Week 13: @ NO (1-2) Week 14: vs. BUF (3-1) Week 15: vs. MIA (0-4) Week 16: @ CHI (3-1) Week 17: vs. HOU (0-4) Week 18: vs. DET (2-2) The only sub-.500 teams left on the Packers’ schedule right now are the Saints in Week 13 (New Orleans hasn’t played in Week 4, and could be 2-2 by the end of Monday’s action), the Dolphins in Week 14 and the Texans in Week 17. For perspective, 0-4 Houston has been able to keep games closer this year, as they have a -25 point differential compared to the 2-2 Packers’ -32 point differential. The Saints only have a -2 point differential, despite being 1-2. The only team left on Green Bay’s schedule with a worse point differential than the Packers is the 0-4 Dolphins, who have by far the worst mark in the league at -55. We all knew the Packers got a good break to start the season coming in, considering their injury situation. What we didn’t fully see was the team going just 2-2 to start the year and suffering four season-ending injuries in the first four weeks of 2026. Green Bay needs to buckle down for the rest of the regular season, as the schedule difficulty is only going to get tougher.
