title: 4 things we learned from the Giants’ 36-24 victory over the Cardinals
summary: Your NFC East-leading New York Giants defeated the Arizona Cardinals 36-24 Sunday in a game that was much closer (to say the least) than that final score indicates. This game had a lot of the things we fear and that we hope for from this team. Let’s talk about a few of them. Dennard Wilson […]
full_text: Tyler Nubin and Tae Banks celebrate after Sunday’s game. | Getty Images Your NFC East-leading New York Giants defeated the Arizona Cardinals 36-24 Sunday in a game that was much closer (to say the least) than that final score indicates. This game had a lot of the things we fear and that we hope for from this team. Let’s talk about a few of them. Dennard Wilson finally decides to be aggressive – and it pays off Wilson came to the Giants with a reputation as a defensive coordinator who likes to force the action, the polar opposite of the passive Shane Bowen. Through three games, we didn’t see much evidence of that. Wilson’s defense only broke up five passes in the Giants’ first three games. Well Sunday, things changed…a lot. Jacoby Brissett was slicing and dicing (h/t Walt Frazier) the Giants’ defense in the first quarter, and it looked like things might get out of hand in a hurry when the score got to 14-3 before the first quarter was edone. Then Dennard finally started being aggressive. All told, he wound up blitzing on 20 of 39 Brissett dropbacks. Not Brian Flores-level blitzing, but still a lot. Brissett was only 5 of 17 on those dropbacks for 43 yards. When not blitzed he was 16 of 18 for 123 yards. After that first quarter, the Cardinals only had 10 points the rest of the game. The defense broke up 6 passes today, one more than in the first three games combined. Jameis Winston + Matt Nagy = oil + water Last season, when Jaxson Dart went down with a concussion, Jameis Winston took over and the Giants’ offense, though different in nature without the threat of Dart’s legs, didn’t miss a beat. In the two games Dart played before being injured, he threw for 433 yards and two touchdowns. In Winston’s two starts, against Green Bay and Detroit, he threw for 567 yards and two touchdowns. Yes, Jameis comes inevitably with interceptions, but the offense didn’t look noticeably worse or awkward with Winston at the helm other than the absence of the threat of QB runs. This season so far is a completely different story. Winston appears very uncomfortable in the Nagy et al. offense. He’s hesitating after dropping back, bailing the pocket at a moment’s notice. Sunday we saw both good and bad Jameis, with three TD passes and 250 yards but also two interceptions and four sacks. Winston just looks unsure when he drops back in this offense. And maybe with good cause. Obviously the Giants want to run more this year than when Brian Daboll and Mike Kafka were designing the offense, no surprise there. The question, now that Winston is the starter, is whether Nagy can design an offense that will click against the better defenses the Giants will see down the line, or whether his starting days are numbered once J.J. McCarthy gets up to speed. Is Deonte Banks’ career being resurrected? During training camp we heard the coaching staff say nice things about Deonte Banks. I for one took those with a grain of salt and agonized about what the Giants’ pass coverage would look like with Cor’Dale Flott gone and no obvious immediate replacement on the roster. Yes, the Giants signed Greg Newsome (who gave up six receptions Sunday but did have an interception) and drafted Colton Hood (who, to my knowledge, did not see the field Sunday), but none of that gave me faith. Fast forward to Week 4, and we’re seeing something that gives me hope. Banks didn’t look bad in the opener against Dallas and then missed the next two games. Today, though, he was one of the players of the game. The Cardinals picked on him, targeting him eight times. He gave up three completions, for 19 yards, but he had responsibility on two of Arizona’s touchdowns. He came up big late in the game, though. With the Cardinals knocking on the door at the end of the game seeking the winning score, Banks made two consecutive great plays, first getting a hand in to break up the potential winning TD to Trey McBride, and then stepping in front of Michael Wilson for a pick-6 to end the game. I’m not ready to say that Banks will ever justify his first-round pedigree, but he looks like he might finally become the viable cornerback that we saw glimpses of in his rookie year. Speaking of first round picks… It is not taking Arvell Reese long to adjust to playing football at the NFL level. He was a monster on Sunday: nine solo tackles (five of them stops), three passes defensed, and an interception, plus a hit on Brissett. Wilson had Reese rush the passer 13 times, about twice as often as he had in his first three games. He was targeted six times and gave up 6six completions, but only for 36 total yards. He really seems to be the total package as a defensive player, a chess piece Wilson can move all around the board. Meanwhile, the Giants’ other recent top five draft pick, Abdul Carter, is starting to make noise. He pressured Brissett nine times: Without Brian Burns in the lineup against the Cardinals, Abdul Carter led the Giants with nine pressures, including eight coming in less than 2.5 seconds. No other Giants pass rusher had more than two pressures on the day. #AZvsNYG | #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/Q0rNXiMXwT — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) October 4, 2026 As you can see, Wilson lined him up all over the place, both sides, inside and outside, and he got pressures no matter where he lined up. And finally, welcome back, Malik Nabers! Six targets, six receptions, 112 yards and his first TD of the season. This is the first time since his injury that Nabers looked to my eye as if he wasn’t thinking about it anymore. Maybe Nagy will finally start pushing the ball downfield more often. Honorable mention I’m only supposed to get four things for this post, but I would be remiss not to once again mention kicker Dominic Zvada (3 for 3 field goals today and 9 of 9 for the season) and punter Jordan Stout (3 punts, 48.7 yard-average, 2 inside the 20). The Giants’ special teams are finally special.
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: Giants 36, Cardinals 24: Instant position-by-position grades
summary: The New York Giants won one of the sloppiest — yet exciting — games against the Arizona Cardinals, 36-24, with a walk-off Tae Banks pick-six. The Giants’ defense clamped down in the second half, and Jameis Winston had a roller coaster performance with more lows than highs. Nevertheless, the Giants went 7 of 15 on […]
full_text: Arvell Reese (52) had a monster game for the Giants on Sunday against the Cardinals. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants won one of the sloppiest — yet exciting — games against the Arizona Cardinals, 36-24, with a walk-off Tae Banks pick-six. The Giants’ defense clamped down in the second half, and Jameis Winston had a roller coaster performance with more lows than highs. Nevertheless, the Giants went 7 of 15 on third down and outgained Arizona, 270-219 yards. The Giants are now 3-1; here are the immediate grades. Quarterback It was the Jameis Winston roller coaster. He struggled mightily through most of the game. He held onto the ball, threw recklessly, was late, missed, and looked uncomfortable in the pocket. Winston was flat-out bad for much of the first half, but he made an excellent extended play on third-and-4, which led to Malachi Fields’ first touchdown. He then capitalized on Arvell Reese’s interception and found Malik Nabers for a touchdown up the seam in the red zone. Winston threw an interception with less than a minute to go in the first half, which stifled New York’s momentum; Denzel Burke did an excellent job switching leverage pre- to post-snap, and Winston threw it right into his numbers, targeting Malachi Fields on a dig. He then threw an interception to Budda Baker to start the second half. Winston finished the game 18 of 29 for 250 yards, three touchdowns, and a pair of interceptions. He was sacked four times. At least the red zone offense improved. We still need more from Winston, or we may see J.J. McCarthy sooner rather than later. Grade: C – Running back We saw more Najee Harris early in the game, as the Giants attempted to establish the run to move the football, since Winston struggled with most aspects of playing quarterback. The rotation was fine, although neither was doing much on the ground, until Harris fumbled the football early in the fourth quarter. Neither running back was efficient in the game. The Giants averaged a measly 3.1 yards per carry. Cam Skattebo had 18 rushes for 58 yards, and Harris had nine carries for 30 yards with a costly fumble. The split was even until the fumble — we did not see Harris after he put the ball on the ground. Overall, the Giants received little from their rushing attack. Grade: C – Wide receiver Malik Nabers secured a 39-yard catch on the Giants’ first drive to put New York into field goal range; he suffered a shoulder scare, but returned to the game. Nabers caught the go-ahead touchdown, splitting Cover-2 after Arvell Reese’s interception. Nabers caught six passes for 112 yards with a touchdown on seven targets. Malachi Fields scored his first NFL touchdown on third-and-4 and bailed the Giants out of a third-and-twenty after the Cardinals’ rookie safety blew a Cover-2 assignment. He finished with two important catches for 53 yards on three targets. Darnell Mooney was missed a few times by Jameis Winston; he got the football to Mooney over the middle of the field on third down, but Budda Baker nailed the receiver, and the ball was not secured. Mooney did not record a catch; still, Nabers and Fields made MASSIVE third-down plays that helped the Giants secure the win. Grade: A Tight end Both Isaiah Likely and Theo Johnson did their part in Week 4. Likely caught seven of twelve targets for 66 yards, and Theo Johnson caught his one target for 11 yards and a touchdown. The group blocked adequately but not great, and both tight ends did enough when their numbers were called. Grade: A – Offensive line Jameis Winston was under pressure against a defense that struggled to generate it, but much of the pressure came from Winston holding onto the football too long. Francis Mauigoa had a miscommunication on the back side of a third-and-two Skattebo run that was blown up in the red zone. Overall, the blocking was not great up front in the run game, albeit Arizona was loading up the line of scrimmage and crashing hard on the run. The pass protection wasn’t perfect, either, but Winston did not help the line out at all. Grade: C Defensive line The Giants’ run defense on the inside was solid – the outside is a COMPLETELY different story. The defensive line had several STOPs near the line of scrimmage against inside runs. Shelby Harris had a key PBU that led to Reese’s interception, and C.J. Okoye got a big sack on a heavy blitz by Dennard Wilson. Overall, the defensive line played very well up front. Grade: A Edge The Cardinals SLICED and DICED the Giants with their rushing attack on their first two drvies. Mike Lafleur certainly watched the tape and saw how vulnerable the Giants were against outside runs over the last two weeks. Lafleur pulled, and the Giants had no answers – this isn’t just an edge problem, but they’re tasked with setting the initial defense, albeit crack-toss was a big strategy, and the rest of the defense was not in position to fit the run. Terrible run defense to start. The defense, however, stabilized. They shut down the runs to the outside, and they got consistent second-half pressure, as Dennard Wilson dialed up the blitz. Abdul Carter took over the game in the second half, and he was an absolute menace for the Cardinals. Overall, the edge group was carried by Carter’s performance, but it was VERY impactful. Grade: B + Linebacker Arvell Reese — wow! The linebackers were picked on early in this game. They were late to fit the outside runs; they weren’t gaining depth in their zone drops. However, the linebackers changed the Giants’ fortunes in the second quarter; Tremaine Edmunds blew up a Tre McBride screen, and then Arvell Reese hit Brissett’s arm, leading to the Newsome II interception. Reese then tackled Tyler Allgeier in the flat on a third-and-9 ; he’s done well guarding the flat since struggling in the first two weeks of the season. Reese was EVERYWHERE and put the defense on his back for much of the game. It was a slow start, but the edge and linebacker group stabilized well. Grade: A Cornerback THE TAE BANKS REDEMPTION ARC IS HERE! A game-sealing pick-six for Banks after losing earlier in the game to Marvin Harrison Jr. on a touchdown. Banks also had a second-down PBU in the final goal-line stand for the Giants. The Cardinals ran the football outside consistently; while the cornerbacks weren’t out of position, they weren’t making plays to stop the run. Newsome recorded an interception on an underthrown Brissett pass, though he surrendered 24 yards in the final seconds of the first half, leading to Chad Ryland’s 60-yard field goal. Giving Wilson the outside was tough, and it helped halt the positive momentum that the Giants had established. Newsome also held Marvin Harrison Jr. in the end zone, which led to the Cardinals’ third touchdown, but his fourth-quarter PBU against Michael Wilson was clutch. Dru Phillips got away with a defensive hold on Tre McBride on third down late in the game, forcing a punt and giving the Giants the ball in advantageous field position. Phillips made a MASSIVE play in the end zone against Michael Wilson. It wasn’t a perfect performance by the corners, but it was enough with impactful splash plays. Grade: B + Safety Tyler Nubin returned to the lineup and started by making an impressive pass break-up versus Tre McBride, but he struggled early to fit the run in the alley. We didn’t hear much from Jevon Holland in the game; I’ll need to see more on the All-22. Grade: B Special teams Tyrone Tracy Jr. had a 55-yard return when the Giants were down 14-3, which was MUCH NEEDED. The Giants’ kick coverage did allow a good return to start the second quarter. Charlie Jones replaced the injured Braxton Berrios and returned it 23 yards, which was impressive. Jordan Stout had three punts, averaging 48.7 yards per punt, with two pinned down between the twenty-yard lines. Dominic Zvada booted a 52-yard field goal to give the Giants a six-point lead with just over two minutes left. Zvada was technically 4-for-4, but a controversial…

title: The Jets, the Rabbit-Duck Illusion, and Why Fan Perceptions Are Shifting Again
summary: The picture below is known as the rabbit-duck illusion. Depending on your perception, you might see a rabbit or a duck. The illusion first appeared in a German magazine in the 1890s, and it has been dissected by scholars in numerous academic fields since. Fans of the television series How I Met Your Mother may […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Roschon Johnson #23 of the Chicago Bears reacts during the fourth quarter against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The picture below is known as the rabbit-duck illusion. Depending on your perception, you might see a rabbit or a duck. The illusion first appeared in a German magazine in the 1890s, and it has been dissected by scholars in numerous academic fields since. Fans of the television series How I Met Your Mother may recognize the illusion as it played a central role in an episode that aired in 2010. This speaks to something basic. Our perceptions of a person, event, or place can change even if little has changed on the surface about that entity. It’s tough to believe, but there was a brief window in 2024 when the Aaron Rodgers-Robert Saleh Jets seemed to be right on track. The team lost its opener in San Francisco to the 49ers, a game few expected them to win. The Jets followed that loss up to back-to-back wins against the Titans and the Patriots. The team was 2-1 heading into Week 4. Of course that year nobody thought Tennessee or New England would be very good, but the Jets were doing what good teams did. They took care of business against bad opponents. Then came Week 4. The Jets lost to a Denver Broncos team they were supposed to beat. The next week they lost in London to the Vikings, and their head coach was fired. Next up was a loss to the Buffalo Bills. The team made a desperation trade for Davante Adams, but that didn’t help the Jets avoid a loss to the Steelers and then the next week that same Patriots team. After the third week of that season, it was perfectly reasonable to look at the Jets’ 2-1 record and feel like they took care of business against bad teams. A few weeks later, those games looked different. The Titans were on their way to earning the number one overall pick, but they had outgained the Jets in Week 2. The Jets needed a late goal line stand to secure a win against a dreadful team. The Week 3 win against the Patriots was more decisive, but New England was indeed awful in 2024. Still they were able to avenge their loss to the Jets a few weeks later. It quickly had become clear that the 2024 Jets were also a very bad team. They would win only three more games the rest of the way, one of which was against a Jaguars team that also earned a top five pick. Another was against a Dolphins team in Week 18 playing its backup quarterback. I’m not sure which one of duck or rabbit represents a good team on its way and which represents a really bad team that had a soft early season schedule, but it’s fair to say perceptions changed about that Jets team. An NFL season is a fragile thing. A team can seem to be on a good trajectory and then completely fall off and have a disastrous season. The 2026 Jets weren’t playing spectacular football heading into Week 4, but they more or less had looked like a professional team, which was something to be appreciated. The record might have only been 1-2, but this team looked a cut above your recent Jets club. They were coming off a Week 3 game where they stood toe to toe with a quality Lions team. Up against a backup quarterback in Chicago, I don’t think a win was an unreasonable ask. At the very least, the Jets should continue to look professional. Instead fans were treated to a catastrophic loss. The Jets were horrible in all phases of the game. In recent years this team has had an uncanny way of becoming a footnote like this. And there’s this:￼ The Bears had more 1st downs (34) than the Jets had plays (32). It's the 2nd game in the Super Bowl era (since 1966) in which one team had more first downs than its opponent had plays. H/t ESPN Research #jets ￼ — Rich Cimini (@RichCimini) October 5, 2026 This was the kind of game that makes you question whether the progress of the first four weeks was actually progress. Maybe that win over the Tennessee Titans that seemed promising in the moment was just this team’s version of the Week 3 2024 game against New England, catching a horrific opponent at the perfect moment on the schedule. Blowing a 10 point lead to Green Bay in the fourth quarter in a game they otherwise dominated perhaps could be excused since the Jets did play at a high level. Losing a back and forth road game to the Lions because Detroit made one more play? It happens. But when you combine these results with that ghastly effort in Chicago, you get a 1-3 record. You could be excused for wondering how real the progress of the first three weeks really was. When I say progress, I’m not talking about merely being better than the Brady Cook Jets of the final five games from 2025. That legitimately might have been the worst five game stretch of football a team has played in NFL history. The Jets could have done literally anything this offseason and been improved from that. The question is whether the Jets are on track to become a genuinely good team within the next year or two. You could be forgiven if your answer today is different from what it would have been yesterday. One critical area where fan perceptions might change is on the team’s head coach. It isn’t exactly a secret that Aaron Glenn has struggled in his year and change in charge of the Jets. His 4-17 record is a clear enough indicator of that. Of course Glenn inherited a true nightmare situation, one few coaches could have navigated successfully to this point. There’s nothing wrong with trying to talk yourself into a head coach. Glenn was a legendary player for this franchise. Hoping for the best for him is the right thing to do. So we can point out the horrendous condition the team was in when he took the job. We can talk about focusing on the long-term. We can try to absolve Glenn of the blame. But when you face the Bears, you face Ben Johnson. There is a clear display of what a genuinely good head coach is capable of doing. Johnson, of course, took over a much better situation in Chicago. Still, it isn’t all about his talent. In a six day stretch he just produced two wins with two different quarterbacks playing well. Neither of those quarterbacks is his starter. Compare that with Glenn. Ask what Glenn is doing to make this team better. Your perception of Glenn slowly making progress building this team might change faster than you can say, “Rabbit to duck.” The best thing about the NFL is there’s a game the next week. A victory over the Browns can change perceptions back. But for one week, the Jets have left many of us wondering whether the early stages of 2026 actually represent a meaningful step forward. They earned that through this performance.

title: New York Jets: Slip Sliding Away
summary: The New York Jets got the 2026 season off to a rousing start as they dominated the Tennessee Titans on their way to a 23 – 10 opening day victory. It was their first win since November 30, 2025, and only their third double digit win since the 2023 season. It has been a long […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Head Coach Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets looks on from the sideline during the second quarter against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets got the 2026 season off to a rousing start as they dominated the Tennessee Titans on their way to a 23 – 10 opening day victory. It was their first win since November 30, 2025, and only their third double digit win since the 2023 season. It has been a long time since the Jets have looked dominant. Unfortunately, it didn’t last. Since that big opening day win the Jets’ fortunes have been gradually sliding downhill. They dominated the Titans all game in week 1. In week 2 the Jets dominated the Green Bay Packers for 49 minutes before they collapsed and allowed 13 unanswered points to close the game in an overtime loss. In week 3 against the Detroit Lions the Jets never dominated, but they kept the game close and were in position to tie the score late before Geno Smith lost a fumble on the Jets’ final drive of the game. In week 4 against the Chicago Bears the Jets were thoroughly dominated from start to finish in a 23 – 12 loss that was not nearly as competitive as the final score might indicate. The trend here is not encouraging. The Jets have gotten less competitive with each passing game, culminating in a game against the Bears on Sunday where the Bears outgained the Jets by well over 300 yards and the Bears had more first downs on offense than the Jets offense had plays. That is annihilation. The loss brought the Jets 2026 record to 1-3. Playoff hopes are already growing faint, as teams starting the season 1-3 have only made the playoffs a little over 13% of the time since the 2012 season. For Aaron Glenn the loss was his 17th in a little more than a year as Jets head coach. He has a 4-17 record overall, good for a .190 winning percentage. The Aaron Glenn Jets have lost 8 of their last 9 games and 10 of their last 12. That is a very troubling record. The Jets have had 13 head coaches who have coached the team at least two full seasons. In chronological order they are as follows: Sammy Baugh Weeb Ewbank Walt Michaels Joe Walton Bruce Coslet Rich Kotite Bill Parcells Herm Edwards Eric Mangini Rex Ryan Todd Bowles Adam Gase Robert Saleh Of these 13 head coaches, only Rich Kotite had fewer wins than Glenn after 21 games. Kotite was arguably the worst head coach in Jets history, and one of the worst in NFL history. Only two of these 13 Jets head coaches had less than 10 wins after two seasons: Rich Kotite and Adam Gase. Both were fired after two seasons with the team. For Glenn to get to 10 wins over two seasons he would need to win at least six of the remaining 13 games in the 2026 season. Glenn has a .190 winning percentage in his head coaching career with the Jets. Just one Jets head coach has ever been worse in his first two years: Rich Kotite. Glenn’s Jets had a -203 point differential in his first season as Jets head coach. Not even the lowly Kotite ever posted a worse point differential. In fact there has only been one worse season in Jets history. Adam Gase posted a -214 point differential in his 2-14 2020 campaign. He was promptly fired. The Jets season looks like it is already slipping away. Glenn’s career as Jets head coach may follow suit. It is difficult at this point to identify much that Glenn has excelled at. It is not difficult to point to areas in which he has struggled. With three more first round draft picks in the 2027 draft soon to be made and the Jets very likely selecting a quarterback with one of them, can the Jets afford to allow the Glenn regime to make those picks if we don’t soon see a major turnaround? Six first round picks in two years represent an historic opportunity for a quick turnaround. It would be a major disappointment if the team invested a regime that has shown little chance of success thus far with that opportunity. The Jets have had just 13 playoff seasons in their 66 year history. Only two of them involved a start with 1 or fewer wins in the first four games of the season. It happened in the 1991 season when the Jets improbably sneaked into the playoffs with an 8-8 record with a dramatic overtime victory over the Miami Dolphins on the last day of the regular season. They were then unceremoniously bounced out of the playoffs with a loss in the Wild Card round. The Jets did not return to the playoffs for seven years after that loss. If you’re looking for a silver lining, here it is. In 1981 the Jets had not made the playoffs since the 1969 season, an 11 year drought that was the longest in Jets history until the current 15 year streak. The Jets hadn’t had a winning season during that 11 year stretch, a streak that exceeds any other such stretch in Jets history, including the current 10 year streak. That 1981 Jets team was led by first time head coach Walt Michaels, who had never posted a winning record in his first four seasons as Jets head coach. The 1981 season gave no indications it would be different after the first four games. The Jets opened the 1981 season with a 31 – 0 blowout loss to the Buffalo Bills. After three games the Jets were 0-3 with a -60 point differential. The season was threatening to spiral out of control. Then something clicked. The Jets won in week 4. That started a 10 game stretch in which the Jets lost just one game. By the end of the season the Jets were 10-5-1 and in the playoffs for the first time since 1969. They lost in the Wild Card round to the Buffalo Bills, but that 1981 season was the beginning of the legendary New York Sack Exchange Jets. Seemingly overnight the LOL Jets were transformed into a force to be reckoned with. They went on to make the playoffs four of the next six years, the best sustained stretch of Jets football in their history. Eventually the Sack Exchange grew old and broke up, and the Jets entered a decade of terrible football from the late 1980s through the late 1990s. But for a short time in the early to mid 1980s the Jets were a dangerous football team, led by a head coach in Walt Michaels who had never had a winning season before the turnaround. Can Aaron Glenn follow in Walt Michaels’ footsteps and usher in a new era of sustained Jets success? Based on what we’ve seen from him thus far, it doesn’t seem likely. But Michael’s dramatic turnaround in 1981 seemed just as unlikely after four games of the 1981 season. Then everything changed. Whether Glenn has it in him to engineer such a turnaround is the question the Jets must answer this season. Right now the season, and Glenn’s Jets career, appear to be slip sliding away. Time is running out for Glenn to change this. If we don’t see major progress soon, the Jets will need to once again move on and start over.

title: Jets vs Bears: Jets never competitive in thorough thrashing by Bears
summary: In the New York Jets’ fourth game of the 2026 season, on a beautiful bright and sunny day at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois, the Jets fell to the Chicago Bears, 23 – 12. The game opened with the Jets on defense. It did not go well. The Bears were pinned close to their own […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Kenyon Sadiq #16 of the New York Jets attempts to catch a pass during the second quarter against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the New York Jets’ fourth game of the 2026 season, on a beautiful bright and sunny day at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois, the Jets fell to the Chicago Bears, 23 – 12. The game opened with the Jets on defense. It did not go well. The Bears were pinned close to their own end zone to start the drive. It didn’t matter. Tyson Bagent took whatever he wanted against the Jets secondary, the Bears running game kept the ball moving, and the Bears went right down the field against token Jets resistance until they had the ball inside the Jets one yard line. In an unlikely twist, the Jets defense suddenly became stout, putting up a great goal line stand and holding the Bears out of the end zone. The Jets offense took over on downs at their one foot line. A three and out forced a Jets punt and the Bears marched right down the field again. Again the Jets defense put on a goal line stand before Kyle Monangai punched it in on fourth down for a touchdown and a 7 – 0 Bears lead late in the first quarter. The quarter ended with the Jets having the ball inside their own 30 yard line. At this point the Jets had been outgained 145 yards to 15. It wasn’t a promising start to the game. The Jets went backward and were forced to punt. The Bears got the ball and started driving. Then something happened that hadn’t happened in forever and a day. Minkah Fitzpatrick intercepted a Tyson Bagent pass, the first Jets interception since 2024. The Jets got the ball deep in Bears territory but they couldn’t do much with the opportunity. The Jets drive fizzled and they had to settle for a Jason Sanders field goal. That made the score Bears 7, Jets 3 midway through the second quarter. The Bears then drove the ball down the field, grinding away on the ground against a Jets defense that seemingly had few answers. After the Bears drive was stopped deep in Jets territory the Bears kicked a short field goal to take a 10 – 3 lead with just over two minutes left in the half. The Jets took over in a two minute drill situation. Previous efforts this season in this situation did not bode well for the Jets. In another spectacular end of half possession by the Jets, they went three and out, with Geno Smith throwing a ball on third down that should have been intercepted. The Bears took over on offense with just under two minutes left in the half, plenty of time to extend their lead. Unlike the Jets, the Bears are not completely incompetent in two minute drill situations. They drove the ball down inside the Jets 20 yard line before settling for a short field goal. Jets went into the locker room at halftime down 13 -3. It could have been much worse after the Bears completely dominated the action. The Bears outgained the Jets in the first half 274 yards to 34. The Jets had five(!) net yards passing. It felt like the Bears could do whatever they wanted on offense and the Jets couldn’t do anything. Not being down by three touchdowns felt like a moral victory. If the Jets didn’t make some adjustments and find some answers at halftime this game could get out of hand quickly. The Jets opened the third quarter on offense. They put together a couple of first downs on the ground before Geno Smith got sacked and the Jets were forced to punt. Then fortune smiled on the Jets. D’Andre Swift fumbled on the Bears’ next possession and the Jets recovered, giving the Jets the ball in scoring position. The Jets squandered a golden opportunity however, as they had to settle for a short field goal. The score was now Bears 13, Jets 6. The Jets were down by a touchdown despite winning the turnover battle 2 – 0. Not great Bob. The Jets would soon pay for their inability to take advantage of their opportunities. On their next possession the Bears drove right down the field. Kyle Monagai ended the drive with his second touchdown run of the game as the Bears went up by two touchdowns at 20 – 6. At this point there was a little over two minutes left in the third quarter and the Jets defense had yet to force a Bears punt. The Bears turnovers were the only thing stopping the Bears from putting this game completely out of reach. The Jets put together a brilliant three and out drive as the clock wound down in the third quarter. As the fourth quarter opened the Bears were on the move near midfield, leading by two touchdowns. A third straight Jets loss seemed all but inevitable. The Bears put together another scoring drive, getting inside the Jets five yard line before settling for a short field goal and a three score lead at 23 – 6 with 10 minutes left in the game. The Jets then came to life on a quick 70 yard drive ending in a long Geno Smith touchdown pass to Isaiah Williams to get the Jets back within two scores with a little more nine minutes left. Jason Sanders botched the extra point to make the score Bears 23, Jets 12. The good feelings didn’t last. The Bears proceeded to go on a long, grinding drive in which the Jets were helpless to stop the Bears running game. They ran out the clock with a more than 9 minute drive to end the game. Final score: Bears 23, Jets 12. This game was nowhere near as close as the final score indicated. The Bears completely shut down the Jets offense save for the one long touchdown pass to Isaiah Williams. The Bears offense was never forced to punt all game. Outside of a couple of turnovers the Bears offense took whatever they wanted whenever they wanted it. They outgained the Jets by more than 300 yards and put up more than 230 yards rushing against an overwhelmed Jets defense. You rarely see this level of domination in the NFL. It was a humiliating performance by a lifeless Jets team. The loss brought the Jets’ record to 1-3. The Jets return home next week to take on a 3-1 first place Cleveland Browns team that is proving to be a much more formidable challenge than they seemed before the season began.

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 27: Elijah Moore #8 of the New York Jets runs for yards in the first half of a game against the Chicago Bears at MetLife Stadium on November 27, 2022 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week the New York Jets suffered their second straight heart-breaking loss. They faced off against the Detroit Lions and had the ball in Lions territory, driving for a game-tying score late in the fourth quarter when disaster struck. Geno Smith was sacked on a Lions blitz and fumbled. The Lions recovered and that was the end of the Jets chances for an upset victory. The loss gave the Jets a 1-2 record on the season. Today the Jets try to get back on the winning track as they stay on the road against the Chicago Bears. Kickoff is scheduled for shortly after 1 PM at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois. The Bears opened the 2026 season with a resounding 59 – 37 blowout victory over the Carlina Panthers. They followed that up with a thud, losing to the Minnesota Vikings 9 – 3 in a game that saw Bears starting quarterback Caleb Williams exit the field with an injury. Williams remained on the bench last week as Case Keenum made his first NFL start since 2023. Keenum played surprisingly well, leading the Bears to a 27 – 7 thrashing of the Philadelphia Eagles last week. Join Gang Green Nation on game day! Stay on top of every Jets update and debate every snap with other diehard fans. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . The 2-1 Bears enter this game expecting to field their third different starting quarterback in the last three weeks. 26 year old Tyson Bagent is expected to start his first NFL game since he made four starts in his rookie year of 2023. Despite the backup quarterback Bagent starting for the Bears, this game will likely be a formidable challenge for the Jets. The Bears head coach Ben Johnson is an outstanding offensive mind and will no doubt cook up some interesting wrinkles to best use Bagent’s talents at quarterback. In addition, the Bears come into this game with the #1 running game in the NFL. Throw in a defense that has allowed no more than 260 yards and 9 points to each of their last two opponents, and you have a difficult matchup for a Jets team struggling with injuries. The Jets are missing almost half of their offensive starters today, and they will be without four wide receivers. That is unfortunate against a Bears pass defense that has been a weakness for them thus far this season. The Jets’ best chance for victory today involves limiting the Bears’ chunk plays on offense, confusing the inexperienced Bagent enough to create some sacks and turnovers, and throwing the ball as much as possible to Garrett Wilson and Kenyon Sadiq while grinding away on the ground with Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis. Can they pull off the upset? We’ll find out soon enough. It’s the Jets and the Bears in game 4 of the 2026 season. Enjoy the game everyone.

title: Eagles-Rams Takeaway: Injuries complicate search for identity
summary: DeVonta Smith. Saquon Barkley. Lane Johnson. Landon Dickerson. Dallas Goedert. Tank Bigsby. Quinyon Mitchell. Jonathan Greenard. Zach Baun. Marcus Epps. Nine starters and one vital back-up. All injured either coming into the Eagles’ fall-from-ahead 24-20 loss to the Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday or hurt during an excruciating afternoon that dropped the Birds […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 4: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles screams prior to an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 4, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images DeVonta Smith. Saquon Barkley. Lane Johnson. Landon Dickerson. Dallas Goedert. Tank Bigsby. Quinyon Mitchell. Jonathan Greenard. Zach Baun. Marcus Epps. Nine starters and one vital back-up. All injured either coming into the Eagles’ fall-from-ahead 24-20 loss to the Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday or hurt during an excruciating afternoon that dropped the Birds to 2-2 on the still-young-but-getting-older season. Even if the Eagles came into the game with an offensive system that had been in place for four or five years and knew what they wanted to be, losing that many players in one game would be difficult to overcome. But when you’re under yet another first-time offensive coordinator and playcaller, and when you’re going up against one of the most high-powered offenses in the NFL, sometimes the attrition and misfortune of injuries is too much to overcome. For most of three-and-a-half quarters yesterday, the story of the day was “resilience.” No, the Eagles had not played well on offense, but it was somewhat understandable without Smith, their No. 1 wideout, and Johnson and Dickerson, both of whom anchor the offensive line. When Barkley went down on the first series of the game, Bigsby, Will Shipley and Darius Cooper stepped up and made enough plays to take advantage of L.A. mistakes and put up a 20-10 lead. Their depth was being tested but they were hanging in there. The numbers, including a ghastly 0-for-12 on 3rd downs, would be less important than the grit showed by Jalen Hurts and an offense trying to cobble things together while short-handed. But with Sean Mannion calling plays in just his fourth NFL contest, it became clear he, and Hurts, are still searching for easy-button set of layup plays that can help them convert short distances in pressure situations. In seven of their 12 failed third down opportunities, they needed less than five yards, and on the all-important 4th-and-goal from the 2 in the fourth quarter, there was nothing dependable or reliable in the playbook for Mannion and Hurts to turn to. No security blankets. Even without Smith in the lineup, there should still be at least 2-4 plays the offense can choose from in order to pick up five yards, or give themselves a real shot at the goal line. But there is nothing in the bag they feel good about yet. It all comes down to forming an identity. The Eagles searched for one all last year under Kevin Patullo and never found one. That search continues through four games under Mannion. And while some patience should be reserved for the new OC, it is reasonable to expect some improvement as the weeks move along. Nick Sirianni is correct that progress is not always linear, but it also should look better than it has over the last two weeks. Their struggles in the second half of football games is truly concerning. One week after being outscored 17-0 after halftime, the Eagles were shut out 14-0 in the second half against the Rams. That’s 31-0 over the last two weeks. Now, it’s fair to wonder how things might have gone had Hurts not bobbled the snap on 3rd-and-2 at the goalline late in the 4th quarter and managed to hand the ball off to Bigsby, who was still in the game at this point. It looked as though Bigsby would have at least been able to get it close to the goal line, if not score. Had he done so, the game would have been over. But if wishes were horses, then beggars would ride. Mannion was supposed to craft an offense that would put defenses into conflict, never knowing when the Eagles were going to run or pass. But so far, it’s pretty much a guarantee that if Hurts is under center, they’re handing it off to a running back. They’re only going to pass out of the shotgun, and that’s problematic. Is that a function of Hurts’ comfort or a lack of imagination from Mannion? We asked many of these same questions last year under Patullo. Those questions, and the quarterback, remain. It is difficult to find an identity without a competent offensive line and, right now, they don’t have one. They haven’t had one since the Super Bowl 59 squad walked off the field. Dickerson’s absence forced a reshuffling of the offensive line that pushed Cam Jugens to left guard and Drew Kendall to center. Kendall has been fine, but Jurgens has struggled. And with Lane Johnson out and Tyler Steen also finding difficulty, as well as a predictable pattern for defenses to hone in on, it’s been almost impossible for the Eagles to form the kind of run-first identity Mannion would ideally like to have. As such, there is no play-action. Nothing to put defenses in conflict. Should Hurts have been able to do a little more against the Rams in the second half? The film grinders will watch on All-22 and let us know if meat was left on the bone, but it didn’t look as though Hurts had much of a chance in the passing game on Sunday. The makeshift offensive line couldn’t hold up to a superior Los Angeles pass rush and, with the game on the line, wilted. The search for an identity on offense will clearly be hampered by the loss of star players and key offensive linemen. Defensively, even without Mitchell, Greenard, Baun and Epps, the defense should have been able to hold a 10-point lead with 6 minutes left and the Rams backed up to their own 2-yard line. Quick aside: Sirianni’s decision to go for it at the goal line was the right call. Had he kicked the field goal, the Rams still could have gone ahead with two touchdowns, which is what happened anyway. Sirianni had to believe that, even if the Eagles fell short there, the defense would at least force a struggling Matt Stafford to take more time off the clock to travel 98 yards than they did, and he had to believe they would be able to prevent the Rams from scoring twice in that short amount of time. But Vic Fangio’s unit, who had played admirably to that point, was unable to get the job done. Mitchell’s absence in the secondary was felt, as was Baun’s play-making and ability to cover receivers out of the backfield. The pass rush, which had been so effective all day, suddenly ran out of gas. Jalen Carter’s name was barely uttered on Sunday. Ultimately, the losses on defense were too much to overcome. Moving forward, the concern is how long these missing players will be out. Reports indicate Smith’s hamstring injury is one that could keep him out for multiple weeks. The injuries to Barkley and Biggs didn’t look good. No one knows, as of this writing, what forced Johnson to miss the game on Sunday, and even when Dickerson comes back, no one is sure how he’s going to look. Will the defense be without Mitchell long-term? How about Greenard? Baun’s concussion? There is a real danger of this football season looking like the 2005 Eagles who, coming off a Super Bowl, ran into a calamity of injuries (and Terrell Owens’ nonsense) and suffered a lost season under Andy Reid. Sirianni and Hurts have never had a losing season. This Eagles roster is top-heavy and, when the top is hurt, there’s not much there waiting in the wings to replace them. It is in situations like these that Mannion has to prove that he can be a creative problem-solver and Hurts can be adaptable. They must work together to find an identity or, at the very least, a collection of plays they can rely on to get them 5-7 yards throughout a game. Perhaps that’s easier said than done but, that is why the Eagles hired Mannion, after all. The NFL season is one-quarter of the way done. The training wheels need to come off now. If we’re going to see a fully functional Mannion offense, it has to start now, even if they are under-manned. Yes, injuries complicate the search for an identity. But an identity still must be found if the Eagles want to avoid…
author: John Stolnis

title: Eagles News: “The Nick Sirianni hot seat is real, or at least it should be”
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! There’s plenty of blame to share but the head coach is lacking answers and that’s a pretty big problem. The team isn’t that far off from 0-4; they narrowly won their first two games. Of course, you can also say the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 4: Head Coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts after a play during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 4, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! There’s plenty of blame to share but the head coach is lacking answers and that’s a pretty big problem. The team isn’t that far off from 0-4; they narrowly won their first two games. Of course, you can also say the Eagles were close to being 3-1. But that record would be masking a team that’s just not playing very well right now. We might be heading down a path where a reset is needed. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL winners and losers: Nick Sirianni sucks – SB Nation The Sirianni hot seat is real, or at least it should be. This team has churned through offensive coordinators since its Super Bowl win, routinely causing them to get blamed when things go wrong and the offense doesn’t reach its potential. This has to come back to Sirianni at some point, and it’s fair to question whether or not he’s lost control of the offensive side of the ball. One of the best traits the Eagles had at their zenith was a perfect understanding of who they are, their strengths, and not getting outside of that rubric. Lately it’s felt as if Philadelphia is playing aspirational football, forcing what they want to be, rather than accepting who they are right now — and playing to those strengths. It’s a weird situation, because Sirianni actually does have a lot of fantastic traits. He’s an excellent motivator, he developed a locker room culture that had more of a swagger an edge, but he’s sorely needing someone to assist with the strategic elements of the game. It’s not that Sirianni is incapable, but more that he looks like a coach who is underwater right now, trying to do too much at once. If he doesnt find a way of swimming soon, it’ll sink this entire season. Roob’s Observations as Rams take advantage of injury-riddled Eagles – NBCSP Second half. Again. Good lord. The Eagles have now been outscored 54-20 in the second half this year, 31-0 the last two weeks and they’ve been outgained by an average of 202-103. That’s insane. The Cowboys scored more second-half points today (28) than the Eagles have all year. The Rams outgained them 260-72 Sunday. How does an NFL team not understand you have to play 60 minutes to beat a good team? How can an entire team just fall to pieces when the game is on the line? How can so many players just stop making plays at crunch time? The Eagles on Sunday had four first downs in the second half and the Rams had 16. Seriously? Come on. And I put the blame for this squarely on the coaching staff, Nick Sirianni in particular. He’s responsible for everything we see on the football field. And what we’re seeing after halftime is a football team that’s inept, unprepared, overmatched and embarrassed on a weekly basis. Pathetic. Eagles vs. Rams: 9 winners, 9 losers, and 4 IDKs – BGN The Philadelphia Eagles didn’t really deserve to beat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday afternoon. The Birds were outgained by 243 yards. That’s typically not a recipe for success. Neither is failing to convert a single third down despite having 12 chances to do so. Despite these struggles … and despite entering this game with a lot of key absences and only suffering more injuries during the day … the Eagles almost managed to steal this game. Almost. They were two yards away from going up 17 points with about 7.5 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. If they score a touchdown in that spot, the conversation is a lot different than it is right now. But that’s not our current reality. The Eagles lost their second game in a row and one can only wonder if there are more losses on the way. Handing out 10 awards from the Eagles-Rams game – PhillyVoice They were 2-for-9 last week against the Bears. Add it up, and they are 2-for-21 on 3rd downs the last two games. #Math. Is it execution? Play calling? Scheme?”Everybody contributed to that,” Nick Sirianni said. “Everybody. There’s execution errors. There’s coaching errors. Everybody contributes to that.” It feels like “Everybody contributed to that” is a common answer too often, from the back half of the 2025 season, carrying through into 2026. What made the third-down ineptitude so egregious was that they weren’t even in a lot of third-and-long situations. […] They were in 3rd and 5 or less on seven of those 3rd-down opportunities. Other than the Tush Push (which also failed today), the Eagles just don’t seem to have anything they can go to to sustain drives. Good Start Goes Bad – Iggles Blitz I don’t know how to feel about the Eagles right now. I was impressed with the first half. I was depressed by the fourth quarter. And I’m definitely concerned by all the injuries. While I’m not confident in them, I don’t want to dismiss the positive signs from the Rams game. The safeties played well. The pass rush was good at times. The STs gave the team a big boost. Rookie Markell Bell did some good things in his first NFL start. But the offense…yikes. Regardless of who is out, the offense must handle the blitz better. That is on the OL, Hurts, the skill players and the coaches. Everyone owns some of the blame for those struggles. Teams will continue to attack until the Eagles show they can block it and/or burn it. Sean Mannion, or Nick Sirianni, or Jalen Hurts has to decide on offensive identity after ugly Rams loss – Inquirer After nearly reaching the quarter pole of the season, it’s become evident that Sean Mannion’s Eagles offense is disjointed, unimaginative, and ultimately, ineffective. Or is it Nick Sirianni’s offense? Or Jalen Hurts’? Or does it even matter who is given ownership of a unit that failed to capitalize on an impressive defensive performance against the Los Angeles Rams? Of course, everyone played a part in a 24-20 loss on Sunday. Vic Fangio’s defense could have gotten a stop on the Rams’ two late fourth-quarter touchdown drives. The Lane Johnson-less offensive line could have opened more holes and given Hurts more time. The wide receivers, running backs, and tight ends could have done something to convert just one third down. But the offense has reached an inflection point after its regression in each of the first four games, and it’s on the figureheads at the top to decide where to go from here. Should Sirianni allow Mannion to fully implement the Kyle Shanahan scheme that was at the core of his hiring? Or should they just abandon the under-center heavy system that has been woefully unproductive thus far? What is the Eagles’ offensive identity? Not ‘good enough,’ says Nick Sirianni after loss to Rams | The Early Bird – PHLY Eagles An optimist’s view would also point to the fact that the Eagles have been here before with Hurts under center and Sirianni at the helm. You might remember the team also got off to a 2-2 start in 2024. The offensive line implored Sirianni to pivot toward more of a run-first approach, Sirianni shaved his head, and the Eagles went on a magical run to Super Bowl LIX and left Caesars Superdome with the organization’s second Lombardi Trophy. That page doesn’t seem to be in Sean Mannion’s 2026 playbook, though. The Eagles ranked fifth in EPA/rush through the first four games of 2024. This season, they’re 24th. They’ve had moving pieces along the offensive line in three of the first four games and Barkley has now suffered a stinger and a hamstring injury already this season. Backup running back Tank Bigsby also suffered an apparent injury late in the fourth quarter. What is apparent is that the Eagles now have an urgency to figure out what this year’s about face is going to look like. A training camp spent harping on under-center formations and play-action passing…
author: Brandon Lee Gowton

title: Eagles vs. Rams: 9 winners, 9 losers, and 4 IDKs
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles didn’t really deserve to beat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday afternoon. The Birds were outgained by 243 yards. That’s typically not a recipe for success. Neither is failing to convert a single third down despite having 12 chances to do so. Despite these struggles … and despite entering this game with […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 4: Darius Cooper #80 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 4, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles didn’t really deserve to beat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday afternoon. The Birds were outgained by 243 yards. That’s typically not a recipe for success. Neither is failing to convert a single third down despite having 12 chances to do so. Despite these struggles … and despite entering this game with a lot of key absences and only suffering more injuries during the day … the Eagles almost managed to steal this game. Almost. They were two yards away from going up 17 points with about 7.5 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. If they score a touchdown in that spot, the conversation is a lot different than it is right now. But that’s not our current reality. The Eagles lost their second game in a row and one can only wonder if there are more losses on the way. Time to hand out winners, losers, and I don’t knows. For even more analysis, check out my appearance on the PHLY Eagles postgame show along with Brandon Graham, Bo Wulf, and others! WINNERS DARIUS COOPER September 21, 2026 : “I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again: good things happen when Hurts throws the ball to Cooper.” My love for Cooper isn’t just a bit! He’s proving to be a useful player. Three of his five receptions this season have resulted in touchdowns. On his first touchdown, Cooper made a great effort to snag the ball out of the air to prevent an interception and put points on the board for the Eagles instead. Cooper then managed to get wide open in the back of the end zone for Hurts for his second score. Cooper finished this game with a team-high seven targets. That volume speaks to Hurts’ trust in him. It’s pretty silly that this guy saw zero targets in Week 1. And that he played the fifth-most snaps of any Eagles receiver in Week 3, when he also logged zero targets. Cooper can make plays as a pass-catcher. He’s the Eagles’ best blocking receiver. He’s among the NFL leaders in special teams tackles. The Eagles need to stop messing around and get him more regularly involved. It’s really a shame they lost this game because Cooper would be getting much more shine if they won. MARKEL BELL Bell graded out better as a run blocker than a pass protector. The rookie tackle was able to use his size and strength to pancake some defenders. Bell wasn’t perfect. But he had to start this game on short notice after Lane Johnson did not play due to personal reasons. It’s not like he got a full week in practice to prepare for this situation. Bell did not look totally lost out there. He did not wreck the game. That might sound like a low bar but it’s an encouraging starting point. ANDREW MUKUBA Mukuba has drawn a lot of ire but he made a really nice diving interception for a 21-yard return that allowed the Eagles’ offense to set up at the plus 28-yard line and ultimately score three points. Mukuba’s playmaking ability is part of his purported appeal, so, that was good to see. He did was charted for two missed tackles, which isn’t ideal. But those mistakes are a little more easy to live with if he’s generating big plays. COOPER DEJEAN DeJean has bounced back since a rough Week 1. Impressive focus to stay with a tipped ball and make the grab for a pick and 25-yard return to set up an Eagles touchdown right before the end of the first half. JEREMIAH TROTTER JR. Tackles aren’t a perfect stat but Trot Jr. led the team with 15 total, 10 of which were solo. A team-high three of his tackles were classified as “stops,” which are tackles that constitute a failure for the offense. Trot Jr. did miss a key tackle on Kyren Williams’ touchdown run that gave the Rams the lead. Shame, too, because he had the running back lined up for either no gain or a loss. Didn’t make the play. Still, more good than bad from a player making his first NFL start in a game where the Eagles weren’t resting their starters. NOLAN SMITH Smith timed up the snap count well to get to Matthew Stafford unblocked for a sack. His second sack of the season accounts for the Eagles’ total of four sacks through four games. Smith also had two “stops. One of them was a TFL. Also worth noting that Smith officially started this game as one of two edge rushers … with the other being Jonathan Greenard. MICHAEL CLAY Part of the reason why the Eagles were in position to steal this game was because their special teams unit played well. We’d be ripping Clay if his group had a rough day, so, it’s only fair to give the Eagles’ special teams coordinator credit here. JAKE ELLIOTT Including training camp practices (28/31), preseason games (7/7), and the 2026 regular season thus far (13/13), Elliott is 48/51 on all kicks dating back to the offseason. That’s pretty good. Elliott drilled a 56-yarder in the rain and wind today. He has two makes from 50+ yards on two tries this season. He was 5/15 from 50+ in the past two seasons combined. Elliott also did his part to help pin the Rams back deep with a kickoff that hit the landing zone and bounced into the end zone to force LA to take over at their own 20-yard line instead of the standard touchback at the 35-yard line. BRITAIN COVEY Covey set the Eagles up at the plus 17-yard line with his 41-yard punt return. Two plays later, Hurts hit Cooper for Philly’s first touchdown of the game. Covey is logging 13.5 yards per punt return this season. That figure would rank eighth among qualified punt returners from last season. Good stuff. LOSERS TEAM HEALTH The Eagles have a long list of players who are injured coming out of their Week 4 loss. Far from ideal. Especially with an international trip coming up this weekend. SEAN MANNION This offense flat out sucks. Is that entirely Mannion’s fault? No. We all know there are major injury issues. We can allow some room for growing pains. But he is the offensive coordinator and the results were very, very bad. The Eagles have failed to convert their last SEVENTEEN third down attempts. 0/17! They were 0/12 in this game. One year after leading the NFL in three-and-out percentage, the Eagles continue to look pathetically inept. A bunch of stats to back up the eye test: The Eagles have 15 three-and-out drives this season, the most in the NFL. 11 of their 15 three-and-out drives have come in the 2nd half, 3 more than any other team in the NFL. (Via NFL Research) — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) October 5, 2026 Out of 5,638 games since 2016, here are the 2026 Philadelphia Eagles offensive EPA/play game rankings and percentiles, per @SumerSports Wk 1: 2,940 | 48th percentile Wk 2: 2,458 | 56th percentile Wk 3: 5,252 | 7th percentile Wk 4: 5,188 | 8th percentile — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) October 4, 2026 Eagles with 172 yards of total offense — their lowest total in a game in the last 12 YEARS (!!!). 68 net passing yards — their lowest total in a regular-season game in the last 23 YEARS (!!!). — Sheil Kapadia (@SheilKapadia) October 4, 2026 The #Eagles have the worst under center offense in the NFL. https://t.co/AMlqiP6k3M pic.twitter.com/UNnzdrSQ8G — Deniz Selman (@denizselman33) October 5, 2026 It's only been 4 games so there will surely be reversion, but here's a look at the 192 offenses since 2021 in success rate on dropbacks with and without play action. Even if we just look at the first 4 weeks of each season, 2026 #Eagles rank 190th of 192 teams with play action. pic.twitter.com/1RZVsA0NIX — Deniz Selman (@denizselman33) October 5, 2026 The Eagles offense has hit rock bottom Data via @SumerSports pic.twitter.com/wWAYNFFpRp — Eagles Eric (@EaglesXsandOs) October 5, 2026 JALEN HURTS Not exactly one of the prettier box scores you’ll see: 12/27, 68 net passing yards, two touchdowns, zero interceptions, and a 78.2 passer rating.…

title: Jalen Hurts cited “poor execution” for the Eagles’ offensive struggles
summary: The Eagles offense was able to get some things going against the Rams, at least enough to go up by almost three scores, but ultimately, they stalled in the second half (again) and ended up losing. Quarterback Jalen Hurts spoke after the game and didn’t blame injuries or the new scheme for their uneven performances, […]
full_text: Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images | Getty Images The Eagles offense was able to get some things going against the Rams, at least enough to go up by almost three scores, but ultimately, they stalled in the second half (again) and ended up losing. Quarterback Jalen Hurts spoke after the game and didn’t blame injuries or the new scheme for their uneven performances, and expressed confidence that the group will continue to grow together. Hurts didn’t need a lot of extra words when asked about the offense’s struggles in the second half, and on third downs, citing “Poor execution” for both. “Poor execution. I don’t think there’s any other way to put it.” Here’s what else the QB had to say: On injuries stacking up Hurts said that those skill players always have an immediate impact when they are on the field, but it’s still up to the people out there to execute at a high level, regardless. “I’ve got to be better. I’ve got to figure it out. However it looks, whatever that means, find a way to win the game. We had our opportunities, and we didn’t take advantage of them. This is an event that we can learn from, that I’ll learn from, and we’ll use. I’ll use.” The QB was also asked about Lane Johnson being unavailable on Sunday, and Hurts said it was very unfortunate, but they have a next man up mentality. They kept the focus on the team and on trying to go out there and do their best. “A lot of respect for everyone that stepped in unexpectedly and even throughout the week, different roles, new opportunities, taking advantage of those in the end. This is one that you can learn from, obviously.” He also later rejected the idea that the injuries held them back at all, with the QB saying he never felt that they were too much to overcome. They still had an opportunity to make it a three-score game, and they didn’t do it, so he’s not going to blame injuries. On the 4th-and-2 failed QB sneak “Well, we had a bad exchange on the snap the play before. Comes down to very little things, executing at a high level. So, I think in the end, it comes back to alignment, connectedness to what we’re doing and everybody executing. I think in the end, it comes down to executing. Third down was not good enough, not good enough at all. Situationally, we were not good enough. So, us as a team, we’ve been really good when we’ve been able to be dominant in situational football and we’ve just got to be better and point towards the little things. We point towards the small things that build up to those moments, kind of clean things up when we get in those situations typically. We’re not doing that right now.” On their struggles in the ground game Hurts said that they are still finding their flow, and ultimately it all comes down to execution. He expects everyone in the locker room to first look internally when asking those questions, and then controlling the things they can control and execute better. The QB didn’t want to blame the new scheme for their issues, and said it was an executing thing, instead. On his message to the team “Get up.” On his confidence in the team “I think it’s less about being even-keeled and more about doubling down on the work and controlling the things that you can. This is a team that is building and finding its way — it’s obviously a work in progress. I have the utmost confidence in this team. I have the utmost confidence in this group. We just have to remain enduring, be persistent, keep committing to one another, and keep committing to the work of becoming a better group together. We’ve just got to continue to grow and go on that journey.”
author: Alexis Chassen

title: Nick Sirianni says Eagles’ third-down failures are on everybody
summary: The Eagles lost another ugly game on Sunday against the Rams, and will move forward 2-2 with a growing number of injured players adding to the issues. Head coach Nick Sirianni spoke to reporters after the game and talked about the offense’s inability to convert third downs, what he thinks of the play-calling, and why […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on from the sideline during the second quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles lost another ugly game on Sunday against the Rams, and will move forward 2-2 with a growing number of injured players adding to the issues. Head coach Nick Sirianni spoke to reporters after the game and talked about the offense’s inability to convert third downs, what he thinks of the play-calling, and why they went for it on 4th-and-2. When asked about the identity of the Eagles offense through four games, Sirianni was honest about that being unresolved. “You’re trying to make sure as you find out who you are that you’re playing with detail and you’re playing together and you’re playing with toughness, and we’ve still got a ways to go there and it’s obvious that we’re still trying to figure that out.” Here’s what the head coach had to say: On third down inefficiency Sirianni said that everybody shared the blame and contributed to their lack of success on third downs – there were execution errors and coaching errors. “Some of our problems offensively has been [that] we’ve been behind, but it wasn’t quite the same case today where we were in second-and-long and all those different things. It was more we couldn’t convert on third down for multiple different reasons. So again, there’s always a lot of contributors to that.” He explained that he needs to watch the tape before commenting further, but admitted that when you convert zero third downs, everybody has a hand in it. The head coach also said that it’s their job to figure out what happened and get better from it, but also noted that it’s not to assign blame. It was later pointed out that the Rams blitzed on every third down, highlighting the issues they were having at pass protection. Sirianni explained that there are different things that go into that, and it’s very rarely a simple, one-item solution. “But again, 0-for on third down, that hurts. It hurts your drives. It hurts you being able to do the things that you want to do on offense. It can put you in a pressing situation at times. One of them obviously turned into a fourth down conversion that did lead to points, but that to me is where we had our biggest issues here today, was there.” Sirianni also pointed to the offense not being able to finish advantageous situations. He explained that they had the short field thanks to Drew Mukuba’s interception, but weren’t able to put the game away. “We lose yards on a run play there playing that kind of like, ‘Hey, you have four downs, two more downs to get it on third down, then we lose yards.’ And then third-and-two at the two, to not finish that one, you’re essentially putting the game away there in that scenario and we didn’t in that particular case. I think what has to happen at the end of the day, what I told our guys is that when you’ve got a team down, you’ve got to finish it. That’s everybody. Coaching, playing, everybody.” On going for it on 4th-and-2 “In that situation right there, try to make it a three-score game. It was a two-score game, up 10. We would’ve gone up 13, but I wanted to make it a three score game right there. Fourth-and-two from the two, you leave them in a true backed up scenario. I’m very well aware of how the fourth down decisions go as the head coach. You go for it and you get it, great. You go for it and you don’t get it, that’s on the head coach. We didn’t get it, so that’s on me. A lot of things that we’ve got to look at and see what went down on that particular play, obviously same deal. It wasn’t good enough as coaches and wasn’t good enough at playing there.” On rookie Markel Bell Bell had to play when Lane Johnson was abruptly inactive for Sunday’s game, and while Sirianni said he still needs to watch the tape, the rookie didn’t stand out in a bad way. “I didn’t feel like, ‘Hey, that one was on Markel.’ We’ll see. We’ve got to watch the tape. But I thought he battled and went in there and played his butt off. I know he was coming off the field every time, just having given it his all. He was ready to play and you love that about him. We’ll have to look at the tape, but I think he battled and played his butt off.” On the play-calling Sirianni was asked why they didn’t run as much outside zone, especially after having some success with it in the first half. The head coach explained that he’d have to see how many times they called it, but they have checks built into it sometimes, too. Ultimately, though, “I felt like we had it called a handful more times. I feel like we got to some of the gap things that we ran today that compliment that, that we hit a couple of those out of there. At the end of the day, not good enough on our part offensively and put the defense in some bad positions.” Still, he emphasized that when they had zero third-down conversions, the offensive issues belong to everybody – not just OC Sean Mannion. “I’ve got a ton of confidence in Sean [Mannion] and he’s going to wear a lot of this. There’s no doubt. I’m going to wear a lot of this. Our offense is going to wear a lot of this. You win together, you lose together. I have no complaints on what happened there today. There’s opportunity for us all to grow following this game, win, lose, draw. There’s always opportunities for growth and then we’ve got to be committed to continuing to get better, and that will be the emphasis this week.” On the effect of injuries The head coach was adamant that the growing list of injuries were in no way an excuse, and that he has confidence in every next man up. “Life hands you a lot of different scenarios. Football hands you a lot of different scenarios. You’ve got to be accountable to who you are and to what you do, each and every one of us. You’ll never hear me say a word about an injury. I have a lot of faith in everybody on this football team. There’s a reason they’re Philadelphia Eagles. I’ve got to do a better job. We’ve got to play better. We’ve got to coach better. All of us have things to get better from. I don’t care who’s on the field.”
author: Alexis Chassen
