title: Eagles vs. Rams: The good, the bad, and the ugly
summary: The Los Angeles Rams waved goodbye, laughing hysterically at the raucous midnight green denizens that filled Lincoln Financial Field on an overcast, raw Sunday. The Eagles held two 10-point leads over the desperate, mistake-prone Rams, and somehow, someway, blew it. The Eagles dropped to 2-2, though appear in far more trouble than their record indicates. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams waved goodbye, laughing hysterically at the raucous midnight green denizens that filled Lincoln Financial Field on an overcast, raw Sunday. The Eagles held two 10-point leads over the desperate, mistake-prone Rams, and somehow, someway, blew it. The Eagles dropped to 2-2, though appear in far more trouble than their record indicates. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni can no longer get away with the chances he once took, squandering two fourth downs during critical junctures, and quite literally handing the game over to the Rams. Where once Sirianni’s bold fourth-down decisions made him look like he was a sideline swashbuckler, now, the choices appear flat out inane. It seems apparent the Sean Mannion experiment is not working. Jalen Hurts was sacked four times for minus-25 yards and barely had time to look down field behind a porous offensive line, and the defense, which had carried the Eagles for much of the game on Sunday, has not played up to their overall capabilities. Knowing how to tackle would help. The Eagles were working out of a triage unit on Sunday, with DeVonta Smith, Zack Baun, Lane Johnson, Marcus Epps, Fred Johnson and Dallas Goedert out before the game, and Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Jonathan Greenard and Quinyon Mitchell leaving during the game. When the Eagles fly over the Atlantic to play the Jacksonville Jaguars this week, they may arrive in London with a red cross emblazed on the plane. The Eagles lost to a Rams team that committed eight penalties for 100 yards and turned the ball over twice. Although, the Rams outgained the Eagles 415 yards of total offense to 172, which included being pummeled by the Rams to the tune of 260 yards of total offense and 16 first downs in the second half to the Eagles’ 72 yards of offense and four first downs. The Rams ran off 77 plays to the Eagles’ 58. The Rams had four plays of 20 yards or more. The Eagles had one. The Rams scored on touchdown drives of 67, 79 and 98 yards. The Eagles’ two touchdowns came on drives of 17 and 35 yards. Sirianni began his rookie season in 2021 at 2-5, before putting together the pieces of a promising team and running the ball behind a stalwart offensive line. He and the Eagles may be heading in that same 2-5 direction with Jacksonville, Carolina and Dallas up next—with little or nothing to be optimistic about. The difference this time is Sirianni is the captain of a listing ship, plagued by injuries, an offense that does not work under a first-year coordinator, and has been shutout in consecutive games during the second half, compounded by a cracking, tired defense that can no longer bail them out. The Rams had to win on Sunday. So, too, did the Eagles, if not for anything but to prove they still belong among the NFL’s elite. Since the Eagles started last season 4-0, they have now gone 9-8, and 9-9 if you include the Wild Card round playoff loss to San Francisco. This proves they are no longer elite, and far closer to being mediocre. The question that needs to be asked, hypothetically, is if Sirianni were to be fired tomorrow, what NFL teams would line up to grab him? Here it says not many— if any at all . He was able to stay out of the way and win with superior talent. That talent has now thinned and is hurting. His decisions seem to be getting more in the way (like the two times he opted to for it on fourth down against the Rams) than clearing the way for the Eagles. The Rams’ victory also marked the first time Los Angeles coach Sean McVay beat Sirianni. There was a lot of good—for three quarters, some bad and another ugly mess in the Eagles’ 24-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. The Good Jalen Hurts completing 10 of 18 passes for 83 yards and two touchdowns in the first half, completing passes to five different receivers. He went 2-for-9 the rest of the game for 10 yards—yep, that’s right, 10 yards passing in the second half . Makai Lemon coming through in the first half with three catches for 27 yards. Darius Cooper’s two catches for two touchdowns, two weeks after he caught the first touchdown of his career. On Cooper’s first score, he leaped over and literally grabbed the ball out of safety Quentin Lake’s hands for his second career TD. Later in the second quarter, Hurts found Cooper like he did on his first TD in the last seconds against Tennessee, wide open in the middle of the end zone. The Eagles getting 10 points on the first two turnovers the Eagles created this season. Andrew Mukuba’s interception on the Rams’ first drive led to a field goal, and Cooper DeSean’s pick near the end of the first half let to a touchdown and a 20-10 lead at intermission. Tank Bigsby’s 19-run to open the fourth quarter, and get the Eagles’ their first first down since Trent McDuffie was flagged for interference against Dontayvion in the last minute of the first half. Britain Covey’s tightrope 41-yard, second-quarter punt return to the Rams’ 17, which set up Cooper’s first TD. Cooper DeSean’s interception to set up Cooper’s second touchdown near the end of the first half. Safety Andrew Mukuba coming up with the Eagles’ first turnover this season , an interception at the Rams’ 49-yard line on the Rams’ first possession. The Eagles entered the game minus-5 in turnover differential. This time, Mukuba, whose play as been sporadic at best in the first three games, set up Jake Elliott’s 29-yard field goal—the first time the Eagles scored in the first quarter this season. Linebacker Jeremiah Trotter Jr. filling in nicely for the injured Zack Baun with game-highs 15 tackles and 10 solos, solidifying the middle of the field , along with further proving he deserves to be an NFL starter for someone. The Eagles scored for the first time in the first quarter this season. Up until Jake Elliott’s 29-yard field goal with 8:38 left to play in the first quarter, the Eagles had been outscored 17-0 in the first quarter. They at least scored for the first time this season in the first quarter and now have been 20-3. Rookie third-round draft pick Markel Bell doing a great job in place of Lane Johnson at right tackle. The Bad The Eagles started the game with a three-and-out and lost Saquon Barkley for the game with a pulled right hamstring on the first play of the Eagles’ second drive. Losing Quinyon Mitchell for the second half, leaving the Eagles with Jon Jones at one corner. Tank Bigsby leaving the game with a leg injury with 3:48 to play. The Ugly Blowing a 10-point fourth-quarter lead. The Eagles led by 10 twice, 13-3 with 5:44 left in the first half, and 20-10 entering the fourth quarter. Kyren Williams scoring the winning touchdown with 1:10 to play running through Trotter, who overall played well, DeJean, who also played well, Jalyx Hunt, who is becoming a liability, and safety Michael Carter II. Tackling has been an issue with the Eagles this season (see: Tennessee’s Tyjae Spears ripping down the sideline for a 27-yard run—on a fourth-quarter third-and-22 play). The Eagles going 0-for-12 on third-down conversions. It was an all-time worse for the Eagles at home, since they went 0-for-10 on third-down conversions in Week 7 in 2001 against the Baltimore Ravens. The Eagles did not have a passing first down in the second half. Backup corner Jon Jones (who?) nailing Williams out of bounds for a personal foul with just over 5 minutes to play, which brought the Rams to the Eagles’ 13. It led to Los Angeles scoring a 1-yard Williams’ touchdown and bringing the Rams to within 20-17 with 3:59 to play. It finished a 98-yard, 10-play drive that put the Rams within a field goal of tying the game. Linebacker Jihaad Campbell can’t cover anyone it seems. Completion after completion on Monday and again on Sunday…

full_text: Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images | Getty Images We are just about a quarter of the way through the 2026 NFL season already, and while the Eagles seemed to avoid injury issues in the first two weeks, they’ve really stacked up in their last two games. Heading into the Week 4 matchup against the Rams, the Eagles had six players inactive due to injury: DeVonta Smith Dallas Goedert Hollywood Brown Fred Johnson Zack Baun Marcus Epps And then, things spiraled completely out of control during the Rams game, with Saquon Barkley suffering a hamstring injury early in the first quarter: Saquon Barkley (hamstring – ruled out) Quinyon Mitchell ( knee – never returned ) Jonathan Greenard ( ankle – ruled out ) Tank Bigsby A few guys were also evaluated in the medical tent before ultimately being cleared to return: Drew Kendall Cooper DeJean It wasn’t due to injury, but Lane Johnson was inactive for Sunday’s game too due to personal reasons , so his status moving forward is also questionable. All-in-all, the Eagles will have a lot of questions to answer as far as the roster goes moving forward, and hopefully some of these starters will be able to return soon.

title: Steelers Week 4 grades in loss to Browns
summary: After four weeks, the Pittsburgh Steelers find themselves in third place in the AFC North, holding a tiebreaker over the Cincinnati Bengals, who lost on Sunday to the Jacksonville Jaguars. It makes it that much more frustrating that the Steelers were unable to take care of their own business and get to 3-1. Instead, Pittsburgh […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images After four weeks, the Pittsburgh Steelers find themselves in third place in the AFC North, holding a tiebreaker over the Cincinnati Bengals, who lost on Sunday to the Jacksonville Jaguars. It makes it that much more frustrating that the Steelers were unable to take care of their own business and get to 3-1. Instead, Pittsburgh dropped their Week 4 game to Cleveland 27-24 on Thursday. With Week 4 wrapped up, we give our grades for the Steelers. Let’s dive in. Aaron Rodgers Jarrett Bailey: It was a mixed bag for Rodgers. On one hand, he had a great fourth quarter that featured two touchdown passes. On the other hand, he failed to pull the trigger on a pair of throws that would have changed the outcome. DK Metcalf got behind the Browns defense for what would have been an easy score, but Rodgers didn’t see it. Metcalf was also open on the Steelers’ final play in regulation that could have put them in range for a potential game-tying field goal. He also held the ball too long, which made him responsible for more than one of the five sacks he took. Grade: C+ Joey Bray: This is a very tough grade for me. On the one hand, Rodgers brought the team all the way back down 14 in the 4th quarter by making one impressive throw after another. His quarterback sneak on the 2-point conversion attempt late in the contest capped off one of the best quarters of football Rodgers has played in a Steelers uniform. With that being said, it was quite obvious throughout this game that Rodgers’ lack of mobility put the Steelers in tough situations too often. The veteran quarterback was sacked 5 times and took 10 hits. While some of that is on the offensive line, the lack of mobility makes Rodgers an easy target for teams that love to blitz like Cleveland. There is only so much Rodgers can do at his age, as he is simultaneously digging the Steelers out of holes that he puts them in. Grade: C Offensive Line Jarrett Bailey: The offensive line wasn’t perfect. Max Iheanachor made Sam Williams look like Lawrence Taylor, and Rodgers was sacked five times. However, the fault can’t all go on the shoulders of the guys up front. The Steelers’ receivers couldn’t gain any separation, which led to Rodgers having to try and create. When you hold the ball longer all night, naturally more sacks will happen. They could have been better, but could have been worse, as well. Grade: C+ Joey Bray: After an impressive game from the offensive line with Max Iheanachor and Brock Hoffman making their Steelers debuts, it was a bit of a different story in Week 4. As we talked about with Rodgers, I think it is more than fair to say the offensive line is responsible for some of the sacks and quarterback hits that Rodgers endured. However, Rodgers’ immobility does his line absolutely no favors. The run blocking was more than fine, as the Steelers averaged just under five yards per gain. The important thing to keep in mind is that this offensive line is incredibly young and still gelling together. There will be plenty of ups and downs with this unit in the early stages of the season. Grade: C Jaylen Warren Jarrett Bailey: Warren continues to show that the offense should run through him by putting up a second consecutive game of 100+ scrimmage yards. He averaged 5.5 yards per carry and continues to be a strong receiver out of the backfield. More of No. 30 will lead to more wins. Grade: A- Joey Bray: Are you kidding me? Jaylen Warren is having a career year in 2026. With fellow back Rico Dowdle still nursing a toe injury, Warren once again took care of the Steelers’ rushing duties. Coming fresh off a game in which Warren averaged over seven yards per carry, the running back once again proved why he deserves to be the Steelers’ feature back even when Dowdle is fully healthy. Warren used his 17 carries to pick up 93 yards and added 33 yards on three receptions. He should, and will continue to be, the engine of the Steelers offense. Grade: A+ Pass Coverage Jarrett Bailey: If only the Steelers gave a fair contract offer to their good press-man cornerback and didn’t lowball him on guaranteed money. For a group that came into the year very deep, they are all of a sudden very thin, and struggled immensely to slow down the Browns passing game. With Jamel Dean dealing with an ankle injury, they need to bring in someone from the outside. Grade: D- Joey Bray: This secondary desperately needs a bump. I find it hard to be on Daylen Everette like most are right now, given the fact that the play in which Denzel Boston ran by him for a chunk gain downfield was a miscommunication and not all on the rookie corner. Jaylen Ramsey came into the contest playing on a broken wrist on just three days’ rest, and Jamel Dean aggravated an ankle injury that kept him out for most of the contest. All of that said, this is not a strong unit right now, but they are nowhere near healthy. However, this was a rough showing from them. Deshaun Watson was quite efficient, with a 94.0 passer rating, but he was far from perfect. There were often receivers open downfield as Watson extended the play. There is a little bit of hope, as safety DeShon Elliott is eligible to come off of injured reserve as early as next week, which would be a massive boost to a secondary that needs help fast. Grade: D ​Pass Rush Jarrett Bailey: The Steelers had the seventh-worst pressure percentage in Week 4 entering Monday before the Saints and Falcons could be considered. That said, when they did get pressure, they got to Watson quick, ranking seventh in time to pressure. I don’t blame the pass rushers for a largely down night as much as I blame the lack of blitzes. The Steelers only sent five or more rushes on 18.9 percent of snaps, and the Browns got rid of the ball in an average of 2.42 seconds, which was the fifth-fastest rate in the league in Week 4. Grade: C+ Joey Bray: I thought the pass rush got home and pressured Watson quite a bit on Thursday, but Watson’s legs allowed him to escape more often than not. TJ Watt continued his Defensive Player of the Year-caliber start to the season with a sack and a forced fumble in the contest. Jack Sawyer got his hand on a pass that ended up causing an interception. I am becoming just a tad worried about Nick Herbig, who has yet to record a sack this season after signing a massive extension in the offseason. Herbig did make several plays in the run game on Thursday Night, so there is no real reason to panic just yet. Grade: B- Tackling Jarrett Bailey: A big part of waiting to put out our grades was because I wanted to see where the Steelers ranked in terms of miss tackles in Week 4. Entering Sunday night, they missed the most tackles of any team with 14. Inexcusable performance from the defense. Grade: F Joey Bray: According to Pro Football Focus, the Steelers missed 14 tackles in Week 4. Comparatively, the unit missed seven tackles in their Week 3 contest against the Bengals. This was not an isolated issue for one position group, as just about every unit on the defense missed several opportunities to bring Cleveland down at some point in the game. This was an overall poor showing from the defense who is still struggling with basic things like communication and tackling. Grade: F Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Snap Reactions: Emanuel Wilson capitalizes on Jadarian Price’s absence
summary: On Sunday afternoon at Lumen Field, the Seattle Seahawks moved to 3-1 on the season by holding on to defeat the Los Angeles Chargers 30-23 after having jumped out to a three-touchdown lead in the third quarter. When the Seahawks had the ball, Emanuel Wilson saw the bulk of the work at running back, playing […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Seattle, Washington, USA; Seattle Seahawks running back Emanuel Wilson (23) runs for a touchdown against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first half at Lumen Field. Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Sunday afternoon at Lumen Field, the Seattle Seahawks moved to 3-1 on the season by holding on to defeat the Los Angeles Chargers 30-23 after having jumped out to a three-touchdown lead in the third quarter. When the Seahawks had the ball, Emanuel Wilson saw the bulk of the work at running back, playing 60 percent of the offensive snaps, with George Holani at just 37 percent and Velus Jones seeing the field for his first two offensive snaps of the season. Wilson turned those snaps into 21 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown, to go with three receptions for 39 yards and a receiving touchdown. Wilson’s 81 yards marked the fourth time in his career he’s broken the 75 yard rushing mark in a game, including the second time in the past three weeks. At right guard the rotation between Christian Haynes and Beau Stephens continued with yet another week of a roughly 60/40 split. At times Stephens has looked good, and at other times he has looked like a rookie fifth round pick. However, perhaps the most notable stat from the rotation is the fact that of the eight pressures credited to Seattle offensive linemen Sunday, four of them were allowed by Haynes. Whether it was simply a poor matchup, opponents have enough tape to know the weaknesses to exploit when Haynes is in pass blocking or some other reason, whatever the reason for the struggles Sunday, with Anthony Bradford out for at least two more weeks right guard will continue to be a spot to keep an eye on. Lastly, while fans call for more Tory Horton, the coaching staff seems to have other ideas. After missing the season opener, Horton’s snap counts and the percentage of offensive snaps played has decreased in each of the past two weeks: Week 2: 22 snaps, 31.4% of offensive snaps Week 3: 15 snaps, 22.4% of offensive snaps Week 4: 10 snaps, 16.7% of offensive snaps The most likely culprit to point a finger at would likely be the simple fact that even as some receivers are producing more at a younger age, wide receiver remains one of the slowest to develop positions in the NFL due to the complexity of NFL route trees compared to most college systems. Whether that is what is preventing Horton from seeing more snaps or not is something to which fans are almost certain to be paying attention in the coming weeks. On defense, the secondary looked revitalized with the return of Julian Love, who played every snap. Notably, Trevon Diggs saw his first regular season action of the season after earning an elevation from the practice squad, while Nehemiah Pritchett played less than he had in any game so far this season. In spite of that limited playing time against the Chargers, with just five more snaps over the remaining 13 regular season games Pritchett will set a career high. And, as always, special teams continues to belong to Brady Russell, as he led the Seahawks with 30 special teams snaps played. Interestingly, though, former wide receiver turned defensive end turned linebacker Connor O’Toole finished right behind Russell with 29 special teams snaps. From there Mike Morris, A.J. Finley, Patrick O’Connell and Tyrice Knight all played 24 special teams snaps, with Julian Neal right behind them with 23. And now it’s on to Week 5 and an opportunity to take over first place, via tiebreaker, in the NFC West.
author: John Gilbert

title: Seahawks won’t have Zach Charbonnet, Leonard Williams a maybe versus 49ers
summary: Sunday the Seattle Seahawks defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 30-23 at Lumen Field to keep pace with the San Francisco 49ers, who sit alone atop the NFC West at 4-0. And now comes Week 5 and a matchup against those undefeated 49ers, which means an opportunity for Seattle to take over first place in the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 04: Leonard Williams #99 of the Seattle Seahawks receives medical attention against the Los Angeles Chargers during the fourth quarter at Lumen Field on October 04, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday the Seattle Seahawks defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 30-23 at Lumen Field to keep pace with the San Francisco 49ers, who sit alone atop the NFC West at 4-0. And now comes Week 5 and a matchup against those undefeated 49ers, which means an opportunity for Seattle to take over first place in the division by knocking the Niners out of the top spot. However, when the teams face off Sunday, the Seahawks will once again be without 2026 first round pick Jadarian Price, who is on injured reserve for at least another three weeks. That brings the discussion to 2023 second round pick Zach Charbonnet and a potential return from injured reserve, but any hopes for that were shot down by head coach Mike Macdonald Monday. Mike Macdonald injury updates on @SeattleSports "Zach Charbonnet will get team reps this week, and that’s exciting. He will not play this week." Leonard Williams: “ It’s an ankle; we are optimistic, and we will see this week.” @CascadiasportsN @Seahawks — MazvitaMaraire (@MazvitaMaraire) October 5, 2026 Thus, barring the addition of a veteran free agent, such as Joe Mixon, it appears as though Seattle fans have another week of the former undrafted duo of Emanuel Wilson and George Holani, with Velus Jones seeing situational spot snaps. However, what could be even more important news on the injury front is the availability of All-Pro defensive lineman Leonard Williams. Williams suffered an ankle injury in the second half against Los Angeles and Macdonald was noncommital regarding Williams’ availability for the showdown against San Francisco. Williams is a huge piece of the Seattle defense, and while Macdonald says he is optimistic, Macdonald is a dad, and “we will see” more often than not tends to be dad speak for “no.” Should Williams be unable to play against San Francisco it would be a big blow for a defense that has given up far more points than they would prefer the past couple of weeks to opponents of a far lower caliber than the 49ers offense the Seahawks defense will face in Week 5. And now it’s on to the Wednesday injury report.
author: John Gilbert

title: Seahawks-Chargers post-game recap: NFL at last completes decades-long transition to flag football
summary: In the last 120 minutes of their young season, we’ve seen the worst the 2026 Seattle Seahawks have to offer. The three turnovers in Washington that sank an offensive renaissance. Then, early defensive domination was undone by untimely mistakes and lack of discipline back at home. Sloppiness in all three phases on critical downs gifted […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Seattle, Washington, USA; Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh greets Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike MacDonald after the game at Lumen Field. Mandatory Credit: Steven Bisig-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect In the last 120 minutes of their young season, we’ve seen the worst the 2026 Seattle Seahawks have to offer. The three turnovers in Washington that sank an offensive renaissance. Then, early defensive domination was undone by untimely mistakes and lack of discipline back at home. Sloppiness in all three phases on critical downs gifted points to opponents in close games, repeatedly. In their last 120 minutes, more things went wrong than a fan can count, even a Sea-soned Hawks fan, and still Seattle earned a split. Depending on your point of view, that’s either a reason to rejoice or to worry. Ah, who am I kidding — been doing a bit of both myself and I’ll guess you have too. It’s reassuring to be able to win even playing under your talent level. These aren’t the Dolphins or Cardinals, who have basically room for error if they want to post the W. Speaking of inferior teams, whooping the winless Los Angeles Chargers 30-13 as the fourth quarter begins is usually the recipe for a final quarter of self-congratulations, toasts in the crowd, and everyone in Seahawks Nation looking ahead to a Week 5 clash with the 49ers. Instead, one near-meltdown later, on the heels of stubbing your toe the week prior, the whole enterprise suddenly feels shaky. Seattle converted exactly one third down on the ground, did not sustain drives after building a three-score lead, and did not defend well enough to slam the door well before the final minute, but at least they did that. Uchenna Nwosu provided the capper on a big revenge game (those are real): Stay for the last split second though — John Fraley (@johndavidfraley.bsky.social) 2026-10-04T23:46:31.168Z LA was in position to win because of Justin Herbert’s excellent second half, implausible toughness, and a veritable plague of personal fouls — seven in total for Seattle. One early soft call on Brady Russell stomped on a drive before it had a chance to bloom. Connor O’Toole drew one for a borderline helmet-to-helmet when the punt returner unwisely declined to make a fair catch. Nick Emmanwori’s inexplicable headbutt with five seconds before half left stopped the clock and put the Chargers in comfortable field goal range. Devon Witherspoon tackled a dude four steps out of bounds, Emmanwori grabbed a facemask in the open field, DeMarcus Lawrence hit Herbert low and Derick Hall hit him late on the same drive. And that’s not counting the offsetting personal fouls somewhere in that first quarter, well before the game descended into a parody of itself. The 150 yards in penalties were a new franchise record. (More than any Raiders game back in the AFC West days, even.) Fortunately, the Chargers arrived with an entire case of beers, and at the contest’s most critical moments, they’d casually pull one out and ask the Seahawks to hold it. When Los Angeles was perfectly poised to conduct a proper game-winning drive with all three timeouts, Justin Eboigbe landed on Sam Darnold after his slide, freshening the downs for Seattle and forcing longtime Seahawks sufferer Jim Harbaugh to burn them after all. There’s a sequence in the third quarter that captures the essence of this flagfest better than any. Do note the expressions on Jason Myers’ and Michael Dickson’s faces — “What are we even doing, guys.” You probably saw these at your watch party, in your row at the stadium, or on your own face at some point Sunday afternoon. Putting this whole Seahawks-Chargers sequence on tape because it's emblematic of the day — John Fraley (@johndavidfraley.bsky.social) 2026-10-05T00:11:57.867Z You can watch the video, but just in case you don’t: Greg Zabel isn’t on the field until the play clock hits 10, so he hurries to his assignment. The kick is snapped at zeroes, Myers pushes it right, giving LA excellent field position EXCEPT NO, there’s a late leverage call against the defense, first down Seattle instead. (The drive would end soon thereafter in three points, which seemed superfluous at the time but ended up pretty dang important.) Anyway. It’s fun to complain about a win, sure beats the alternative. Thirty penalties and countless bullet wounds in everybody’s feet later, the Seahawks had emerged with their third victory of the year. Truly, ‘bout the only surprise is their victory formation went off without a flag. The recap will omit most of the fouls, if possible. Before we get there! It would be criminal to not mention Emanuel Wilson’s big day. Not by choice entirely, Mike Macdonald and Brian Fleury traded their explosive but risky running attack for a more reliable, albeit boring dose of Wilson and George Holani. It frickin’ worked. (I will never stop quoting Pete Carroll no matter how many Super Bowls [four] Macdonald wins here.) Wilson rewarded his coaches, teammates and himself with a tough, tough 21-81-1 line and that first-quarter touchdown reception that sent the Chargers chasing the hosts for the rest of the afternoon. Factor in 51 more yards from Rashid Shaheed and Holani and you have the makings of a respectable running game. Which you’ll need. Q1: Seahawks 7, Chargers 3 Predator: The officiating crew Prey: Anyone watching How: We didn’t know it yet, but maybe we should’ve. Like when the officials found offsetting personal fouls that instant replay couldn’t locate. That should’ve alerted viewers. Then, Russell was dinged 15 for this “offense”: First quarter recap: this is a 15 yard penalty — John Fraley (@johndavidfraley.bsky.social) 2026-10-04T21:19:15.564Z Later, O’Toole’s personal came for leading with the helmet but you can see him pull up. Maybe it’s a flag but that exact hit is performed on every drive and Derius Davis never put his hand up. I don’t know what a crew can do when a team like the Seahawks repeatedly toes the line with over-aggressiveness some might call dirty. But it was hard to watch the parade of yellow. Action: In the most mulligan-y of starts conceivable, Herbert and Darnold traded interceptions on successive plays. What to say about that, except you’d like to win the turnover battle from there on out, and the Seahawks did. The Chargers offense settled in first though, with two rapid-fire first downs, one semi-explosive pass play and one questionable offsides against Nwosu to creep into field goal range. An eight-play, 30-yard drive off the pick resulted in three points. And when Seattle’s real opening possession ended in an awkward intentional grounding, the hangover from that Commander got real rear view mirror-like: objects are closer than they appear. No matter, O’Toole reached into his special toolebox and pulled out a timely fumble recovery. First O'Toole in the right place at the right time since Lawrence of Arabia — John Fraley (@johndavidfraley.bsky.social) 2026-10-04T20:48:08.068Z The game was barely five minutes old, and each possession was a whiplash. Add Weeks 3 and 4 together and a fan could be forgiven for believing they were watching the 2010s Chaoshawks again. (Recite the Kevin Clark tweet from memory, if you know what I mean.) Yet the pattern of this particular meeting had already manifested: the Chargers were happy to beat themselves, the Seahawks happy to oblige. Off the giveaway, it took exactly one play for Wilson to tilt the field. Little screen to the right, and with ball in hand he turned and went north-south with more determination than a Blackpoll warbler (safe to Google it, go ahead). Seattle ended up six points richer. The next seven possessions ended in punts. Emmanwori and Lawrence helped kill drives with tackles for loss, and as the second quarter took off, so did the Seahawks pass rush. title: Seahawks Droppings: Uchenna Nwosu mercifully ends repulsive game vs old team
summary: A win is a – hold on, there’s a flag. As I was saying, you can’t complain – wait, did I just see yellow fly again?  Let me try this again, beggars – oh for the love of God, there’s another one?!? That’s what the entire game felt like today…a sloppy, disjointed mess. It was […]
full_text: A win is a – hold on, there’s a flag. As I was saying, you can’t complain – wait, did I just see yellow fly again? Let me try this again, beggars – oh for the love of God, there’s another one?!? That’s what the entire game felt like today…a sloppy, disjointed mess. It was like preseason with the amount of stupid penalties committed by the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Chargers as each team tried to give the game away. However, the Seahawks were just a little smarter about being less dumb, barely holding on to a 30-23 win that had no right being as close as it was. Los Angeles came in with an 0-3 record, and played like it for the first three quarters. The Seahawks took advantage of turnovers, racing out to a 21-point lead in the third quarter. That should’ve been a comfortable cushion with the Dark Side defense, but it wasn’t. Seattle continued to commit asinine penalties and allow long third and fourth down conversions. Los Angeles had the ball with over 1:30 left only down seven points. Luckily, former Charger Uchenna Nwosu strip-sacked Justin Herbert with Derick Hall recovering the ball to preserve the win. It was pretty ugly. Seahawks Droppings The refs were flag happy, but I thought all of the calls were legit. That means that the Seahawks have a penalty – and by extension – a discipline problem right now. Many of those penalties were personal fouls. Many of those extended drives. You just can’t do that against good teams and win. Seattle racked up 14 penalties for 150 yards which is inexcusable. This is a pattern that has been relatively consistent this season going back to preseason. It will need to turn around or Seattle will lose games because of it. Jason Myers missed an extra point, got bailed out by a penalty after missing a long FG, and had another kickoff out of bounds penalty . I’m trying not to get too concerned, and give him the benefit of the doubt, but that’s becoming more difficult each week. The defense wasn’t up to its standard today in the second half. That late 4th and 7 conversion was the stuff of nightmares. Yes, they forced four turnovers…yet to do that and only win by seven points isn’t ideal. Part of the reason for the defense running out of gas was the offense taking their foot off of it in the fourth quarter . Seattle had 30 points prior to the final frame, adding none in the final 15 minutes. Even an extra field goal or long drive would’ve made this game much more comfortable. Seattle had the ball twice in the last 5 minutes and couldn’t close out the game. Emanuel Wilson was quite good as the feature back today with over 100 total yards and 2 TDs . He always seems to finish forward and has shown decent hands out of the backfield. Seattle will need him to hold down the fort until Zach Charbonnet can play. Sam Darnold had only 13 completions, and was under pressure quite a bit . He made a few plays with his legs which was nice to see coming off of his injury. The slant throw to Tory Horton was a thing of beauty. His boneheaded INT on the first offensive play was not. Jaxon Smith-Njigba didn’t get to the 100-yard mark for the first time in 2026, yet was still a factor in the game with a huge early third-and-long conversion . He led the team with 76 yards, followed by Emanuel Wilson’s 39 yards. Rashid Shaheed was more active today, especially out of the backfield where he contributed 33 yards a TD. Shaheed also fumbled again on a kickoff, but got the ball back. I don’t like to see that. What I would like to see, however, is Tory Horton getting more run. All he does is seemingly catch TDs, with another one today. I feel like he could be a much bigger weapon with all the attention that JSN, Shaheed, and Cooper Kupp get. Maybe Horton will be a bigger part as the season rolls on. Ernest Jones IV had a pretty awesome game with 12 tackles, 1 TFL, 1 Sack, and 1 INT . Nick Emmanwori also had a nifty sack…and a dumb penalty that helped the Chargers have an even more makeable FG . I thought DeMarcus Lawrence had a much bigger impact than his 3 tackles and 2 TFL stat line suggests. I’m not too mad at him for his low hit on Herbert since he was already going down to the ground and there wasn’t much he could do about it. Plenty of players took turns being boneheads on defense. Seattle has a hell of a lot to shore up prior to playing the San Francisco 49ers next week. You better believe that the undefeated Niners will be a much bigger test than anyone the Seahawks have faced thus far in 2026. Hopefully Leonard Williams’ ankle injury isn’t serious, as the team will need him in a big way. Coming off of a terrible loss last week, it would’ve been nice to see the Seahawks make a statement and close the Chargers out in the fourth quarter. Oh well, it could’ve been – oh get the f— out of here with the flags, the game is over!!

title: Seahawks vs. Chargers flag-fest was historically ugly in multiple ways
summary: The Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Chargers playing to a 30-23 scoreline would suggest an entertaining game. It was certainly dramatic toward the end when the Seahawks’ 27-6 lead dwindled, but entertaining it was not. Between countless undisciplined penalties, very questionable calls on both teams by Scott Novak’s officiating crew, and a healthy serving of […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Chargers playing to a 30-23 scoreline would suggest an entertaining game. It was certainly dramatic toward the end when the Seahawks’ 27-6 lead dwindled, but entertaining it was not. Between countless undisciplined penalties, very questionable calls on both teams by Scott Novak’s officiating crew, and a healthy serving of failed third downs, this was not one that will go down as an NFL Throwback channel classic. We should’ve known we were in for a wild day when the game started with Dueling Interceptions, the worst ever sequel to Dueling Banjos . Drake Thomas will not get fooled by your play action attempts. pic.twitter.com/gf3Rq6cCt1 — Billy M (@BillyM_91) October 4, 2026 first career interception pic.twitter.com/9nSXvk8mY1 — Los Angeles Chargers (@chargers) October 4, 2026 First time since at least 1978 that an NFL game began with two picks in two plays From Seahawks.com senior reporter John Boyle : Two plays, two interceptions; making it the first time since at least 1978, per the Elias Sports Bureau, that both teams threw interceptions on their first play from scrimmage in the same game. Neither pick was a good decision and frankly Herbert’s was so bad that if Drake Thomas had an invisibility cloak then Josh Jobe probably gets the interception instead. Seahawks vs. Chargers had most penalties in NFL regulation game in 26 years You’ve lived the story by now. Scott Novak’s crew was flag happy from the start, and the Seahawks and Chargers were both heavily punished. There were 30 total accepted penalties for a whopping 280 yards, with multiple drive-extending infractions called on both teams. Seattle’s 150 penalty yards was a team record. According to Stathead , the Seahawks and Chargers had the most accepted penalties in a non-overtime game since the New Orleans Saints and St. Louis Rams combined for 31 penalties in November 2000. It looks like it’s only the 12th ever non-OT game to have north of 30 penalties. Only one Seahawks game has ever had more penalties The year was 1976. It’s year one of the Seahawks in the National Football League. They’re 0-5 while the fellow newcomers, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, are also 0-5 and on their way to 0-14. Seattle prevailed 13-10 for its first win in franchise history, but not without committing 15 penalties for 120 yards. Not to be outdone, the Buccaneers had 20 penalties for 190 yards. The Seahawks won on a blocked game-tying field goal in the final minute, punctuated by a personal foul penalty on the Bucs after the play was over. It remains the franchise record for most combined penalties (35) in a game, and had the Seahawks and Chargers played to overtime it really would’ve put that “record” under threat. Hey, the Seahawks won. There are no style points like this is for the College Football Playoff. You’d just rather not have a game look like this.
author: Mookie Alexander

title: Winners and Losers from Seahawks’ needlessly close win vs. Chargers
summary: Hey, the Seattle Seahawks got a win over the Los Angeles Chargers. Was it borderline unwatchable because of all the penalties, punts, and the near collapse from a 27-6 lead to a 30-23 score? Yeah. Is it still a win? Yes it is. Given the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers both won, it […]
full_text: Hey, the Seattle Seahawks got a win over the Los Angeles Chargers. Was it borderline unwatchable because of all the penalties, punts, and the near collapse from a 27-6 lead to a 30-23 score ? Yeah. Is it still a win? Yes it is. Given the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers both won, it was pretty important for the Seahawks to stay ahead of the Rams and not lose contact with San Francisco ahead of the big Week 5 showdown. Let’s get to Winners and Losers while this game is still etched in my brain. Seattle Seahawks Winners Emanuel Wilson’s first start is one of his best performances in the NFL If I could give a game ball to anyone on the Seahawks offense, it’s Emanuel Wilson. He had 81 hard-earned yards on 21 carries, his first Seahawks rushing TD, and he took a 23-yard screen pass (!) to the house. Over 100 scrimmage yards for Wilson on a day when Seattle’s offense was far from crisp. He’s not fast or particularly great with lateral quickness, but he runs hard and can play through contact well when he gets downhill. Rashid Shaheed makes the most of his limited touches Only three touches on offense for Shaheed, but one was a 28-yard touchdown run, another was a five-yard carry on a 1st and 10, and his lone reception was a 20-yard catch. Given his slow start to the season, he showed up in a major way even on a low volume of offensive plays. I thought he was agonizingly close to breaking a big punt return, too. Tory Horton is back in the end zone How about a touchdown for the first time since last year’s Commanders game? It was Horton’s only catch and only target, but it was a smooth slant on a Sam Darnold check at the line of scrimmage. Hopefully we see more of Horton in the offense as the weeks progress. Uchenna Nwosu saves the day There was a real chance the Seahawks could’ve given up a tying touchdown, if not a winning touchdown on that final drive. Uchenna Nwosu closed the show by haunting his former team, strip-sacking Justin Herbert and sealing the win. Nwosu has played well throughout the season and now has the sack to show it, plus he’s as good as it gets when it comes to edge-setting in the run game. I would walk through walls for Ernest Jones IV Ernest had a sack and an interception, and there’s a chance he could end this weekend as the NFC Defensive Player of the Week for a phenomenal performance. The Seahawks defense (when they weren’t getting flagged) stifled the Chargers offense, and Jones was a big part of that stifling. He’s one of the leaders on the team and he is a premier inside linebacker. Drake Thomas bounces back Last week was not one of Thomas’ better days at the office. He started this game with an interception on the first play from scrimmage, and had a TFL on a screen pass. Thomas is just a fireplug of a linebacker and is extremely fun to watch. Nick Emmanwori looked like Nick Emmanwori, albeit with two bad penalties E-Man had a normal snap count and had made them count. He picked up a sack, a pass defensed, nine tackles (with two TFLs), and even generated pressures while lined up as an edge rusher. I’m not pleased with the headbutt penalty (more on that later) but otherwise he was dominant against the Chargers offense. Connor O’Toole is on the spot Derius Davis muffed a punt, and O’Toole was there for the recovery (which led to a touchdown). While he’s not part of the defensive rotation, he is a valuable special teams contributor when active on game days. I will not hold the helmet-to-helmet penalty against him because that was just bogus. Join Field Gulls on game day! Stay on top of every Seahawks update and debate every snap with other members of the 12s. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . Seattle Seahawks Losers Seattle has to clean its penalties up As awful as Scott Novak’s crew was, many of those Seahawks penalties were legit. The headbutt penalty by Nick Emmanwori on Cole Strange was a silly one to commit, especially given how flag-happy the refs were for other penalties earlier in the game. Emmanwori committed a face mask that extended a drive, Devon Witherspoon was flagged for unnecessary roughness, Derick Hall got a roughing the passer (which I didn’t like, but I think is correct by the letter of the law) on 3rd and 24, it’s all got to be fixed. Likewise for the pre-snap penalties like Jalen Sundell rocking in his stance before snapping the ball. The Seahawks are one of the league’s most penalized teams and they were their own worst enemy at the moment. When they run into a crew as flag-happy as Novak’s, that is a cause for concern. Brian Fleury needs to figure a couple of things out Seattle’s offensive coordinator has been put in a tough spot with injuries at key positions. The Seahawks third-down passing game is not consistent enough to threaten teams, and if Seattle is going to continue to get blitzed into oblivion then he needs to identify and find better blitz beaters. They’re otherwise not equipped to come out on the positive side of obvious passing situations. Additionally, too many drives are ending because of 2nd and long runs to nowhere, and he needs to figure out what plays are better run for Emanuel Wilson versus George Holani. The latter should never ever be the short-yardage option, and certainly not to the weaker side of the line. On the plus side, Fleury has fixed the screen game which looked like an impossible task. That’s a big plus for the first-year playcaller. Enough of the Christian Haynes/Beau Stephens rotation If Christian Haynes cannot be trusted to handle a full game of action then I don’t know what to say. Your backup guard cannot be in a time-share deal because you want to give Beau Stephens rookie reps in non-garbage time situations. Haynes has been fine and to my recollection hasn’t given up a pressure yet. Start Haynes until Anthony Bradford comes back. End of story. There was one series where Stephens got worked on multiple run plays, and I’m just exasperated that we’re still doing this. More special teams inconsistency Jason Myers missed an extra point, missed a field goal (and was given a second life thanks to a Chargers penalty), and had another kickoff short of the landing zone. Coverage continues to be an issue on kickoffs, although at least they took advantage of Derius Davis’ muffed punt. Something is not clicking with this ST unit on a consistent basis and it has to tighten up. George Holani is a good “everything but running the ball” running back I’ve harped on Holani a lot because John Schneider made glowing comments about him over the offseason after Kenneth Walker left. There was even some idle chatter among fans that George could get significant workload. Holani is ordinarily a very good pass-protecting back, a good special teams player who can return kicks, and a quality receiving back. When he actually has to run the ball he is so limited because he’s not fast, doesn’t break a lot of tackles, and can’t push piles. Holani had 7 carries for 18 yards and now has 153 career rushing yards on 47 attempts. His longest carry to date is still 9 yards. These are fullback numbers. When Zach Charbonnet comes back, it should be Emanuel Wilson and Charbonnet splitting the touches and Holani only in for the most situational snaps (third and obvious passing, maybe two-minute drills, etc.). Hopefully Zach is back sooner rather than later. A rare off day for A.J. Barner Not one, but two drops for Seattle’s normally sure-handed tight ends. Three targets, one catch, two drops. Speaking of tight ends, what is up with Elijah Arroyo? Is he ever going to seriously get involved in this offense? Eric Saubert has more targets than he does! Monitoring closely Sam Darnold was nowhere near his best The opening play interception was gross and inexplicable. Darnold sort of settled down the rest of the way and did throw a couple of touchdowns, but he was nearly picked again…
author: Mookie Alexander

title: Leonard Williams injury update: Seahawks star believed to have avoided serious ankle injury
summary: After having multiple key starters sidelined across their first three games, the Seattle Seahawks’ front looked poised take a hit after star defensive tackle Leonard Williams went down with an apparent injury against the Los Angeles Chargers, but it seems as though he avoided the worst case scenario. According to head coach Mike Macdonald, Williams’ […]
full_text: After having multiple key starters sidelined across their first three games, the Seattle Seahawks’ front looked poised take a hit after star defensive tackle Leonard Williams went down with an apparent injury against the Los Angeles Chargers, but it seems as though he avoided the worst case scenario. According to head coach Mike Macdonald, Williams’ ankle injury is not believed to be serious. However, it remains unclear if he’ll undergo further testing or will be required to miss any time. Coach Mike Macdonald’s said it’s going to be “through, not around” for the #Seahawks next 2 days after team-record penalties, including 7 personal fouls. “Not acceptable.” Also says Leonard Williams’ injury the win over Chargers doesn’t look serious. @thenewstribune @933KJR pic.twitter.com/nFc2sCQC9c — Gregg Bell (@gbellseattle) October 5, 2026 The veteran defensive tackle exited the game just over halfway through the fourth quarter and was deemed questionable, but did not return. Although he finished the game on the sideline, Seattle had a comfortable 30-13 lead at the time he went down which could’ve possibly played a factor in their decision to keep him off the field. The injury occurred on a Justin Herbert goal line run and Williams remained on the turf for just over a minute before being helped to the sideline, where he entered the blue medical tent. Omarion Hampton punched it in for a score on the ensuing play and Williams was seen out of the tent and on the sideline before the Seahawks offense took the field, seemingly boding well for a potential return in the team’s Week 5 divisional clash against the San Francisco 49ers. A key piece of Seattle’s dominant top six, Williams recorded just one quarterback hit prior to his exit. It’ll be worth monitoring his status when Seattle releases their first injury report of the week on Wednesday night.

An ultra-physical battle of wills in which the 49er offense had to be very patient in grinding down the Broncos’ vaunted defense, […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Deebo Samuel Sr. #19 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after scoring a touchdown in the third quarter against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers knew what to expect from their Week 4 matchup with the Denver Broncos, and it played out exactly as they anticipated. San Francisco’s 24-14 win over Denver was a rock fight. An ultra-physical battle of wills in which the 49er offense had to be very patient in grinding down the Broncos’ vaunted defense, and which turned on a key special teams play from Siran Neal in the third quarter. They were able to pull out win in no small part thanks two players whose physicality was missing from the roster last season after they each made the decision to explore pastures new, only to find their way back to the 49ers this year. Dre Greenlaw and Deebo Samuel each opted to leave the 49ers in 2025. Greenlaw signed with the Broncos as a free agent, while Samuel requested a trade and was dealt to the Washington Commanders. Neither move worked out, and the 49ers made the decision to reunite with both players on one-year deals. Doing so is looking like an increasingly astute call by San Francisco, with their value to the team laid bare as they both produced key performances brought on by the same motivating factor. Greenlaw successfully channels extra emotion For Greenlaw, the motivation was obvious. The Broncos cut him in March, one year into a three-year deal, seemingly put off by an injury-affected 2025 season for the linebacker who infamously tore his Achilles running onto the field in the second quarter of the 49ers’ Super Bowl 58 defeat to the Chiefs. This was a revenge game for Greenlaw, and he made sure to make his presence felt. Greenlaw was everywhere against his former team, making 12 tackles, forcing a fumble and recording three pressures, all while regularly talking trash to Broncos head coach Sean Payton, whom he had to held back from confronting at the end of the game. Being deemed expendable by the Broncos lit a fire under a player who needs excuse to play with aggression, though the 49ers were happy he was able to keep it in check enough to avoid any costly unsportsmanlike penalties. Said head coach Kyle Shanahan of Greenlaw: “We knew he’d be excited going into this game. Dre’s excited going into every game, but this one meant a little more to him. I was a little nervous there in the first half. We told him, ‘You can get close, but don’t be so excited you give them an explosive with 15.’ And I really thought someone was going to get one in the second half of one of the teams, just challenged our team to make sure it wasn’t us. I don’t think anyone ended up getting one, but Dre held his emotions good enough today and led the team in tackles and had an unbelievable game. He’s had an unbelievable season so far and we’re so happy to have him back at home.” Fellow linebacker Fred Warner added: “There was definitely something a little extra for him this week. He got banged up last game. Everybody was asking him, ‘Hey, are you going to be able to make it?’ And he said, ‘I wouldn’t miss this one.’ He had extra emotion going into this game. I told him just to use it wisely, which he did. I was proud of him and he played a heck of a game. He’s played great all year. He’ll continue to play great for us. I’m glad he’s on our side now.” Greenlaw heeded those words, his display was full of emotion and energy, channeled in the right way, and it provided the 49er defense with something it arguably lacked last season when he was in Denver and Warner missed most of the season to an ankle injury. Pressed to elaborate on his feelings about Greenlaw, Shanahan replied: “I think people know, but like if I had to wear a jersey, I’d probably wear his. Just the way he plays, what he’s done for us over these years, going back to his rookie year and getting us the number one seed in Seattle with the play he made on the goal line. Just the way he inspires people because the way he plays. I think he’s an intimidation factor for the other side of the ball because of the way he plays, and it’s hard for us not to be as aggressive as possible with how he is out there. So, we missed him for the year, but it was good to, as we feel, get a family member back.” That intimidation factor was clear for all to see on Sunday and, in Samuel, the 49ers had a playmaker providing it on the other side of the ball. Samuel produces vintage display Greenlaw was given additional fire from the emotion of being doubted by one franchise. For Samuel, his impressive start to the season — which has seen him score three receiving touchdowns already — looks to have stemmed from a desire to dispel the notion that he had lost a step. After an indifferent 2024 with the 49ers, Samuel looked a long way from his devastating best during his sojourn with the Commanders, and San Francisco fans would have been forgiven for being somewhat skeptical about the idea of a second spell with the Niners. But his signing on a one-year, $7 million deal already looks like one of the best moves of the offseason, and left tackle Trent Williams believes the success Samuel has enjoyed through four games is a product of the wideout’s abilities being questioned. “I think knowing him as well as I do, this offseason was probably the first time in his career that he was doubted,” Williams said. “He’s always been supremely talented, always been a playmaker, and this league, it turns on you quick. I think him having to feel that doubt for the first time, I think it lit a fire in him.” Deebo breaking tackles and picking up 20 yards 😤 DENvsSF on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SiAgd5A8eB — NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026 The 49ers are reaping the benefits of Samuel’s desire to prove the skeptics wrong. There is an evident explosiveness to his play and, against the Broncos, his trademark bruising style of running with the ball in his hands was crucial to the Niners wearing Denver down. Samuel’s most tangible contribution to the win was, of course, his touchdown reception in the third quarter that gave the 49ers a lead they did not relinquish. But he also had a 22-yard run in the first quarter, a 20-yard rush in the second on a drive that led to a game-tying field goal, and an eight-yard reception that set up third-and-short on a scoring drive that ended in a Christian McCaffrey touchdown. In doing so, Samuel displayed the tackle-breaking ability that has underpinned his success in the NFL, leading to significant praise from Shanahan after the game. Kyle Shanahan is paying homage to Bill Walsh Shift & Motion to a Split Back Pro Set to run Counter Solid with Deebo Samuel👌 pic.twitter.com/oOaQt8GZGo — Coach Dan Casey (@CoachDanCasey) October 4, 2026 “I thought Deebo was huge today,” Shanahan said. “Those two runs in the first half that he had, I don’t think many people get the amount of yards that he got on that. I think both of them, I think they were about eight yards, but he does something amazing to get over 20 on both of them. “He was really big at the end on a couple. They’re all less than 10-yard catches, but they were big catches that kept us ahead of the sticks. Then Brock finding him to get in the end zone was huge too.” In bringing back Greenlaw and Samuel, the 49ers took calculated, low-risk bets on players they developed and whom they trust. Four games into the season, both bets are paying significant dividends, with Sunday’s hard-fought victory perhaps the best illustration yet of their worth to this team. Greenlaw and Samuel have had very similar journeys in recent times. On Sunday, they both thrived amid the same urge to silence those who doubted what they had left in tank. Now, back with the team that never lost faith in them, their shared desire has the chance to help make their reunion season with the 49ers a very…
author: Nicholas McGee

full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported that the San Francisco 49ers will be without Kyle Juszczyk for a ‘couple of weeks’ due to a hyperextended knee. Those were the initial tests. Juszczyk will undergo an MRI on Monday to confirm whether those initial tests were accurate. Juszczyk has played a pivotal role for the 49ers this season. They ask him to do everything . He caught a slant route from Brock Purdy that led to a first down, and the other reception also moved the chains for the offense. But it’s been the blocking and usage on dash motion that have helped the running game take off this season. Juszczyk is a big reason why. In Week 3, the 49ers had Juszczyk covering punts. If the team is short on depth in one area, Juszczyk is probably the backup. Short on wide receivers and with Jake Tonges going down, Juszczyk has lined up everywhere on offense. Here’s a look at his snap alignment through four weeks: Tight end – 44 Slot/stack WR – 35 FB -23 Wing (attached off-tackle) – 14 WR – 6 RB – 3 It’s a huge loss for an offense that prides itself on multiplicity. Brayden Willis played 10 snaps and ran three routes for Juszczyk. Willis missed one of his 7 run-blocking snaps. And now he’ll go against the best defense in the league. We’ll see whether he is the fullback or they ask more of Luke Farrell. Kyle’s update, 11:47 a.m. PT: Ian Rapoport shared that Juszczyk has a bone bruise that will keep him out for 2-3 weeks. Juszczyk is also dealing with a knee sprain.

title: 3 stars from the 49ers win over the Broncos: Siran Neal saves the day
summary: It wasn’t the most convincing of wins, but it was a win nonetheless, as the San Francisco 49ers withstood the Denver Broncos and the heat, moving to 4-0 on the season with a 24-14 victory. A slow first half for both sides ended with a blocked Eddy Pineiro field goal, which added to the slow […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images It wasn’t the most convincing of wins, but it was a win nonetheless, as the San Francisco 49ers withstood the Denver Broncos and the heat, moving to 4-0 on the season with a 24-14 victory. A slow first half for both sides ended with a blocked Eddy Pineiro field goal, which added to the slow start, but things woke up late in the third quarter to San Francisco’s advantage. And with such a close game, it only took a couple of big plays to swing the momentum the 49ers’ way. We use two of Sunday’s stars to acknowledge who made those game-changing plays: 3rd star: TE Georgie Kittle It wasn’t the big momentum swing, but it was the play that put things to rest for the 49ers. Kittle was held to a relatively quiet game up until the 2:25 mark in the fourth quarter. Until then, he was targeted five times for three receptions and 14 yards before the 49ers took a three-point lead late in the game. Facing a second-and-8 with a chance to run the clock down to the two-minute warning, the 49ers went to Kittle. A slow-developing screen gave the tight end oodles of space, and after making the first man miss, it was a footrace to the end zone. Kittle outpaced Talonoa Hufanga for a 56-yard score and gave the 49ers an insurmountable 10-point lead. The speed looked good for a player nine months removed from an Achilles injury. Kittle’s day was boosted by the big catch, finishing with 70 yards on four receptions and a touchdown. 2nd star: DB Siran Neal Kittle’s play might have sealed the win, but Neal’s special teams play first swung the momentum toward the 49ers. The third quarter started the way the first half did for the 49ers offense: slow. San Francisco opened the third quarter with two drives totaling six plays for four yards. That’s when Corliss Waitman was called onto the field for his fourth punt of the game and second of the third quarter with Marvin Mims back to return. Waitman launched a 61-yard punt with Neal gunning down towards Mims. Mims decided to take the return even with Neal closing in, and the decision was a poor one. Neal held Mims to just a one-yard return, but before Mims’ elbow could hit the ground, the impact of his wrist hitting the ground jarred the ball loose, and Neal was able to recover. After a quick review, the call was confirmed, and the 49ers regained possession at the Denver 28-yard line. Nine plays later, the 49ers took the lead 10-3 with their first touchdown of the afternoon. The 49ers offense was floundering, but the field-position swing of Neal’s forced fumble changed things. Before Neal’s heroics, the offense had scored only three points through nearly three quarters. After the forced fumble, the 49ers scored 21 points in a little over a quarter. Neal’s takeaway completely flipped the game in San Francisco’s favor, and for that he earned Sunday’s No. 2 star. 1st star: WR Mike Evans Maybe his ribs are broken, maybe they aren’t, but you could tell that Evans was in pain on Sunday. And despite the pain, Evans still led all pass-catchers in receiving yards. In the gutsiest performance since Mac Jones in Los Angeles last season, Evans hauled down five passes for 76 yards, wincing and hobbling his way through Sunday. Evans was responsible for some of the biggest plays in the 49ers’ offense, with three receptions for 15 or more yards. He started his day with a big 18-yard gain to open the 49ers’ fourth drive. The catch-and-kick started what turned out to be the 49ers’ first scoring drive of the game, resulting in an Eddy Pineiro field goal. His next catch was his longest reception of the game. With 38 seconds left in the first half and the offense inside its own 20-yard line, Evans flipped the field with a 26-yard reception, getting the ball near midfield. This catch also led to a Pineiro field goal, but this kick was blocked, holding the drive without points. Evans’ last big play led to the game-winning score, after starting the 49ers’ first drive of the fourth quarter with a nine-yard grab to move the offense into plus territory. Several plays later, Evans almost got into the end zone, but a 17-yard reception moved the ball to the goal line, setting up a Christian McCaffrey touchdown to put the 49ers up 17-6. It’s not the most eye-popping line we’ve seen from Evans, but with the ribs obviously bothering him, it boosts the performance that much more. Throughout the season, we will track the three stars of the season by tallying points for each star award using a complex scoring system: three points for being the first star, two for the second, and one for the third. Through Week 4, the standings are: QB Brock Purdy – 7 points LB Fred Warner – 3 points WR Deebo Samuel – 3 points
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: NFC West Recap: 49ers remain in first place, Rams and Seahawks win
summary: 4-0. That’s all. The San Francisco 49ers are 4-0 and look like a 4-0 team. The Denver Broncos were the first big test for the 2026 offense, and they passed with flying colors. Yes, there were injured defensive backs with the Broncos, but the 49ers don’t have their starting wide receivers 100 percent healthy either. […]
full_text: (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images 4-0. That’s all. The San Francisco 49ers are 4-0 and look like a 4-0 team. The Denver Broncos were the first big test for the 2026 offense, and they passed with flying colors. Yes, there were injured defensive backs with the Broncos, but the 49ers don’t have their starting wide receivers 100 percent healthy either. The 49ers were nearly mistake-free, with a single penalty for five yards all game. Brock Purdy’s numbers were a bit more pedestrian with 19 for 30 and 218 yards, but his 107.4 passer rating has him now four games in without dropping below 100 for the metric. Oh, and another streak? Brock Purdy has yet to be sacked in 2026. Every game isn’t going to be pretty, but Purdy delivered where it mattered, especially that final touchdown to George Kittle. Unfortunately, the 49ers play in a competitive division, and two of the other three teams also notched wins. Arizona Cardinals (1-3) When the score had the Cardinals with a 14-3 lead over the New York Giants toward the end of the first quarter, I was going to repeat how the Cardinals were much better than their record was—and also that the Los Angeles Rams beating up a Giants squad without their starting quarterback wasn’t near as earth-shattering as some may want to believe. Then the Giants came back. At the end of the half, it was 19-17; the Giants and the Cardinals would be trading leads before the game ended. While Giants quarterback Jameis Winston did Jameis Winston things, like throwing two interceptions and taking four sacks, Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett threw three interceptions and only averaged 4.7 yards per completion. Ick. Arizona put up 123 yards of total rushing. And 166 yards of total receiving. I don’t mean to make this math class, but that’s under 300 yards of total offense. It’s very hard to win football games with that and three interceptions to boot. The sad part is, the Giants weren’t exactly efficient either, getting 337 yards of offense. Once they had a successful two-point conversion near the end of the third quarter, it was pretty much all over, even if up by two points. The good news? The Cardinals are no longer tied. They now have last place in the NFC West all to themselves. Seattle Seahawks (3-1) Well, this is a weird way to start a football game: First Chargers play: Interception First Seahawks play: Interception Wild scenes in Seattle! 🤯 Watch Chargers v Seahawks on Sky Sports and NFL Game Pass on DAZN 📺 pic.twitter.com/qx5DVZfWFl — NFL UK & Ireland (@NFLUKIRE) October 4, 2026 Sure, when the first plays from both offenses are interceptions, that’s a sign of the weirdness to come. The commentating team said it best: “Two plays, two picks.” And I say: “ Endless possibilities .“ Funny thing is, for the next three quarters this was all Seahawks. Then the fourth quarter rolled around, that’s when they let their foot off the gas. How did this happen? Well, the Seahawks getting 14 penalties for a franchise-record 150 yards through the game certainly doesn’t help. This batch of laundry includes a facemask call and some roughing-the-passer flags, allowing the Chargers to sustain drives and get back into the game in the fourth quarter. The Chargers also o utgained the Seahawks 138 yards to 11 in that same quarter. Yes, you read that right. 11 yards in the final quarter of the game for the Seahawks offense. With under a minute left, the Seahawks managed to sack Justin Herbert and force a fumble to end the game and get out of there. Had the Seahawks not played such a tremendous three quarters, that game could have been a disaster. Then again, that was a hell of a three-quarters. Regardless, that was not four quarters of football from the Seahawks. It was, however, a win that puts them to 3-1. Los Angeles Rams (2-2) This marks the first game the Rams played on a Sunday afternoon. Four weeks into the season, they play a game that isn’t on prime time. After this, I think I’ll take the prime time games since the Rams have only won one of those. And for a bit, they may have had no business winning this one. I mean when you have a catch like this, it’s just a bad sign for the visiting team: OH MY DARIUS COOPER 🤯 pic.twitter.com/adE7VVSDSo — Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) October 4, 2026 I don’t care who you root for—that catch was awesome. So how did the Eagles blow this? Beyond the points, the Rams dominated in several areas, including time of possession, third-down conversions (the Eagles didn’t convert a single one), first downs, and more. The Eagles had two turnovers, but they also suffered from some bad playcalling. And when you have that on top of you not converting a third down, two touchdowns seems more like a gift. The first half had the Eagles up 20-10. The Rams were not going away, but the Eagles had their turnovers and their lead. Just no mistakes, no getting cute, and manage the game. Just manage the game. Make good play calls: The Rams stop the tush push‼️ 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/7siNXhy8D4 — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 4, 2026 That was not managing the game or making a good play call. Credit to the Rams for stopping a play that is rarely stopped. But no credit to the Eagles for running that. That looks like a looooong fourth and 1, to the point that it’s fourth and 2. Call me crazy, but that doesn’t seem like a good time to run that when you are on your own side of the field. Reminds me of another failed QB sneak I saw Sunday that probably should have been left on the playsheet. But even with that blunder, the game stayed 20-10. Until the four-minute mark of the fourth quarter. That’s when the Rams scored not one but two touchdowns to take the lead and the win. That’s right, with four minutes left in the game, the Rams scored 14 unanswered points. And their second touchdown came with nearly a minute remaining. So in reality, the Rams scored two touchdowns in three minutes. When you are up 10, and that happens? Is that the Rams or the Eagles? Who knows. Even with the differential in stats, I’m wondering how the Eagles managed to meltdown in five minutes. Onto Week 5 The Rams go back to prime time in Week 4. This time they host the Buffalo Bills. The Bills lost to the New England Patriots Sunday, so don’t expect them to be too happy with life a week later. Maybe the Bills can use the Rams to get right and hand them another prime-time loss. The 49ers have their second test of the season against the Seattle Seahawks and that Seahawks defense. They are in Seattle and much healthier than they were last time, in the NFC Divisional. The Seahawks defense has given Kyle Shanahan fits in the past, but if the 49ers offensive line can keep Brock Purdy upright when the Seahawks rush four, then there could be an opening. The Seahawks are favored by three points this time, which is practically the “home-field” points. If the 49ers manage to win here, they are 3-0 in the division, and you could not ask for a better start. Also, can we keep Brock Purdy at 0 sacks into Week 5? Please? The Cardinals host the Detroit Lions. The Lions are favored by five points, so that should tell you what to expect. Given the defenses, I expect this to be a pretty high-scoring one. The over/under is at 52.5 points—so the oddsmakers tend to agree with me. The Lions lost to the Panthers Sunday night so expect them at 2-2 to come out with their hair on fire. 1st: San Francisco 49ers Next at Seattle Seahawk s 2nd: Seattle Seahawks; Next: vs. San Francisco 49ers 3rd: Los Angeles Rams; Next: vs. Buffalo Bills (Monday Night Football) 4th: Arizona Cardinals; Next: vs. Detroit Lions

title: 49ers prove age is just a number with unique piece of NFL history
summary: In recent years, 49ers GM John Lynch has spoken regularly about San Francisco’s roster needing to get younger, and the front office has made plenty of moves with that goal in mind. But four weeks into the 2026 season it is the still plentiful old heads on the San Francisco offense that have powered the […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In recent years, 49ers GM John Lynch has spoken regularly about San Francisco’s roster needing to get younger, and the front office has made plenty of moves with that goal in mind. But four weeks into the 2026 season it is the still plentiful old heads on the San Francisco offense that have powered the 49ers to a 4-0 start. The 49ers were made to work very hard for their 24-14 win over the Denver Broncos, with their experienced cast of skill-position players coming through when it mattered. Deebo Samuel caught his third touchdown of the season to give the 49ers a 10-3 lead in the third quarter, before a Christian McCaffrey goal-line plunge and a spectacular 56-yard catch-and-run from George Kittle on a screen clinched the victory for the 49ers. The scores by Samuel and Kittle sealed a unique piece of history for a 49er offense that, with the likes of De’Zhaun Stribling and Ricky Pearsall sidelined, is hugely reliant on ageing veterans. Indeed, per CBS Sports’ Doug Clawson , the 49ers have 11 receiving touchdowns scored by players aged 30 or over. That is the most through four games in NFL history. Kittle has accounted for four of them, with Mike Evans scoring two in addition to Samuel’s treble. Demarcus Robinson and Kyle Juszczyk each have one. Of course, in an ideal world the 49ers would love to have Stribling, who was injured in his NFL debut and is likely looking a late November return, and Pearsall (out for the season) making key contributions and developing into long-term assets. But this is still a team very much focused on the now and, for the time being, the 49ers’ veteran pass-catchers are a huge reason why they look like the best team in football through four weeks. You’re only as old as you feel, and the 49ers are feeling very good heading into their Week 5 matchup with the Seattle Seahawks.

full_text: (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images What absolute freaking warriors. They showed so much grit and resilience today that I feel like my expectations are immediately raised for the rest of the season. It was good to see what it looks like when the 49ers offense faces a serious defense. It won’t always be fireworks and big runs. But when the going gets tough, these guys come through.
