title: How to bet Falcons-Saints on MNF: Analysis, tips and top prop plays
summary: Odds and analysis to help you bet Falcons-Saints on "Monday Night Football."
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons enter "Monday Night Football" feeling like they have a new lease on life.

 After a disastrous first two weeks of the season with Cooper Rush starting at quarterback (with Michael Penix Jr . still recovering from ACL surgery and Tua Tagovailoa  also injured), the Falcons looked like one of the worst teams in the league. But with Penix back in action in Week 3, the Falcons delivered a shocking 35-14 blowout of the Green Bay Packers . The Packers have plenty of their own problems offensively, but Penix played well (posting an 84.9 QBR) and the Falcons earned that win, giving them hope going forward.

 

 The New Orleans Saints , meanwhile, sit at 1-2, but they were competitive in all three of the games they played. They lost to the Detroit Lions in overtime in Week 1, beat the Baltimore Ravens  in Week 2 and then lost a back-and-forth affair with the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 3. QB  Tyler Shough has delivered in key moments and ranks 15th in QBR so far, exceeding my expectations for him entering the season. The defense, however, has struggled. It ranks 28th in EPA per play, though perhaps part of that is because they have played against both the Lions and Ravens.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 The sneaky unit to watch here is the Falcons defense. It ranks 10th in EPA per play, fifth in run stop win rate and third in pass rush win rate. This is a group that is, quietly, dramatically exceeding expectations and should be able to slow down the Saints' offense.

 

 Another reason I believe that? The Saints have converted third and fourth downs at a 56% clip, third best in the NFL. Even if I feel reasonably good about the Saints offense this year, that's not a category in which I would expect them to be among the league leaders. Late downs have all the leverage in terms of effect on a game, but are they as predictive of future offensive success than a team's entire breadth of work? I'm skeptical.

 So while I won't be on either side here -- or even the total, because I worry about the Saints defense's ability to stop Penix and the Falcons offense -- one way I can take advantage of the analysis above in a team-level bet is to wager against the Saints' team total.

 Bet: Saints team total UNDER 24.5 (-110)

title: Is Bijan Robinson the NFL's top RB? He is when he's in primetime
summary: Bijan Robinson has the most scrimmage yards per game in primetime, and he'll get a chance to keep it rolling on 'Monday Night Football' this week.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski shows high school football highlights of his players to the team on Fridays. For most, the glory days of high school set a bar few could match against NFL competition.

 Then there's Bijan Robinson .

 To be clear, Robinson was a superstar at Salpointe Catholic High School in Tucson, Arizona. He was the Gatorade Player of the Year as a senior in 2019. But Robinson's highlights on Friday nights don't match what he has done under the lights in the NFL.

 Since the 1970 NFL/AFC merger, no player has more scrimmage yards per game in primetime than Robinson (145.4 in 11 games) with a minimum of five games, per ESPN Research. Barry Sanders is second with 126.3 scrimmage yards per game in 20 contests. OJ Simpson (123 in six games) and Jonathan Taylor (121.8 in 12 games) are third and fourth, respectively.

 Robinson will try to keep it rolling Monday when the Falcons (1-2) travel to New Orleans (1-2) to face the Saints (8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN).

 

 "For me, whether it's primetime, whether it's a 1 o'clock game, they're all the same in terms of my mentality," Robinson said. "Everybody watches you on TV, and they watch you in the stands.

 "I love what Kobe [Bryant] said: 'They paid to watch you, so you got to do your job on the field.'"

 Robinson was remarkable against the Green Bay Packers on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 3, leading Atlanta to a 35-14 road win. He had 29 carries for 194 yards and two touchdowns, and added another 19 yards on two receptions.

 "He's an elite player," Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said. "He's one of the best in the league at any position." The Falcons signed Robinson to an offseason extension that briefly made him the highest-paid running back in NFL history. Robinson, the No. 8 pick in the 2023 draft, is under contract for three years with a base salary of $66.75 million ($22.3 million per season), which could go up to $75 million. The Detroit Lions ' Jahmyr Gibbs has the highest average per year at $22.5 million.

 "Bro, I don't know what to say," Packers running back Kaleb Johnson said after the Week 3 game. "He deserves every penny of that."

 Robinson has picked up where he left off in 2025, when he was named first-team All-Pro. He once again leads the league in yards from scrimmage (467) and is second in rushing yards (349).

 Last season, he had the two longest runs of his career -- 93 yards against the Los Angeles Rams and 81 yards against the Buffalo Bills -- on "Monday Night Football." Against the Minnesota Vikings on "Sunday Night Football" in 2025, Robinson had 168 scrimmage yards. Since Robinson debuted in 2023, he has over 20 scrimmage yards per game more than any other running back in primetime. More than Derrick Henry (123.9). More than Saquon Barkley (119.5).

 In his past four primetime games, Robinson is averaging 213.8 scrimmage yards. Robinson can't explain why he has excelled in primetime. He said he's not necessarily a night person, usually going to sleep around 11 p.m. "When it's time to [play], no matter what time it is, it's time to go," Robinson said. "So, the game can be played at 12 midnight, and I'm locked in, ready to go."

 That same mentality is evident when Stefanski shows high school clips of Robinson.

 

 "Our players love playing under the lights, and that takes all of us back to high school days and Friday night lights," Stefanski said. "And every Friday team meeting, I show high school highlights of one of our players.

 "We've done Bijan before, so I've seen what it looked like [under] Friday night lights out there in Arizona. It was pretty special."

 Even more so against the best players in the world. It's enough for recently acquired defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. to put an exclamation mark on the praise. "He's the best player I've ever seen play football."

title: The punt block that unified New Orleans and a Falcons-Saints rivalry
summary: Ahead of Monday's Falcons-Saints game, players and coaches reflect on the storm, the game and a play from 20 years ago.
full_text:
NEW ORLEANS -- The  Saints  and Atlanta Falcons will carry the weight of history between them when they meet at the Caesars' Superdome on Monday night ( 8:15 ET, ESPN ).

 Hurricane Katrina made landfall along the Gulf Coast on Aug. 29, 2005, killing more than 1,300 people, decimating the region and impacting lives in the area forever.

 The Superdome, which was used as a shelter of last resort during the storm, was inoperable for more than a year because of extreme roof damage.

 The indoor stadium reopened to the public on Sept. 25, 2006 ahead of a Week 3 game featuring the Saints and Falcons on "Monday Night Football." Former Saints quarterback Archie Manning and a group of first responders were among those who ceremonially ushered fans back into the Dome ahead of a performance by the Goo Goo Dolls. The pregame celebration continued inside with performances by Green Day and U2.

 

 Pregame shots showed the building surrounded by water in the days after the storm before transitioning to a live shot showing fans counting down the seconds until reopening, clearly ready to move forward to a new chapter.

 While the fanfare included former President George H.W. Bush, who oversaw the coin toss, the real star of the night was a 29-year-old Saints player named Steve Gleason. The core special-teamer blocked Michael Koenen's punt less than 90 seconds into the game.

 Gleason came rushing up the middle, stretched up his arms and hit the football with a solid thwack! Gleason's teammate Curtis Deloatch ran down the ball and fell on it in the end zone for a touchdown.

 The momentum never let up. When the game was over, ESPN analyst Stuart Scott noted "not a soul has left this building," as the camera panned a stadium still packed with fans.

 That block -- in a game that snowballed into a 23-3 Saints rout -- would make history, eventually being ranked No. 28 on the NFL's "100 Greatest Plays" list . It symbolized a new beginning for New Orleans.

 There have been 5,216 regular-season games, 45,983 punts and 247 punts blocked since that night. Perhaps none of those blocked punts have had as much of an impact on one city as the one by Gleason, whose moment is now commemorated in a statue outside the Superdome titled "Rebirth."

 It was the start of a run of success for the Saints, who made it to the NFC Championship Game that season and went on to win Super Bowl XLIV during the 2009 season.

 For the Falcons, it was another chapter in a rivalry that burns bright 20 years after that game.

 

 Gleason, who was diagnosed with ALS in 2011, became a hero in New Orleans and still considers the blocked punt a defining moment of his life.

 "Here's what the blocked punt means to me now. It means I'm alive," Gleason told NFL Network's Steve Wyche. "... If I don't block that punt I'd be dead. Before the punt block I was just a pretty good special teams player, but I wasn't Lou Gehrig or Stephen Hawking. I was just a dude. If I don't block that punt, I'm just another has-been football player. The odds are high that I fade away and die anonymously. Instead, that play connected me permanently to New Orleans."

 Gleason is expected to be in attendance at Monday's game, ready to remind everyone of one of his signature phrases: "Never punt."

 Though many of the current Saints and Falcons were too young to recall the anniversary of the game, they certainly understand what the rivalry means and its significance.

 Here's how "Rebirth" lives on, 20 years after that special night.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 'Last cool rivalry' | 'Greatest moment in Saints football' 
 'Didn't seem real to play' | 'Sound that belonged to city' 
 'Got to stay up and watch the game' 
 'To know a Steve Gleason' | 'It's a sense of hope' 

 
 
 How players feel about the Falcons-Saints rivalry 
 It was no coincidence the league scheduled a primetime game around the 20th anniversary of the return to the Superdome. The 10th anniversary of the game was also aired on "Monday Night Football," with the Falcons winning 35-32.

 As the Saints (1-2) and Falcons (1-2) approach this season's game, they have a chance to stake their claim in the NFC South. The Saints, who are slight favorites, are coming off a 35-27 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders , and the Falcons beat the Green Bay Packers 35-14 on Sept. 24.

 The rivalry has only intensified since 2006. Since that day, there have been more blocked punts: (Michael Mauti blocked a punt against the Falcons with Gleason watching in 2014, and  Taysom Hill had one in 2019). There have been broken goal posts, egged buses , a defensive tackle stiff arm , a touchdown out of victory formation , records broken and numerous jokes about each team's respective failures .

 Saints and Falcons players and coaches, including those who are experiencing the rivalry game for the first time, shared their thoughts.

 Saints quarterback Tyler Shough : "Everybody talks about the Atlanta game. They don't care if we win or lose any other game, depending on the fan you're talking to. ... I feel like it's one of the last really cool rivalries in the NFL."

 Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr .: "It's a nice dome. That's probably like the only nice thing I can say about them."

 Falcons running back Bijan Robinson : "I expect it to be the loudest it'll be, packed-out stadium, super hostile. ... Not only is it the 20th anniversary of that [game], but it's the Saints and the Falcons. It's one of those rivalry games that you get geeked up for."

 

 Saints wide receiver Devaughn Vele : "Especially with the home opener that we lost, I think we owe it to the fans to win this game. And so I feel like guys have a chip on their shoulder this time around and there's a lot of emotion in this game."

 Saints defensive end Cameron Jordan : "The city turns up after we win. ... We got Atlanta coming in. You know what that means to us. Old ladies at Canseco's [grocery stores] don't care about nothing but ... LSU beating Bama [and] New Orleans Saints beating Atlanta."

 Falcons defensive tackle Maason Smith : "I wasn't ever really a Saints fan, but my mom was a Saints fan. [The Saints] was the only thing really the city had because you had the Hornets, but the Hornets was ass back then. So, it was kind of like the thing that unified the city, the state."

 Falcons linebacker Harold Perkins Jr : "S---, I ain't like the Falcons [being from Louisiana]. Now it's vice versa. I hate the Saints."

 Falcons tackle Jake Matthews : "The thing that always stands out with New Orleans is just the environment and the fan base. ... I remember as a kid watching the first game back with Katrina. Obviously just a moment for the city. But nothing but respect for that scene of that stadium."

 Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich: "A lot of people talk about rivalries in the NFL, but I think a lot of that is just, it's false. It's just trying to build some hype -- some fictitious hype -- but this is a real rivalry. ... Whether we're playing here, whether we're playing there, the fans have embraced it and I think the players have embraced it as well, which a lot of times you just don't see in the NFL."

 Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux : "This is one of the biggest rivalries in football. Dirty Birds vs. the Saints. ... A lot of smack-talking going on."

 

 Jordan: "New Orleanians are always going to be heavy with the Saints. And they carry it in their blood. ... They're like, 'No, my granddaddy took me to my first game. My momma took me to this.' And it's a bloodline thing."

 Falcons kicker Nick Folk : "It'll be a night game in New Orleans and that anniversary, the stadium will be rocking, a great atmosphere. It'll be a lot of fun."

 

 Ulbrich: "It's always that place where your ears hurt when you leave, but it's extra special when it's these two organizations."

 
 Remembering Hurricane Katrina and its impact

title: 'Unacceptable': Ravens steaming after most penalty yards in 6 years
summary: The Ravens were flagged 13 times Sunday for 131 yards, which was their most in a game in six years.
full_text:
BALTIMORE -- After the Baltimore Ravens ' 24-18 win over the Tennessee Titans , coach Jesse Minter didn't hide his frustration when asked about his team's increasing number of penalties. 
 
 "It's obviously unacceptable," Minter said, shaking his head. "At the end of the day, we have to get out of our own way." 
 
 The Ravens were flagged 13 times Sunday for 131 yards, which was their most in a game in six years and repeatedly kept Baltimore from pulling away from winless Tennessee.  
 
 In the first quarter, Nate Wiggins ' illegal contact penalty gave a first down to the Titans in the red zone on the opening drive, which resulted in a touchdown. 
 
 In the second quarter, Lamar Jackson 's 29-yard scramble was reduced to a 7-yard gain because of wide receiver Elijah Sarratt 's holding penalty. 
 
 In the third quarter, Baltimore cornerback Chidobe Awuzie 's 39-yard pass interference penalty was Tennessee's biggest play on a drive that ended with a field goal making it 24-10. 
 
 "It's very frustrating," offensive tackle Ronnie Stanley said. "And drives here, drives there got stopped by penalties or miscommunications. Those things can't happen. And I think those things kind of get overlooked because we're up two possessions, but those drives are very important." 
 
 Minter said two weeks ago that reducing penalties was a "major point of emphasis." But the problem has gotten worse. 
 
 The Ravens' 39 penalties are tied for the most by a Ravens team through four games since 2000. Baltimore's 329 penalty yards this season rank behind only the Green Bay Packers (344). 
 
 The Ravens' offense has accounted for 61% of the team's penalties with 24. Baltimore's 11 false starts are the second most in the NFL. 
 
 This shouldn't come as a major surprise. In early August, the Ravens were called for eight false starts in a two-hour training camp practice because quarterbacks were working on a different cadence. 
 
 Ravens left guard John Simpson said the issues with penalties are being addressed in practice. 
 
 "We've been doing as much as we can, just trying to bring it up on film and just talk about it," Simpson said. "For instance, our cadences, just reminding each other when we break the huddle what our cadence is and stuff like that so we're all on the same page." 
 
 
 The Ravens have chalked up some penalties to being either questionable or unfortunate. Last week, Wiggins was called for pass interference on Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb when it looked like Lamb was the one who interfered with Wiggins. 
 
 On Sunday, Baltimore safety Kyle Hamilton was flagged for unnecessary roughness when he sacked Titans quarterback Cam Ward after the play clock had run out. But the officials blew the whistle just before Hamilton hit Ward. 
 
 "That's just one of those plays. It is what it is," Minter said. "I do respect the fact that the league wants to protect the quarterbacks, so I want to start with that, because if that happened to our quarterback, I'd be sitting there saying the same thing." 
 
 This marked the 12th time since 2000 that the Ravens committed 13 or more penalties in a game. 
 
 "When you have penalties, you shoot yourself in the foot, and that lowers your chances," middle linebacker Roquan Smith said. "It takes all of us, not just one of us. It takes all of us, play in and play out, to play [with] clean technique and fundamentals. When we do that, things normally go in our favor. But obviously if we do not, we allow teams to stay around." 
 
 A high rate of penalties have produced mixed results for Baltimore. In the six seasons where the Ravens have totaled over 120 penalties, they didn't have a winning record three times (2005, 2015 and 2016) and they won the AFC North three times (2003, 2012 and 2024), including a Super Bowl title in 2012. 
 
 "If we can get out of our own way," Minter said, "I think there's a high ceiling for us."

title: Cowboys' Texas-themed jabs at Houston tops Week 4 trolls
summary: The calendar shifted to October, and the trolls are becoming a little more impactful, led by the Dallas Cowboys.
full_text:
Welcome to the first weekend of October, when the games get a little more meaningful and the trolls follow suit. Week 4 of the NFL season proved exactly that.

 

 The Dallas Cowboys defeated the Houston Texans 34-30 on the road. Facing a four-point deficit with 2:23 left, Dallas went on an 11-play, 74-yard drive that concluded with a 12-yard touchdown catch by wide receiver CeeDee Lamb .

 It put the Cowboys up for good and capped a stellar performance from Lamb. He had a whopping 17 catches -- second most in franchise history -- for 189 yards. It's the most receptions by any player since Keenan Allen had 18 in Week 3 of the 2023 season, according to ESPN Research.

 Dallas had clever jabs lined up for the in-state matchup. The Cowboys referenced country star Ella Langley's hit track, "Choosin' Texas," in a social media post, adding "Dallas" ahead of "Texas."

 Then, Dallas put a spin on the opening sequence from the sitcom "King of the Hill," which is set in Texas. The illustration featured Lamb, Dak Prescott , wide receiver George Pickens and safety Caleb Downs hanging out together with "Kings of the State" written above them.

 

 Here are the other top trolls from Week 4.

 

 Carolina Panthers 32, Detroit Lions 26 
 It required one final stop, but the Panthers survived for a "Sunday Night Football" win against the Lions.

 Carolina held a six-point lead when Detroit regained possession with 2:06 left. Four plays later, the Lions turned it over on downs, clinching the Panthers' victory. Panthers quarterback Bryce Young threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns -- both to wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan , who had 14 catches for 192 yards. Their teammate, running back Chuba Hubbard , had 122 yards on the ground and two scores.

 Carolina understood the assignment postgame when poking fun at Detroit. It shared an image of a Panther standing on a ledge and growling over a lion, writing in the caption: "The Lion's king."

 

 

 Seattle Seahawks 30, Los Angeles Chargers 23 
 Seattle held on to beat Los Angeles in a bounce-back victory.

 The Chargers had a chance to tie the score with 1:42 remaining, but the Seahawks sacked quarterback Justin Herbert to force a fumble, which they recovered to secure the win. Seattle forced four turnovers -- three came from Herbert and two led to touchdowns.

 The Seahawks had multiple lightning- and charging-related trolls after the win.

 Their first post was simple with the caption: "Lights Out," a reference to the nickname of Chargers legend Shawne Merriman. Seattle's victory comic included a robot out of charge. Seahawks defensive end Leonard Williams  was labeled "The Lightning Thief," the title of a popular Rick Riordan novel. Then there was an image of a charging cord with tattered wires, captioned "0% battery," and another of a charging error with safety Nick Emmanwori sacking Herbert in the background. 

 

 

 Los Angeles Rams 24, Philadelphia Eagles 20 
 Los Angeles stormed back late to beat Philadelphia on the road.

 The Rams outscored the Eagles 14-0 in the second half. The winning touchdown came on a 7-yard run by Kyren Williams  with 1:10 left. The Eagles then had a turnover on downs, giving the Rams the ball and the win.

 Even though the result was still up in the air, Los Angeles soft launched its troll with a post earlier in the day. The Rams shared an image of their players with "Rams in Philadelphia" written above them in a font evoking the hit comedy "Abbott Elementary," which is set in Philadelphia.

 Just over five hours later, Los Angeles posted a test paper with scantron bubbles filled in to spell out "W."

 

 
 San Francisco 49ers 24, Denver Broncos 14 
 The 49ers remain undefeated following a win against the Broncos.

 San Francisco's defense shined, allowing just one touchdown and 296 total yards to Denver. The 49ers' offense played its part, too, specifically the offensive line -- the team has yet to give up a sack this season. The Niners are the first team to allow zero sacks through four games since the 2005 Indianapolis Colts , according to ESPN Research.

 The Broncos' home stadium is Empower Field at Mile High, and even though the 49ers won at home, they highlighted the "mile high" component with a jab.

 

 
 Jacksonville Jaguars 22, Cincinnati Bengals 17 
 Jacksonville's wire-to-wire win over Cincinnati prompted a simple, yet effective, troll.

 Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence had 223 passing yards and one score, and Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow threw for 428 yards, one touchdown plus two interceptions. Cincinnati put up a whopping 437 yards of offense but had only two touchdowns to show for it.

 In a battle between Jaguars and Bengals, Jacksonville highlighted its win by writing "Jungle Cats" in its postgame caption.

 

 
 Cleveland Browns 27, Pittsburgh Steelers 24 
 The Browns have won three straight games for the first time since 2023 after defeating the Steelers on "Thursday Night Football."

 Pittsburgh tied the score with 1:42 remaining, but Cleveland responded by kicking a winning field goal with 10 ticks left. As a result, Deshaun Watson became the second Browns quarterback since 1970 to lead three straight winning drives in the fourth quarter or overtime, according to ESPN Research.

 At first glance, Cleveland's Minecraft-themed post after the win seemed something ordinary. But it was a reference to former Pittsburgh head coach Mike Tomlin revealing his Minecraft world  Wednesday. The Browns capitalized on the moment by building out an "L" in Minecraft blocks and writing: "Pittsburgh was defeated by the Dawg Pound."

title: Joe Burrow after 2nd straight loss: Not 'Armageddon'
summary: Another Burrow fourth-quarter turnover helped bring the Bengals back to .500, but optimism remains.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- Even if the exact message was muffled, the intensity from Cincinnati Bengals coach Zac Taylor certainly wasn't.

 In the immediate aftermath of the team's second straight loss, a 22-17 home defeat to the Jacksonville Jaguars , Taylor's voice could be heard bellowing through the wall that separates the locker room from the media room where news conferences are conducted. Beyond the volume, Taylor's remarks were among the longest following a home loss in recent memory.

 When the eighth-year coach left the locker room to speak to the reporters, Taylor characterized it as encouragement to a team that will need to fight through one of the season's most important stretches.

 For the second straight year, the Bengals are back to .500 after Week 4 following two wins to open the season. But the stakes are a bit higher this year.

 Breaking a three-year playoff drought, if not at least winning a game or two in mid-January, will be needed to eliminate the mounting pressure on Taylor and the franchise. After Sunday's loss, the Bengals are now tasked with regaining momentum and making this season feel promising again.

 "We had our opportunities in the last two weeks, but this isn't Armageddon or anything," quarterback Joe Burrow said after the game. "We're still in a great spot [and] feel really good about our team."

 If anything, the comments show Taylor's postgame message resonated throughout the locker room following a comeback attempt that fell 12 yards short. The Bengals trailed 22-10 with 6:35 left in the fourth quarter before Burrow and the Bengals made a late push at an improbable victory.

 After a touchdown and a defensive stop, the Bengals made it all the way into Jacksonville's red zone before running back Chase Brown was stopped on the 12-yard line on a fourth-down catch, one yard shy of a new set of downs to keep the drive alive.

 

 And instead of a win that could have positioned the Bengals well, Cincinnati was left talking about familiar woes.

 According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Cincinnati missed 12 tackles on defense. Jacksonville had six. The Jaguars also had 143 yards after the catch. Both issues plagued the Bengals in 2025.

 "They hit some checkdowns; and checkdowns, they're not supposed to convert a [third down]," linebacker Barrett Carter said.

 Offensively, the lack of a run game was an issue against Jacksonville. The Bengals had 15 carries for 23 yards. Burrow had 58 dropbacks, tied for the fourth most in his career, according to ESPN Research. And in the quarterback's mind, that number could have been higher.

 His response to the idea of having more balanced playcalls?

 "Let's throw it more," Burrow said.

 There is one other trend that is becoming more noticeable. Since the start of the 2024 season, Burrow leads the NFL in the most turnovers in the fourth quarter or overtime, according to ESPN Research.

 On Sunday, Burrow had an interception deep in Jacksonville's territory on a drive that could have given the Bengals a fourth-quarter lead. Burrow was pressured and didn't see Jaguars linebacker Foyesade Oluokun , who secured the interception in zone coverage.

 Burrow came close to making amends with the late-game flourish. Instead, Taylor was left answering questions about his quarterback amid the recent miscues.

 "In no way, shape or form am I concerned about that," said Taylor, who added that he would "go to battle" with Burrow every day with how he played on Sunday.

 That's a good mentality to have. Because while it isn't quite Armageddon, the Bengals are now fighting to show their preseason beliefs and early-season highs weren't an aberration.

 "We're very confident," Burrow said. "We're 2-2, but nobody wins a championship after Week 4."

summary: The Rams, Cowboys and Pats were all looking at 1-3 ... then everything changed. How did a trio of stunning rallies play out -- and are these teams all back on track at 2-2?
full_text:
It's never too early to turn around a season. Ask the 2024 Eagles, who hit their bye at 2-2 after allowing 33 points to the Bucs in Week 4. Vic Fangio inserted Cooper DeJean into the lineup at slot cornerback, the Eagles leaned on Saquon Barkley , and Philly went 16-1 the rest of the way en route to a Super Bowl victory . The 2025 Seahawks lost a 38-35 shootout with that same Bucs team in Week 5, but one week later, they played their best defensive game of the season to that point against the Jaguars . Like the Eagles, they lost just one game over the rest of the season before winning the Super Bowl .

 Sunday of Week 4 might have seen that turning point take place for three would-be contenders. It's possible we just saw the Cowboys, Rams and Patriots save their seasons. At the very least, they put disappointing starts in their respective rearviews with fourth-quarter comebacks. Their flaws might still be real problems, but this could be a jumping-off point for the three teams as they try to launch their way back to the top of the playoff picture .

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Let's take a closer look at all three. And I'll start in Houston, where the Texans were attempting to salvage their own season after an 0-3 start, only for a massive day from the Cowboys'  CeeDee Lamb to sink DeMeco Ryans' team. (Playoff probabilities are via ESPN's Football Power Index .)

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Cowboys | Patriots | Rams 

 
 

 

 Cowboys 34, Texans 30 
 Lowest win probability for the Cowboys: 21.5% (2:00 to go in the game) 
 Chance to make the playoffs after win, per FPI: 82.3%

 The Cowboys might look back at their past two games and feel like they probably deserved, on average, to win one of the two. A narrow loss to the Ravens in Brazil was followed on Sunday with a come-from-behind victory over the Texans, with Dak Prescott picking up five first downs in a two-minute drill before hitting Lamb from 12 yards out for the game-winning touchdown with 43 seconds remaining.

 For the second week in a row, the vaunted Texans defense couldn't come up with a stop with the game -- and potentially their playoff hopes as the FPI now gives them just a 15.8% chance -- on the line. In Week 3 , the Colts needed only a field goal against them, and the 29 yards Indy gained on its final drive were enough to get Spencer Shrader in position for a game-winning kick. This time, after a Woody Marks touchdown gave the Texans a 30-27 lead with 2:26 to go, the Cowboys needed a touchdown to win the game in regulation.

 

 And outside of a fourth-down conversion to Jake Ferguson that extended the contest, the Cowboys marched down the field without much difficulty. Prescott went 8-of-11 for 74 yards, with George Pickens  torching Kamari Lassiter on a double move for the biggest play, a 22-yard completion. Two plays later, Lamb's 17th catch of the game gave the Cowboys a 34-30 lead. One Houston Hail Mary later, Dallas was 2-2.

 Lamb's outing will linger in the memories of Cowboys fans for quite a while. His 17 catches were the most by any Cowboys wide receiver in a single game in franchise history, an impressive feat for a team with six Hall of Fame wideouts. Lamb turned 21 targets into 189 receiving yards and 11 first downs, including three on the drive that won the game for the Cowboys.

 Watching it back, what was remarkable was just how easy it seemed for the Cowboys receiver. There were a couple of tight-window catches or plays where Lamb had to hang on to the ball as he was about to be hit, but those were the exceptions. Great players make the game look easy, and Lamb's route running gave the Texans serious pause, but that doesn't fully explain it.

 Let's look at Houston's approach. The Texans appeared to have come into this game with a plan of not letting Lamb and Pickens -- both of whom have been getting open on deeper passing concepts all season -- beat them over the top. This was a remarkably conservative game plan from Ryans. Eight of Lamb's catches were against soft zone coverage, with the Texans usually in quarters shells and playing off-coverage to keep the Cowboys from attacking downfield. Lamb likely had more uncontested catches on curls and hitches in this game than he has had in any other game as a pro.

 The vertical shots the Cowboys have hit on "989" concepts in weeks past were mostly missing as a result. Prescott hit one deep throw to Pickens, who outmuscled Lassiter at the catch point and brought in a 50-50 ball. It was a rough drive for Lassiter, who then committed two penalties on incompletions on third-and-7 and fourth-and-goal to extend the drive. But mostly, Prescott just picked the Texans and their zone coverages apart. He was 27-of-37 for 296 yards against zone on Sunday, with the Texans limiting him to 39 yards on eight pass attempts when they went with man defense. Every one of Lamb's catches came against zone, with two incompletions against man-to-man looks.

 Coach Brian Schottenheimer and Prescott clearly wanted Lamb to get the ball. Lamb was targeted three times on screens, including a pair of tagged snaps where the Cowboys called and blocked a run play at the line before Prescott elected to pull the ball and toss it up to Lamb because he liked the look. Schottenheimer also dialed up a screen at the perfect time for Lamb in the fourth quarter, with the Cowboys throwing directly into the slot after it had been vacated by a blitz to pick up 17 yards.

 

 The Texans helped with uncharacteristic issues in the secondary, especially on Lamb's biggest plays of the day. Facing a second-and-18, two defenders latched on to Ferguson's clear-out route, leaving Lamb alone underneath for an easy 21-yard pickup. Lamb's 30-yard catch, his longest of the day, came on a slow-developing crossing route where  Derek Stingley Jr . passed off the route to the other side of the field, only for Lassiter and single-high safety Calen Bullock to focus their attention on Pickens. Lamb was completely uncovered.

 The touchdown pass that won the game also seemed like it wasn't what the Texans wanted from their secondary. With Lamb aligned in the slot, he ran a skinny post against Jalen Pitre , who was playing with outside leverage and was seemingly expecting help from a defender on the inside. That help wasn't there, as the Texans had two defenders on Ferguson, who is admittedly a red zone threat but one with 13 fewer catches than Lamb in this game by the time we got to this point of the fourth quarter.

 There are still issues in Dallas. The run game continues to struggle, although Javonte Williams had his biggest day of the season on the ground by scoring three touchdowns from a combined 10 yards out. The Cowboys are 22nd in EPA per play on designed runs, down from ninth a year ago. Williams has just one run of 20-plus yards all season, a 22-yarder against the Ravens last week. The return of star guard Tyler Smith , who is eligible to come off injured reserve as early as this Thursday's game against the Buccaneers after undergoing thumb surgery , should help create holes for the Cowboys on the interior.

 The defense isn't fixed, either, although the run D looked better for the second consecutive week. The Cowboys were able to slow Derrick Henry  and come up with big stops in short yardage last week, with rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham making several notable plays to end drives. Dallas held a moribund Houston rushing attack to 50 yards on 17 designed rushes Sunday, yielding a 23.5% success rate, the second-worst mark posted by any rushing attack so far in Week 4. Of course, everybody shuts down the Texans' run game, but the Cowboys doing so while playing light boxes at a higher rate than league average might be a bit of a confidence boost at the minimum.

 Stopping Nico Collins was more difficult, as the star Texans wideout returned after missing two weeks with a hamstring injury and caught seven passes for 118 yards and two touchdowns. The Cowboys struggled…

title: Cowboys flip script after Rio loss with key win over Texans
summary: A week after everything went wrong late against the Ravens, Dallas rebounded with a winning drive Sunday.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- One week after enduring a 10-hour flight home from Rio de Janeiro after a debilitating 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens , the 45-minute flight back home from Houston on Sunday night had to feel a lot better for the Dallas Cowboys .

 Questions surrounded the Cowboys following the loss to the Ravens -- especially about coach Brian Schottenheimer, defensive coordinator Christian Parker, special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen, and how the coaches managed the final 28 seconds of a game they were 2 yards away from potentially winning.

 Against the Houston Texans  (0-4) on Sunday, the Cowboys were trailing 30-27 with 2:25 left, facing a 1-3 start to the season for the second straight year.

 

 But quarterback  Dak Prescott and receiver  CeeDee Lamb helped lessen the temperature around the coaches and players by connecting on a 12-yard touchdown with 40 seconds to go for a 34-30 must-have victory .

 "Rio doesn't define us as a football team, as a coaching staff here," Schottenheimer said. "I think I was very upfront and honest with that, but I wanted this game. Why? Because these guys came back off a 10-hour trip. The Ravens, I think, played at home today. We played on the road. We play Thursday night [against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers ].

 "We'll play anybody anywhere and we're looking forward to that, but Rio had nothing to do with this game. This game stood by itself."

 

 But the fate of a season might have been on the line with a loss. Since 2000, the Cowboys have never opened a season with one victory in the first month of the season and finished above .500. The best they have done is last year's 7-9-1 in Schottenheimer's first season.

 In the first half, a Cowboys' offense that wants to be considered " The Greatest Offense There Is " failed to score a touchdown. In the second half, they scored touchdowns on their first three possessions, then Prescott delivered with the late winning drive.

 In certain moments, the defense was better. Linebacker  Rashan Gary had his first sack in 12 games, dating to last season with the Green Bay Packers . Defensive end Quinnen Williams had his first sack of the season, dropping C.J. Stroud for an 11-yard loss in the fourth quarter. In the first three games, the Cowboys had two sacks. They had three Sunday.

 But the unit still gave up eight pass plays of at least 20 yards.

 Schottenheimer wasn't concerned about his decision at the end of the half when he opted to have Brandon Aubrey attempt a 65-yard field goal despite the Texans being out of timeouts. When Aubrey's kick hooked a little left, the Texans were able to convert a field goal of their own to take a 16-6 halftime lead.

 "We felt very comfortable that Brandon would make that kick," Schottenheimer said. "And at that point in the game, I had no question that if for some reason he missed it, that we had plenty of time to fight back."

 He was proved correct as Prescott directed the winning 11-play, 74-yard drive that ended with Lamb ( 17 catches, 189 yards ) in the end zone with 40 seconds left. Along the way, the Cowboys also needed to convert a fourth-down play.

 

 Before the game, Prescott acknowledged to thinking what a 1-3 start would have meant.

 "That can't happen," he said. "During the game, I'm the most optimistic guy there is."

 Seven days earlier inside Maracanã Stadium, Prescott had the Cowboys in position to beat the Ravens, but then just about everything went wrong.

 On Sunday, things went right. Prescott credited Schottenheimer's playcall for the Lamb touchdown. The kickoff ran time off the clock. The defense was able to keep everything in front of them, and Stroud's Hail Mary attempt throw fell incomplete.

 For only the third time in Prescott's 10-plus seasons as the starter, the Cowboys overcame a double-digit deficit to win a game. Before Sunday, they had lost 32 straight road games when trailing by double digits in the second half, which was the longest active streak in the league.

 "There's nothing like winning," Prescott said. "I want to say it fixes all the problems, but it doesn't. It makes you feel good at least for a day or so. But at this point, we got to turn the page and get ready for Thursday. We can't sit here and have some winning hangover. It's so early in the season.

 "It's no different than last week's loss. ... Just shows the resilience of this team to win. So now it's about stacking these wins with great momentum and just belief in the team that we've created."

title: With Edgerrin Cooper out, Evan Williams shines for Packers
summary: The Packers lost one of their two young defensive stars in Cooper (Achilles), but Williams delivered a big game.
full_text:
TAMPA, Fla. --  Evan Williams has had interceptions before. Four of them in his first 32 NFL regular-season games before Sunday to be exact. So while the Green Bay Packers safety would like the football he inadvertently discarded after interception No. 5 came early in Sunday's 17-14 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , it was the sack -- his first in the NFL -- on the final series that might have been more meaningful.

 Three times on the final three defensive plays of the game, coordinator Jonathan Gannon called blitzes. Three times, he sent Williams. On the first, Williams came unblocked and sacked rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels . The second forced a quick pass for a short completion. And on the third, Williams got home again and had Daniels in his grasp when the quarterback flung the ball away.

 Game over.

 

 Not only did the Packers (2-2) come away with a much-needed win, but they might also have found a way to make up for the loss of linebacker Edgerrin Cooper , who left the game in the second half with a likely season-ending Achilles injury .

 Yes, the Packers have leaders such as linebacker  Zaire Franklin and safety  Xavier McKinney . And eventually they will get star edge rusher  Micah Parsons back. But Cooper and Williams were the young stars on this defense, both members of the 2024 draft class, and now one of them is likely out of the picture.

 Gannon might not rush Williams as much from the safety spot as he did with Cooper as a linebacker, but for Gannon to give Williams that responsibility -- and for Williams to deliver -- could be a sign of what's to come without Cooper.

 "Shoutout to that guy just because he always preaches players not plays in the biggest situations," Williams said of Gannon. "For him to call my number in that type of situation, it means a lot to me. To understand the coach has that type of trust in you in the big situations, when you have to make a play, that you're the number he calls, that means everything. Moving forward, yeah, it means everything."

 

 It capped the kind of performance by Williams that the Packers are going to need. Isaiah McDuffie and Ty'Ron Hopper took over for Cooper at linebacker Sunday, but Williams took over as playmaker. He already had that first-quarter interception, which wasn't granted until replay overturned the call of incomplete on the field, but Williams finished with seven tackles, the sack (which was one of two QB hits) and two pass breakups.

 "Hell of a game," McKinney said.

 Williams' two pressures on the final drive gave him six for the season after recording two in his first two seasons. Part of that is opportunity. But with opportunity comes responsibility.

 "He can be really f---ing good," McKinney said. "I think just the progression that I've seen him make from when he first came here to where he's at now, he's a mature player. He goes out there and he's versatile and can play different things, and I think you're just going to keep see him progressing. My job is to make sure that he keeps going towards where I know that he's capable of being as a player in this league. I love to see it, and it's good to see it, too."

 

 It didn't surprise tight end Tucker Kraft , who has gone up against Williams as much as anyone in practice.

 "Evan's shown up in critical moments this season -- deep PBUs, fitting the box," Kraft said. "So having a guy as dynamic as Evan on your team, it really alleviates a lot of issues because he brings that physicality and he's a ballhawk."

 As much as the Packers will need someone to make up for the loss of Cooper, Williams must be conscious of one thing: Don't try to do too much. And he knows it.

 "As soon as you start to do too much and feel like you've got to make plays or fill in for somebody that's gone, that's when there's holes in the defense and explosives start to show," he said. "So it's just about doing your job and trusting the man next to you, even though that's not going to be Coop. I've got trust in all the guys in this locker room. We put in a lot of time in training camp to get to this point right here. Regardless who it is, we're going to ride with him all the way."

 Williams said he had a feeling he might be in position to make some plays Sunday, especially the interception, which was his first of the season after he had one taken away by a penalty in Week 1.

 "The ball found me in practice a couple times," he said. "That's always a good sign coming into a game."

 Speaking of finding the ball, Williams would like the ball from the interception. He discarded it after the side judge initially ruled he caught the ball out of bounds.

 "I tossed the ball back to the ball boy," Williams said. "They didn't even review it. I think a challenge flag came out and then like 15 seconds after, they said it's an interception. After that, I was just focused on my celebration. Went to the end zone and started celebrating. And then about 3 seconds later, I'm thinking, 'What did I do with that ball?'"

title: NFL Week 4's best arrivals, led by Lions DE Aidan Hutchinson
summary: NFL stars continue to turn game-day arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
Week 4 of the NFL season has arrived, and the calendar has officially flipped to October. But sweater weather hasn't quite followed everywhere. 

 Unseasonable heat out West could keep layers light for another week, while cooler temperatures settling in across the East are opening the door for more fall-ready fits. That means players have plenty of options as they make their Week 4 entrances. With three weeks of looks already in the books, personal styles are also starting to take shape around the league. Some players have leaned into statement pieces, while others have kept things clean and understated.

 From warm-weather looks to seasonal layers, Week 4 brings another round of game-day style as the calendar officially turns to fall.

 

 Primetime fashion 
Ahead of the Detroit Lions and Carolina Panthers tilt on "Sunday Night Football," Aidan Hutchinson donned a fuzzy color-block sweater vest with black jeans and boots. And, of course, he had his signature gallon water jug in hand.
 
 Sunday style 
 
The best design is in the details. Super Bowl champion Uchenna Nwosu and his celebrity stylist Ini Ikpe prioritize weekly custom game-day looks from Black and Brown designers.

 This week, Ikpe took us inside the Abasi x Jagne denim fit Nwosu is displaying this Sunday -- a partnership with Baba Jagne, a Senegalese Gambian designer based in Los Angeles who is known for silhouettes and patterns that make you look twice.

 "It's a cropped jacket and wide-leg trousers in dark indigo raw denim with copper contrast stitching. The jacket takes the classic trucker and rebuilds it," Ikpe said. "Its front panels snap on and off so they can be rearranged, which leaves an open U-shaped cutout down the front. Panels curve around the body, a buckled strap sits at the hem, and the sleeves sweep down from the shoulder. The trousers have a tan leather belt that dips and curves down the front, darted knees and a long, flared leg. Cognac leather JAGNE patches finish both pieces."

 Nwosu's favorite part is that nobody else has this look; he's the first to wear it and feels unapologetically authentic to his style.

 It's a small glimpse into just how much attention some of the best-dressed NFL players, like Nwosu, put into their game-day tunnel fit. -- Cameron Wolfe 

 
 Sunday's Best 
 Chicago Bears running back Kyle Monangai arrived in a custom matching jacket gifted to him by Brenda, a Bears fan and breast cancer patient at Advocate Health Care. 
 
 Thursday night's fashion 
Players and coaches aren't the only ones showing off their pregame style. Mascots get in on the tunnel fits, too. This week, Brownie the Elf was ready to rock for Cleveland's Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Game, channeling Prince in a purple jacket with a matching guitar.

title: Vikings make history at 4-0 -- without a scoring offense
summary: Minnesota sits atop the NFC North despite its special teams outscoring its offense the past three weeks.
full_text:
MINNEAPOLIS -- The Minnesota Vikings are 4-0, one of three teams in the NFL without a loss, and they've gone about it in a way the league hasn't seen for more than 100 years. 

 Sunday's 15-10 victory over the Miami Dolphins was the Vikings' second game this season without a touchdown. The other was a 9-3 victory in Week 2 at the Chicago Bears . 

 The last time an NFL team started its season 4-0 despite having multiple games without a touchdown was in 1923. The only other time it has ever happened was in 1922, in both cases by the Chicago Cardinals. 

 No team would realistically expect to be undefeated over such a stretch, but the explanation for the Vikings' success is clear. Their defense has limited opponents to an NFL-best 12.8 points per game this season, and over the past three weeks, their special teams have accounted for six times as many points (42) as their offense (seven). 

 That formula hardly seems sustainable, but under coach Kevin O'Connell, the Vikings have demonstrated a knack for stacking wins in unusual and sometimes unprecedented ways. 

 "We've got to own our role in our own aspect of not moving the football more consistently," O'Connell said, "and then go from there. But excited to get back to work at it. Excited to be 4-0 as a team."

 

 In 2022 the Vikings set an NFL record by going 11-0 in one-score games and became the first team ever to win 13 or more games despite having a negative point differential. They have now put together an NFL-best nine-game regular-season winning streak, dating back to Week 14 of the 2025 season, despite averaging 272.8 yards per game, fourth lowest in the NFL over that period. 

 This season's team has had a level of personnel shuffle that merits appropriate context. New quarterback Kyler Murray suffered a concussion on the 11th play of the season, and receiver Justin Jefferson sprained his left ankle seven plays into Murray's return in Week 3. In other words, they have played only 18 snaps together this season. 

 Sunday, they played almost half of the game without left tackle Christian Darrisaw (neck/concussion exam) and left guard Donovan Jackson (knee). In addition, the offense still appears to be adjusting to Murray, who took roughly half of the team's offensive snaps in spring practices and the first portion of training camp while competing for the job with J.J. McCarthy , who was traded  to the New York Giants  on Sept. 28. 

 Right tackle Brian O'Neill said last week that linemen wouldn't have "internal clocks" any longer because of the way Murray can extend plays out of the pocket. The Dolphins sacked Murray three times in the first half Sunday  (marking Miami's first three sacks of the season), and by halftime the crowd at U.S. Bank Stadium was booing the offense with vigor. All told, the Vikings committed five pre-snap penalties on offense, including two false starts, and O'Connell noted there "were some cadence things going on that we have to continue to figure out what the root of that is."

 

 Murray shouldered the blame for those mistakes, which both he and O'Connell called "unacceptable."

 Said Murray: "Obviously all 11 guys have got to be on the same page, but it starts with me. So we'll be better at that."

 An optimist could find reasons to be encouraged by Sunday's fourth quarter, during which Murray completed 12 of 13 passes for 113 yards. He found receiver Jordan Addison on a 27-yard deep crossing route and repeatedly fed tight end T.J. Hockenson , who tied his career high with 13 receptions. That helped the Vikings kill the final 5:41 of the clock while holding a one-score lead.

 To be fair to history, it should be noted that Hockenson smartly decided to slide at the 2-yard line instead of scoring a touchdown on the Vikings' final pass of the game. But O'Connell said: "I told our guys if we want to score, we should do it earlier."

 As they work through their offensive issues, it is reasonable to expect the rest of the team to continue producing at high levels. Their defense limited the Dolphins to one snap on their side of midfield in the first half, and emerging pass rusher Dallas Turner recorded two more sacks to raise his season total to 5.5. 

 

 Kicker Will Reichard , meanwhile, converted all five of his field goal attempts to raise his season total to 12-for-12. In a darkly humorous moment near the end of the game, the crowd at U.S. Bank Stadium gave him a standing ovation when the big screen showed video of him on the sideline. "A stone-cold killer," safety Harrison Smith called him. 

 The crowd let out its frustration frequently, even when O'Connell called kneel-downs from the 2-yard line rather than try to score to end the game. 

 "We want to score points too," Hockenson said, "and it is what it is. We love our fans here. We love playing in front of them. We're frustrated too sometimes, but we're getting it rolling and that is what it is. I understand it, and we're moving forward."

 Will it be any better in Week 5, when the Vikings go on the road Sunday to face the New Orleans Saints ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox )? It's not yet clear whether Jefferson will be ready, and the Vikings might also play without Darrisaw and/or Jackson. But with arguably the NFL's best defense, and a perfect kicker, who needs touchdowns anyway?

title: Who are the winningest NFL coaches of all time?
summary: From Belichick to Reid, there are many iconic coaches in NFL history. Who has the best career record? Check out the stat breakdown now.
full_text:
Only four head coaches in NFL history have won 300 career games across the regular season and postseason. Kansas City Chiefs  coach Andy Reid was the last to cross the 300-win plateau.

 Reid recorded his 300th career victory on Jan. 18, 2025, when his Chiefs defeated the Houston Texans 23-14 in the AFC divisional round.

 Reid, who signed a five-year, $100 million extension with the Chiefs in April 2024, entered the 2026 season looking to add to his career win total and close the gap between him and the NFL's all-time winningest head coach, Hall of Famer Don Shula.

 Let's take a look at which head coaches have the most career victories in NFL history (including both regular-season and postseason play):

 *Active NFL head coach 

 5. Tom Landry, 270 wins 

 Landry was the Dallas Cowboys' head coach for an NFL-record 29 years in a row and the team had 20 consecutive winning seasons, which is also a league record. Landry led Dallas to two Super Bowl wins, defeating the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl VI and the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XII. He was named the NFL's Coach of the Year in 1966 and the UPI NFL Coach of the Year in 1975. Landry was an innovator, with the 4-3 defense among his creations. He was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 *4. Andy Reid, 311 wins 

 Reid is the only head coach in NFL history who has won 100 games with two franchises: the Philadelphia Eagles (coaching the team from 1999 through 2012) and the Chiefs (he has coached Kansas City since 2013). He led the Eagles on multiple deep playoff runs, including a Super Bowl in 2004 and three straight conference finals from 2001 to 2003. However, he wasn't able to hoist the Lombardi Trophy until he arrived in Kansas City. He has turned the Chiefs into a juggernaut, winning three Super Bowls. Reid is an offensive mastermind and quarterback whisperer. He'll likely continue to rack up wins moving forward with Patrick Mahomes , Travis Kelce & Co.

 

 3. George Halas, 324 wins 

 Halas was a co-founder of the NFL and creator of the Bears. For 10 years, he served as player-coach-executive for the Bears (which is how he earned the nickname "Mr. Everything"). In 1930, he retired as a player and focused on ownership, but he would later return to coach the Bears several times. Halas led the Bears to eight NFL championships, tying Belichick's number of titles. Halas coached the team for 40 years and had just six losing seasons. He helped create the T-formation system and used it to set an NFL record for the biggest blowout in league history: a 73-0 win over the Washington team in the 1940 NFL Championship Game. Halas was selected as the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1963 and 1965, and he was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 2. Bill Belichick, 333 wins 

 Belichick is considered by some as the greatest coach in all of professional sports, as he has won an NFL-record eight Super Bowls (six as a head coach with the Patriots and two as an assistant coach with the Giants). He also ranks first among all NFL coaches in playoff wins with 31. Belichick was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 2003, 2007 and 2010. Many franchises have hired away Belichick's assistants and tried to replicate his "Patriot Way," but it hasn't been the same without him. If Belichick returns to NFL coaching, he is just 26 regular-season wins from surpassing Don Shula as the winningest regular-season coach of all time. 

 1. Don Shula, 347 wins 

 After playing in the NFL as a defensive back for seven seasons, Shula decided to retire and become a coach. He got his first head-coaching opportunity in 1963 with the Baltimore Colts, whom he led to the NFL championship in 1968. From 1970 through 1995, Shula had a legendary run as head coach of the Dolphins. Shula led the Dolphins to a pair of Super Bowl victories (in Super Bowl VII and Super Bowl VIII). Miami had a perfect season in 1972, making Shula the only coach in NFL history to go undefeated. He was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1964, 1967, 1968 and 1972. Whether you're just counting regular-season wins (328) or including playoff wins (347), Shula is the winningest coach in NFL history.

title: Wild stats from NFL Week 4 featuring Cowboys, Bears, Eagles, Seahawks, more
summary: Sunday featured wild plays, historic numbers and a game that started with two straight interceptions. Catch up on the day's most interesting stats.
full_text:
There was a moment in Sunday's early NFL window in which the Rams made it a one-score game, the Texans took the lead, the Bills took the lead and the Bengals made it a one-score game all within 60 seconds of one another. If the feeling of watching that were bottled and sold on the market, I would mortgage my house for it.

 Every Sunday, I'll find several of the coolest advanced stats from the day's NFL action to share with you -- stats to explain all the action and what it means. Some call them NFL Next Gen Stats. I call them Next Ben Stats: the data that might not make it on the broadcast but will make you a smarter fan (and laugh a little bit, probably).

 Let's start Week 4's  list with a historic day for a Cowboys receiver, an NFC North offense and game-opening interceptions.

 

 
 Jump to an eye-popping stat on: 
 Lamb tallies 17 catches   
  0-4 teams to make playoffs 
 Rams blitzed Hurts A LOT   
  Bears out-offensed the Jets 
 Back-to-back interceptions 

 

 
 

 17: Number of catches for CeeDee Lamb in the Cowboys' win over the Texans 
 There were only 11 players Sunday with 17 or more rushes . That's the incredible volume at which Lamb was just used. It's only the ninth game in NFL history in which a player had 17-plus catches.

 The Texans spent much of the game letting the Cowboys play Lamb in the slot and hunt nickel Jalen Pitre in space -- and then again with rookie Kamari Ramsey when the Texans were in dime. Lamb saw 42.1% of his targets on the day from the slot, which is the second-highest slot share he has had since Brian Schottenheimer took over as head coach last year.

 

 

 When Lamb was out wide, the Cowboys threw him hitches incessantly -- almost any time they saw off-coverage from the Texans' outside corners. This was a game in which the Cowboys' offensive coaching staff dared the Texans' defensive coaching staff to continue sticking to its characteristically simple defensive approach. Houston refused to blink, and the Cowboys took the free yardage again and again and again.

 Houston's defense was a vaunted group last season. This year, the Texans have had too many easy holes -- especially in end-of-game situations in which the ball is coming out faster than their pass rush can account for it. This Lamb performance is but an extreme example.

 
 

 1: How many 0-4 teams have made the playoffs since the start of the 1990 season 
 The Texans will drive to become the second. To be fair, the Chargers, Titans, Bucs and Dolphins are also trying do this. The Texans' attempt just feels a little more legitimate.

 Houston has lost three of four games by one score, and all three of those losses have had a score change within the final two minutes. In the Texans' 34-30 loss to the Cowboys, Houston had a win probability as high as 78.5% with two minutes left in the fourth quarter.

 

 It isn't just the close losses. In all four of their games so far, the Texans have had a better offensive success rate than their opponents -- yes, including the 14-point loss to the Bengals, in which they held the Joe Burrow -led offense to a 27.6% success rate, the worst number in a game of his career. The Texans' lack of balance is what kills them -- their running game was once again absent against the Cowboys, with 62 yards on 19 carries and a 23.5% success rate. Short-yardage snafus and clock management failures have been another issue. But this is a much, much better team than 0-4 would suggest.

 
 

 16: How many times Jalen Hurts was blitzed in Sunday's loss to the Rams 
 That's the most blitzes the Eagles quarterback has seen since the 2024 season. Hurts had minus-9.3 total expected points added on blitzed dropbacks in this game -- the worst such game of his career by a comfortable margin. He was pressured on nine of 16 blitzes and went 4-for-14 as a passer with one first down.

 The blitz was considered Hurts' Achilles' heel as a younger passer, and it was a heavily featured game plan for opponents in Philadelphia's postseason losses. It's easy to argue that he has put those concerns to bed and that this game -- without WR DeVonta Smith (hamstring), OT Lane Johnson (personal reasons), Saquon Barkley (left game, hamstring) and TE Dallas Goedert (knee) -- is an aberration, not a sign of regression. But it is worth noting that the Bears also blitzed Hurts at a high rate last week (43.3%), and Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula hit Hurts with a lot of blitzes last season (37.8%).

 
 

 This game, in which the Rams sent a blitz on 50% of Hurts' dropbacks, featured the single-highest blitz rate of a Shula-called game. The Rams were able to keep the running back in protection -- a big deal when Barkley is that potential pass catcher -- and overwhelm rookie right tackle  Markel Bell , who was making his first career start. But they also got Hurts to freeze in a couple of clean pockets and bail into a couple of unblocked pressures, which contributed to the Eagles' 0-for-12 day on third down. That's right, 0-for-12 .

 The Eagles (2-2) haven't picked up a third down in their past 17 attempts. This dropback passing game is a disaster.

 
 

 Plus-57: How many more plays the Bears had than the Jets 
 Want to see what a body-blows game looks like? A game in which the rushing attack just leans on the opponent until it crumbles under the sheer weight?

 Chicago ran 89 offensive plays while New York ran 32 -- astonishing. This was only the fourth game with that large of a play differential since the 1970 merger. The Bears had 34 first downs (which is more plays than the Jets had in total) to the Jets' seven, and that 27 first-down differential is the biggest spread in a game in Bears franchise history. It's only the second game in the Super Bowl era (since 1966) in which a team had more first downs than its opponent had plays. The Bears held the ball for 42 minutes, 45 seconds -- over 70% of the game clock -- for the largest time-of-possession spread the Bears have enjoyed in a game since 1994.

 

 

 That this game ended only 23-12 is a total miracle. The Bears' first drive ended on a failed fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line. The three field goals all came at the end of 11-play drives with kicks from the Jets' 3-yard line and twice from the 12. A lot of missed TD opportunities there. Chicago then ended the game on a fever dream: an 18-play, 76-yard, 9:16 clock eater featuring two interceptions by the Jets that were overturned for defensive penalties -- demoralizing stuff.

 The Bears are 2-0 without quarterback Caleb Williams . They've walked out with two dominant game plans and should have enjoyed a second lopsided scoreboard in this one. Ben Johnson for Coach of the Year?

 
 

 2: Number of interceptions thrown in the first two plays of Chargers-Seahawks 
 It's the first game since at least 1978 to start this way -- that's as far back as ESPN and the Elias Sports Bureau can go. The first offensive snap for the Chargers was Justin Herbert dropping back and blindly throwing into blanket coverage. Seahawks linebacker Drake Thomas leaped and snagged it out of the air.

 

 The first offensive snap for the Seahawks -- coming right after Thomas' interception -- featured Sam Darnold dropping back and blindly throwing a checkdown into a peeling Chargers defensive end. Tuli Tuipulotu accepted the gift gratefully.

 

 There's no important analysis here. It was just hilarious to watch.

title: NFL Week 4 uniforms: Browns wearing 'Alpha Dawg' look; Giants go 'Legacy'
summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 4, led by an alternate look from the Cleveland Browns.
full_text:
As the calendar turns to October, NFL uniforms remain as fresh as ever with an alternate-heavy slate in Week 4. 

 

 On "Thursday Night Football," the Cleveland Browns will wear their  "Alpha Dawg"  combination against the Pittsburgh Steelers . Cleveland revealed the all-brown threads in July 2025 with a brand new alternate brown helmet. They debuted last season and marked the first time in franchise history that a brown helmet was worn. Orange-colored numbers run across the front and back of the jersey, as well as on the shoulder. There's also an orange stripe on the helmet.

 In the throwback space, the New York Giants are donning their legacy uniforms against the Arizona Cardinals . New York wore these threads from 1980 to 1999. It was reintroduced in 2022, when the team brought back the navy helmet. Other design elements include classic numbers plus the red-and-blue trim on the jerseys and pants, similar to the uniforms of the 1980s and '90s. Written inside the collar is "Once a Giants, Always a Giant," the words of late owner Wellington Mara. 

 The Carolina Panthers , meanwhile, will bring an all-black look to "Sunday Night Football" against the Detroit Lions . Carolina first debuted this all-black combination in 2022. 

 The Dallas Cowboys are rocking navy blue alternates with silver pants against the Houston Texans , a look the team will wear only a handful of times each season. The Texans will wear liberty white jerseys with deep steel blue pants. It marks the same uniform matchup the Texans and Cowboys wore for Houston's first regular-season game as a franchise in 2002. 

 The New Orleans Saints and Atlanta Falcons on Monday will honor the 20th anniversary of the Saints' return to the Superdome following Hurricane Katrina by wearing the same uniform combinations they wore for the emotional and memorable "Monday Night Football" matchup on Sept. 25, 2006. The Saints will wear white jerseys and gold pants, and the Falcons will be in their red jerseys and white pants.
